According to their respective order, the results for those numbers from one to nine are the squares obtained by the rule "the product of two similar [quantities]," which are:
Thus, the definitions for these are given in the following aphorisms (sūtras):
And having squared the last term, one should multiply that same doubled last term by the remaining terms,
repeatedly removing them according to the rule for squaring.
Thus, by them, the number of squares for the figures ranging from one to nine must be stated.
Why? Because as long as the number of squares is unknown, it is impossible to set down the number of squares for the final term.
For us, however, everything is encompassed by the definition itself.
The square of one hundred is 6,250; that of one hundred increased by ten is 15,625.
The square of a difference is likewise the same.

However, having squared the numerator and denominator separately of two fractions that have been made similar, the square of the numerator divided by the square of the denominator is the square of the fraction.
The problem: [Find the squares] of six and one-fourth, and of one and one-fifth.
And tell me of the creation of my two forms, which are not inferior to the ninefold earth. // 2 //
The placement (nyāsa) is: 6, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 4, 5, 9.
According to the rule "the fractional part is multiplied by the denominator," the result is 25/4.
The squares of these two quantities—the denominators and the numerators—are 16 and [25] respectively.
625. Having divided the square of the numerator by the square of the denominator, the quotient is 39 1/16.
Likewise for the remaining two [fractions], in their respective order: 1 3/11, 46 25/81. //2//
[The Preparation of the Cube] To demonstrate the preparation of the cube, he states the second half of the verse:
"The cube is the product of three like quantities; likewise, it may be based on twelve. (3)
[The product of three similar quantities] is the multiplication of three similar quantities.
The multiplication of three similar quantities is called a cube (*ghana*).
Cube, mass (*vṛnda*), and the repeated multiplication of three similar quantities are synonyms.
And that [consciousness] is "supported by twelve" (dvādaśāśrita);
that which has twelve supports is this "supported by twelve," it would be so.
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he demonstrates that the cube is a regular tetrahedron (equal on all four sides).
This is not so;
for even without the word "likewise," the fact that this cube is a regular tetrahedron can indeed be understood.

Why? Because by the phrase "the product of three similar [sides]," it indicates that the height is indeed equal to the side of that square field, since the volume is the area of the field multiplied by the height.

Alternatively, the term "equilateral quadrilateral" (*samacaturaśra*), which was previously established in the rule "A *varga* is an equilateral quadrilateral," is carried over here; it refers to that whose sides are to be demonstrated by means of clay or some other material.
The problem statement (*uddeśaka*) is as follows:
Tell me the separate cubes of the numbers beginning with one and ending with nine;
also the cube of the eight-fold group of eight (64), and the square of a hundred and the square of a thousand.
The nyāsa is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9; the aṣṭāṣṭakavarga is 4096; the square of one hundred (100) is 390625.

Regarding the sequence beginning with one and ending with nine, the cubes are obtained according to their respective order by the rule "the cube is the product of three similar [factors]," namely: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, and 729.
Furthermore, for those who hold the defining rule that "the cube of the final term shall be... and so forth, the cubic values of the numbers starting from one must be stated.
Why? Because when the cube of a number is unknown, it is impossible to set down the cube of the final term;
for example, the cube of eight-eighths (64) is 68,719,476,736, and the cube of the square of one hundred (10,000) is 59,604,644,775,390,625.

The same applies even when the cube is broken down. The problem-setter says: "O you whose mind is clear in the calculation of cubes, tell me clearly the cubic number resulting from six, fifteen, and eight, each diminished by its own respective parts. (4)
The *nyāsa* (arrangement) is: 5, 4, 9, 7, 5, 4, 9, 7, 6, 5, 10, 8.
The resulting cubes, in their respective order, are: 198, 110, 970, 488, 107, 74, 299, 191, 216, 125, 1000, 512. [Square root]
Regarding the method for extracting the square root, he says:
One should always divide [the current number] by twice the square root from the previous square;
when a square is subtracted from a square, the quotient is the next digit of the root in its respective place. (4)
"Part," "division," "portion," and "reduction" are synonyms.
One should take—that is, grasp—that part.
From what position? He says: from the square root (avarga).
A square is not a non-square;
therefore, from that which is not a square.
In this calculation, an odd place is a square.

When that very uneven position has been negated by the negative particle (*nañ*), the even position remains as "non-group" (*avarga*); for it is from this [even position] that both the uneven and the even positions arise. He asks: "By what should one divide the portion? and answers: "Always by the square root, which is doubled."
That which has two qualities is "twofold" (*dviguṇa*).
What is that? It is the square root. By that twofold square root. How?
Furthermore, it is said that the square root of that is obtained: "When a square is subtracted from a square, the quotient is the root in another place.
This means: when a square is subtracted from an odd place—that is, from a square multiplied by a square.
Whatever is obtained here becomes known as the "root" (mūla) in another place.
"Another place" (sthānāntara) means a place other than the previous place; in that other place, that which was obtained receives the designation "root."
Furthermore, where no other location exists, the designation "root" applies to that very place itself.
Why? Because another location is impossible.
I shall repeat this very sūtra again and again until the calculation is completed.
Thus ends the introductory section.
"O friend, I wish to know the square roots of numbers beginning with one, of previously seen squares, and of the quantity consisting of the squares of six, five, three, and two. (1)
The sequence of squares is: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 625.
The square roots obtained individually, according to their respective order, are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 25.
Here is the problem statement for finding fractional roots:
Having calculated the square roots of six [units], four, thirteen, and nine hundred and forty-four, state them according to the number of soldiers. (2)
The assignment is: 6/13, 1/4, 4/9.
The operation is as follows: having multiplied the two denominators, one should add the numerator. This results in 25/121 and 4/9.
The square roots of these two fractions, consisting of numerators and denominators, are respectively 5/11 and 2/3.
The square root of the divisor-heap divided by the square root of the dividend-heap yields the square root of the fractional part as 2 1/2;
and the square root of the fractional part for thirteen and four-ninths is 3 2/3.
[Ghanamūla] He says this for the purpose of calculating the cube root:
"One should divide by the second [term], starting from the non-cube."
The square of the cube root of the cube [of the last digit] multiplied by three is to be subtracted from the first [digit]; and the cube [is to be subtracted] from the cube. (5)
It is neither dense nor non-dense; therefore, from that which is non-dense, one should divide it— that is, one should take a portion.
The meaning is that one should take a part.
Since there are many places for the cube (ghana), he says "up to the second";
in this calculation, the cube is one.

There are two negative terms (*aghana*). Why is this so? It is stated that "one negative term" and "two negative terms" [are used] because the establishment of the first negative term is by the rule: "The square, multiplied by three and the preceding number, is to be subtracted from the first negative term," and the establishment of the second negative term is by the rule: "One should divide by the second negative term."
The *ghana* (cube), however, is indeed singular, because a second one is not heard of.
He asks: "By what should one divide starting from the second non-cube? and answers: "By the triple."
By the square root of the cube;
"triguṇaḥ" means three times this.
What is it? It is the square of the cube root.
By that square root of the cube multiplied by three,
the square [of the number] preceded by three is to be subtracted from the first [term].
"Multiplied by three and the preceding number" means the square is multiplied by three and by the preceding quantity.
Of what is it the square?
It is the square of that which has been obtained; this is the completion of the sentence.
It is to be subtracted.
It should be purified;
it is to be connected with "from the first solid mass" (*aghanāt*),
and [the phrase] "solid from a solid" (*ghanaś ca ghanāt*) [is also to be supplied].
And the cube must be purified. Why? From the cube; that is, from the cubic place.
Therefore, the phrase "it becomes the cube root" (*ghanamūlam bhavati*) is to be supplied [as the conclusion].
Here,
having observed this very cubic quantity (*ghanarāśi*), one should calculate that "one is a cube and two are non-cubes," and from that which is the cube, one should first determine the cube root.
By the statement "the cube is to be subtracted from the cube," this entire Ārya-sūtra presents itself:
"One should divide by the second [term] minus the cube," and so forth.
The Instructor says:
Tell me separately the square roots of the cube numbers beginning with one;
let the cube root of eight hundred and sixty-four be calculated quickly. (1)
The cube roots obtained in their respective order are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12.

O Bhaṭa, according to the *Bhaṭaśāstra*, correctly state the square root of the number whose value is [calculated as] four, eight, seven, nine, six, four, zero, nine, two, eight, and seven. (2)
The divisor is 8,291,469,824. The resulting cube root is 2,024.

[The Area of a Triangle] Now, for the purpose of calculating the area of a triangle, he says:
The body of the area of a triangle is the product of half the base and the perpendicular bisector.
That field which has three sides (bhujas) is this triangle;
"bhujā," "bāhu," and "pārśva" are synonyms.
Among these, there are three types of fields: equilateral, isosceles, and scalene.
Regarding the phrase "of a triangle," the singular number is used by accepting the genus (jāti) of triangular figures;
[it refers to] that triangle's "body of the result" (phalaśarīra).
The "body of the result" (phalaśarīra) means the magnitude of the result;
it is the product of half the base and half the hypotenuse.
"Equal-petal-peak," *avalambakaḥ*.
Regarding this, some say: "That which has equal petals is *samadalā*."
They describe it as "an equal petal and a tip" (samadalakoṭī). For them,
the accomplishment of the result occurs only in fields that are equal squares or equal triangles, not in fields that are unequal triangles.

Furthermore, for us who speak [of the area] as "half a square with equal sides" (*samadalakoṭī*) by way of etymological derivation (*avalambakavyutpatti*), the calculation of the area for all three [types of triangles] is established.
Alternatively, even for those who perform the etymological derivation, the calculation of the area for these three triangular fields is indeed established.
Why? Because it is said: "In conventional terms, the function of etymological derivation is for the sake of the ritual act, not for the sake of functional utility."
"Bhujārdha" means half of a *bhujā*. Now,

since the word *bhujā* here could generally be understood as referring to any of the three sides— namely, the arm (*bāhu*), the side (*pārśva*) [of a triangle], or the side [of a quadrilateral]— only a specific *bhujā* is intended to be grasped.
It is designated as *bhujā*.

Regarding the principle that "general injunctions are restricted to specific instances," here in the context of mathematics (*gaṇita*), the word *bhujā* is to be understood as derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes.

Otherwise, since the word *bhuja* is prescribed by rule [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.61] as meaning "hand" (*pāṇi*)— specifically in the sense of "tormenting the hand"— it would not apply to the side of a field. *Bhujārdha* means half of that *bhuja*.
The product of half the base and half the perpendicular is the product of half the base and half the altitude;
this constitutes the body of the area of a triangle. The problem [is as follows]:

O friend, the area of five equilateral triangles whose sides are equal to seven, eight, and nine units respectively, is equal to the area of six equilateral triangles whose sides are equal to two units.
Nyāsa, ā,
and parilekha—

The fruit is also by that same means.

One should multiply the depth (*ogāha*) and the width (*vikkhambha*) by one;

One should multiply the immersion by the width. The square root of that product multiplied by four is the chord (*jīvā*) for all fields.
This is also the method for laying out bow-shaped fields.

This is the side (bhuja), the radius (vyāsārdha) is the hypotenuse (karṇa), and the square root of the difference between the squares of the side and the hypotenuse is the perpendicular (koṭi).
That very [perpendicular] is the sine (jyā) of seventeen degrees, and it is 3084.
Because of its inequality, the chord (jyā) is therefore not produced.
Thus, the chords of the eighth parts of the signs have been explained from the triangle.
Now we shall explain them from the quadrilateral.

The sides of an internal square field are equal to half the diameter; the square root of the sum of their squares is the diagonal. That same diagonal is the full sine of twenty-four degrees, and it is 4862.
Half of these twelve *kāṣṭhās* is the chord (*jyā*), which is 2431; one should subtract this from the radius (*vyāsārdha*). The remainder is the arrow (*śara*) of the twelve *kāṣṭhās*.
The square root of the sum of the squares of twelve and eight is the hypotenuse;
that itself is the full sine (pūrṇajyā) of twelve degrees, and it is 2630. Half of this is the sine of six degrees, and it is 1315.
This is the side (bhuja), the radius (vyāsārdha) is the hypotenuse (karṇa), and the square root of the difference between the squares of the side and the hypotenuse is the perpendicular (koṭi).
That is the sine (jyā) of eighteen degrees, and it is 3177.
One should subtract this from the semi-diameter;
the remainder is the *śara* (arrow) of the six *kāṣṭhās*.
The square root of the sum of the squares of the *śara* and the sine of the six *kāṣṭhās* is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).
That same value is the full chord (*jyā*) for six *kāṣṭhās*, and it is 1342.
Half of this is the chord for three *kāṣṭhās*, and it is 671.
This is the side (*bhuja*), and the radius (*vyāsārdha*) is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).
The square root of the difference between the squares of the base and the hypotenuse is the perpendicular;
that itself is the sine of twenty-one degrees, and it is 3372.
Because it is an odd number, a sine [in this context] is not produced.
Then, one should subtract the string of six units from the semi-diameter;
the remainder is the arrow of eighteen units.
The square root of the sum of the squares of that arrow and the string of eighteen units is the hypotenuse.
That same value is the full chord (*jyā*) of eighteen *kāṣṭhās*, and it is 3820.
Half of this is the chord of nine *kāṣṭhās*, and it is 1910.
This is the side (*bhuja*), and the radius is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).
The square root of the difference between the squares of the base and the hypotenuse is the perpendicular;
that itself is the sine (jyā) of fifteen degrees, and it is 2859.
Because it is an odd number, the sine is not produced [from the standard series].
Thus, there are twenty-four chord-sines (jyā) for the eighth parts of the zodiacal signs.
By this very method, as many half-chords as desired should be produced within half the diameter. // 11 //
[The broken sine (khaṇḍajyā) by another method: He speaks for the purpose of demonstrating the division of the sine:
"That by which the second half is diminished—that is, cut away—from the first half of the arc-sine."
The remaining [sines] are diminished by those respective portions of the first half-sine. // 12 //
From the first, that is, from the initial half-chord;
by how many degrees it is deficient—that is, by how many degrees it falls short and has not yet attained similarity—what is that? It is the second half-segment which is divided.
The "broken" [portion] is the second half-chord (jyārdha) of the arc, severed according to the method for cutting described by the previous masters;
it is taken up by as many parts of the first half-chord as there are by which the second half-chord is less than the first half-chord of the arc.
The half of the larger [chord] is the "half-chord" (jyārdha);
that which is both first and a half-chord is the "first half-chord" (prathamajyārdha);
alternatively, that which is both first and a chord is the "first chord" (prathamajyā).
The first sine and that [value] together constitute the "first sine-half";
a portion of the first sine-half is the "first sine-half-part."
The "portion of the first half-chord" means having divided the first half-chord by itself, the result is, for example, a fifth part or a sixth part;
these are the portions of the first half-chord, and thus [the compound] *tat-prathamajyārdhāṃśaiḥ*.
The inclusion of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) in the phrase "by those respective portions" is purposeful.
The remaining [terms] are subtracted;
"subtracted" means deprived of,
and the remaining [terms] are the sines of the third and subsequent [angles].
For example: first, this half-chord of the arc produced by means of the *chedyaka* is 225;
second, the reduction of the half-chord of the arc is 224;
this is less than the first half-chord of the arc by one.
The half-portion of the second bow-sine and the first bow-sine are added together, resulting in 449.
When this is divided by the first bow-sine, the quotient is two and a half units.
Subtracting one from that and from the previous [value], the first bow-sine becomes the third sine.
And that [is] the conjunction of the three (222); 671;
the quotient obtained by dividing this by half the chord of the first arc, increased by one-half.
There are three forms.
By subtracting those previously obtained three from the first bow-sine (cāpajyā), one obtains the fourth sine.
And that is 219.
The sum of four half-chords is 890.
Dividing this by the first half-chord, the quotient is four with a remainder of one-half.
Subtracting these from the previous six [units], the first half-chord of the arc becomes the fifth half-chord.
And that [is stated in verse 215]:
"By these, the remaining [verses] are explained.
And this explanation has been commented upon by the teacher Prabhākara.
And that is improper; it is useless to provide an explanation without first refuting [the objection].
How is it useless?

Here, in this treatise on calculation (gaṇita-śāstra), another aphorism (sūtra) is commenced either for the purpose of demonstrating a concise method or for the purpose of demonstrating an alternative method.
In this case, even a trace of another method is not present.
How so? This operation is performed using the first and second half-chords of the bow, which have been determined by the previously mentioned rule for cutting;
because that operation extends across two strings, there is no simplicity [of calculation].
And it is not a different means because it relies upon the preceding sutra;
for this reason, there is no distinct purpose served by this sutra.
But how, then, are these strings known individually?
This is the speech of one who is extremely foolish,
because they arise simultaneously with that [bow].
The half-chords for two units, three units, four units, and so forth have been established;
that the individual chords arise from the mutual differences between them is known even by one unskilled in calculation, let alone by an astrologer.
And so, for the sake of understanding by those of dull intellect, it is set forth as follows: 225, 449, 671, 890, 1105, 1315, 1520, 1719, 1910, 2093, 2267, 2431, 2585, 2728.

These are the successive individual sines (jyās), excluding each preceding one from the next, in ascending order: 225, 224, 222, 219, 215, 210, 205, 199, 191, 183, 174, 164, 154, 143, 131, 119, 106, 93.
These same values, starting from the last and proceeding in reverse order, are the sines in descending order (utkramajyās). // 12 //
[The determination of areas and so forth: He states the following for the purpose of demonstrating merely the direction of how the determination of areas and so forth is accomplished:
"An area, whether triangular or quadrilateral, is to be determined by means of rotation and by means of the diagonals."
The ground should be made level with water; below and above, it should be [adjusted] by means of a plumb line alone. // 13 //
A circular field is accomplished by means of rotation;
by the word "rotation," the compass (karkaṭaka) is intended.
By that compass, the perfectly circular field is measured according to the dimensions of the drawing.

Both the triangle and the quadrilateral are established by means of the diagonals. First, the triangle: having stretched a cord upon level ground, one should draw a line; and that [line]—ā ā ā ā ā ā ā ā ā ā ā ā ā ā ā ā.
Parilekha 30: Here, one should produce a fish by means of a compass (karkaṭaka) positioned at both ends;
the other thread emerging from its mouth and tail is the suspensor (avalambaka).
Parilekha 31: Having placed one end of this thread at the front and the second end fixed upon the ground's surface, one should draw a line;
one should do exactly the same for the second end as well.
Thus are the ear-lines;
the triangle adorned by those two ear-lines is the diagram (parilekha). 32.
In a quadrilateral, one should extend a cord transversely equal to the desired diagonal of the quadrilateral; that cord is the drawing-line (parilekha). 33.
And this second [line], the svastika produced in the middle, is extended only transversely; likewise, there is a secondary line on the ear-line (karṇasūtra). 34.
The sides of these two have been filled, and a square field has been produced. Diagram 35.
Level ground is prepared with water;
level ground is accomplished by means of water.
For example: on ground leveled with a plumb-line, one should place a water-pot upon three pieces of wood in a windless place and make a hole at the bottom.
Just as that water flows in a single stream, so too,
wherever that flowing water spreads out and moves in a circle on all sides, that ground is level; and wherever that water, having broken its circular flow, comes to rest, that is low ground.
That which does not submerge is "elevated.
By means of the plumb line itself,
that which is the upper portion of what is observed below is [the elevated].
It is established by the suspender alone;
or rather, that which is the lower region of the upper region is also [established] by the suspender alone. And the suspender is a thread attached to a single point of a heavy substance. // 13 //
[The square root of half the diameter of its own circle:
To determine half the diameter of its own circle, he says: "Having added the square of the measure of the gnomon to the square of the shadow..."
The square root of that is the radius of its own circle.
[The Analysis of the Shape and Dimensions of the Gnomon] Regarding this,
the astrologers disagree concerning the shape and dimensions of the gnomon.
Some say that the twelve-finger gnomon is square at one-third of its base.
"In its middle third it is triangular, and in its upper third it has the shape of a trident.

This is not correct, because the body [of the shadow] is so subtle that while the tip of the shadow might be easily observed by a single fine edge, it is difficult to achieve with the remaining parts.
Because there is no provision for a support at the tip of the trident, straightness itself is difficult to achieve;
and in its absence, all other qualities are absent.
As for the one with a rounded belly shaped like a cow's tail, it is rejected precisely because its support has fallen away.

Others say: "Since it is possible to achieve the means of suspension [of the gnomon] in all four directions, and since the tip of the shadow is captured by two extremities, the determination of the directions is established at the desired extremity.
This too is logical;

however, because such an artisan capable of producing a perfectly square field is nowadays difficult to find—even if some person well-practiced in the science might occasionally exist—[it remains impractical].
Nevertheless, because the gnomon must be repositioned toward the sun every moment, the tip of the gnomon would have to be moved again and again;
thus, for one with extremely keen vision, the desired shadow would be exceeded by that much— this is the fault, and for this reason, this gnomon too must be abandoned.
By this very [method], objections have been raised everywhere. Those belonging to the Āryabhaṭīya school, desiring to establish their own view, describe it as follows:

"Indeed, [the gnomon] should be made of excellent wood, non-hollow, free from lines, knots, and blemishes, perfected by turning on a lathe, with equal circularity throughout its base, middle, and tip, neither too narrow in width nor too short in length."
And this is highly recommended.

Its upright position must be established by means of three or four plumb lines; since the central line of the gnomon is not yet established, the stability of the plumb lines is also difficult to achieve. Therefore, the method for establishing the central line of the gnomon is now demonstrated.

For example: having placed a peg firmly in a high place and having determined the distance between the base and the top of the peg by means of a plumb line, one should stretch a thread attached to its tip and draw lines on both sides;
these are the middle lines for both sides.
Then again, having produced a fish by means of an iron pin and the two threads [passing through] the root, the tip, and the middle, one establishes the remaining central lines.
But surely there is still a defect here as well;
because its head and the tip of the shadow are large circles in all directions, the center of the shadow is difficult to discern.
And because of that, there would be an absence of the inclusion of the term "etcetera" (*ādi*).
This is not a fault;
for above the gnomon (*śaṅku*), at the center, [there are] those exceeding half the radius (*viṣkambhārdha*).
A straight stick, made of metal or wood, is used as a central aligner;
in that case, there will be both the grasping of the beginning and the full knowledge of the middle.
Alternatively, for one who is wise, the knowledge of the middle is achieved by slightly lifting the previously placed suspension-string itself.
Then, by means of a sharp instrument, it was slightly split according to the division of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
otherwise, the mention of its measurement would be purposeless.
Therefore, having accepted the well-known fact that the gnomon (*śaṅku*) may be of any desired measurement—such as twelve finger-breadths—it is stated [as follows].
We shall explain this in the introductory sections (*uddeśaka*).
To the extent that this [body] becomes broad and heavy, to that same extent it is not moved by the wind at all.

To the extent that it becomes longer, to that same extent the minute parts of the finger-breadths become well-known; therefore, care must be taken regarding those that are broad, heavy, and long—thus has been stated the form of the *śaṅku*. [The Analysis of the Measure of the *Śaṅku*]
Now we shall explain the measurement.
Some say that half a cubit consists of a body divided into twelve parts;
however, this is not a fixed rule.
However, "having a body divided according to the desired number" means being divided according to the desired number.
Wherever the measurement is taken, there too one must practice skill in the division of equal finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and the division of the center (*kendra*).
[Commentary on the Verse]:
"The square of the measure of the gnomon"—
it has been stated that the mention of the measure of the gnomon, which is thus expanded in detail, is for the purpose of demonstrating a variable measure.
If the measure of the gnomon were indeed fixed, then even by saying "the square of the gnomon," its fixed measure would be understood.
"The square of the measure" means the square of that which is the measure;
[one should take] that square of the measure.
By the square of the shadow;
"chāyāvarga" means the square of the shadow (chāyāyāḥ vargaḥ),
by that [is meant] "by the square of the shadow."
"Having combined," means having unified;
that which is its square root.
The square root of that combined mass is the radius of its own circle.
What is that circle of which this is called the semi-diameter?
It is the semi-diameter of a circle drawn with a compass whose radius is equal to its own root.
If this is so, then every specific number becomes the semi-diameter of its own circle.
This is not a fault;
if every specific number of counts constitutes its own circumference and radius, what of ours is lost?

Furthermore, in this case, only the specific square root of the sum of the squares of the gnomon's measure and its shadow is taken as the radius of its own circle; therefore, the taking of any other radius for its own circle does not at all follow here.
And when a fault has arisen, its remedy is prescribed.

Here, the taking of half the diameter of its own circle is for the purpose of establishing the rule of three proportions (*trairāśika*): "If these gnomon-shadows correspond to this half-diameter of its own circle, then what are the gnomon-shadows corresponding to the half-diameter of the sphere?"—thus the gnomon-shadows are obtained.
These two are called the *avalambaka* and the *akṣajyā* at the equinox (*viṣuvat*).
The problem statement (*uddeśaka*) is as follows:
"A shadow of five, nine, and four and a half was observed on level ground."
At the equinox, on the central thread, [one should place] a gnomon divided into twelve parts. // 1 //
The placement: gnomon 12, shadow 5; gnomon 12, shadow 9; gnomon 12, shadow 3 1/2.
The operation consists of squaring the gnomon and the shadow: 144 and 25, which sum to 169.
The square root of this is the radius of its own circle;
and that is 13.

The laying out of this field is as follows: the diagram (parilekha) 36 consists of a line called "half the diameter of its own circle," which starts from the tip of the shadow and reaches the top of the gnomon.

Following that sūtra, one fixes the gaze on the ground and observes the sun as it rests upon the top of the gnomon. In calculating the sine of latitude (*akṣajyā*), the arrangement for the rule of three is as follows: 13/5/3438; the resulting sine of latitude is 1322.
This is the side (bhuja); the radius (vyāsārdha) is the hypotenuse (karṇa).
The square root of the difference between the squares of the side and the hypotenuse is the perpendicular (avalambaka), which is 3174.
By means of the rule of three (trairāśika) as well: 13 / 12 / 2328.
The quotient obtained is 3174.
There are also other specific fields here.
Regarding the rule of three, the logic of the statement is: if for this...

When the shadow is equal to the base (bhuja) and the gnomon (śaṅku) is equal to the perpendicular (avalambaka) of half the diameter of its own circle, then what are the base and the perpendiculars for half the diameter of this [celestial] sphere? This same method applies for calculating the time in ghaṭikās from the shadow, and for calculating the position of the sun at midday from the shadow, using half the diameter of its own circle.

However, since the determination of time by means of a shadow requires a gnomon, it is the gnomon itself that is brought forth. When determining the sun by means of the shadow on the equatorial plane, that same [gnomon] is used.
When determining the sun by means of the midday shadow, there is a need for the sine of the meridian zenith distance (natajyā); thus, it is the shadow itself that is brought forth.

For the remaining two [latitudes] as well, the sines of the obliquity (akṣajyā) and the secants (avalambaka) are found by means of the rule of three (trairāśika), using their own respective circumferences and semi-diameters (15/12 and 1 2/3): 2063, 2750; and 963, 3300.
The problem statement (uddeśaka) is as follows:

When the shadow of a fifteen-aṅgula gnomon is six aṅgulas plus one quarter (1.5 aṅgulas), this occurs at midday on the equinoctial day; here, the latitude-sine (akṣajyā) and the sines of altitude (avalambaka) are to be stated. // 2 //
The placement is as follows: the gnomon (śaṅku) is 15 units, and the shadow (chāyā) is 6¼ units. The resulting semi-diameter of its own circle (svavṛttaviṣkambhārdha) is 16¼ units.
By means of this semi-diameter of its own circle, the resulting sines of latitude (akṣajyā) and the sines of colatitude (alambaka) are 1322 and 3174 units, respectively.
The Instructor:
When sixteen finger-breadths of shadow are observed from a gnomon measuring thirty [aṅgulas], one must state how much of the day has passed from midday for the sun with its spread rays. (3)
The gnomon (śaṅku) is 30 and the shadow (chāyā) is 16. The resulting half-diameter of its own circle is 34. The obtained sine of latitude (akṣajyā) is 16;18. // 14 //
[The operation concerning the shadow of a lamp] states the rule for the shadow of a lamp:
the product of the gnomon and the multiplier, divided by the difference between the gnomon and the base, [is the result].
That which is obtained is to be known as the shadow of the gnomon from its own base. 15.
That which has the peg as its multiplier is "multiplied by the peg" (śaṅkuguṇam).
To the question "What is that?", he says: "the difference between the peg and the arm. By the word "arm" (bhujā), the height of the lamp is expressed.

The interval between the height of the lamp and the gnomon is the difference between the gnomon and the arm; that [interval] multiplied by the gnomon and divided by the difference between the gnomon and the arm—
where the "difference between the gnomon and the lamp's height" refers to the same difference as that between the gnomon and the arm.
The quotient obtained is the shadow of that very gnomon;
that shadow is found from the base of that same gnomon. The problem (uddeśaka) is as follows:

Tell me the shadow of a gnomon that stands at eighty [aṅgulas] from the base of a lamp-post seventy-two [aṅgulas] high, when the gnomon itself is thirty [aṅgulas] long and positioned twenty [aṅgulas] away. // 1 //
The placement (nyāsa):
the drawing (parilekha) is 37; the distance between the gnomon and its shadow (śaṅkubhujāvivara) is 80.
This is the product of the gnomon, 960; the base is 72, the gnomon is 12,
and the difference between these two is 60.
The product of the gnomon multiplied by this [quotient] is subtracted from the difference between the gnomon and its shadow;
the resulting quotient is the shadow, 16. The second problem statement is as follows:
Parilekha 38: The shadow obtained by the preliminary calculation is 13;5,3.
This operation is a rule of three (trairāśika).

How so? If the measure of the space between the gnomon and the shadow—where the shadow is greater than the gnomon—is obtained as the shadow, then what shadow is obtained by means of the gnomon? By means of inverse calculation, the problem is stated:
the shadow of a lamp seventy-two units high is seen to be sixteen units.
By how much [of its height] should the base of a twelve-finger gnomon be stated by you? // 2 //
The placement (nyāsa) is as follows: the drawing (parilekha) 39;
the calculation (karaṇa): by this [distance] of 60 between the gnomon and the arm, the shadow is obtained.
Therefore, according to the rule "they become divisors and multipliers" (Gaṇita-sāra-saṃgraha 28), the shadow 16,
when multiplied, results in 960.

In this very case, since the gnomon (*śaṅku*) was the multiplier (*guṇakāra*) in the expression "the difference between the gnomon and the base" (*śaṅkubhujāvivara*), according to the rule "the multiplier becomes the divisor" [Gaṇita-sāra-saṃgraha 28], the difference between the gnomon and the base is divided by the gnomon (12). The result is 80.
The problem statement is as follows:
A gnomon is situated at the base of a lamp-post at a distance of fifty cubits; its shadow forms a row. One must state: how large is that lamp? (3)
The assignment (nyāsa) is as follows:
the diagram (parilekha) is number 40.
The calculation (karaṇa) is: “The side (koṭī) multiplied by the gnomon (śaṅku) and divided by the shadow (chāyā) becomes the base (bhuja). [Gaṇita]
Thus, by means of the calculation to be described, the shadow-koṭi (the perpendicular side of the shadow) becomes equal to the sum of the gnomon-arm-difference and the shadow. Here,
the gnomon-arm-difference is 50 and the shadow is 10.
In one case, [the value] is 60; this multiplied by the gnomon (śaṅku) is 720;
divided by the shadow (chāyā), the measure of the base (bhuja) is 72.
[Knowledge of the height of a lamp and its distance by means of two gnomon-shadows:

He states the calculation for determining the unknown height and distance of a lamp by means of two gnomon-shadows: "The difference between the tips of the shadows multiplied by a shadow, divided by the shorter one, is the *koṭi* (the vertical side)."
The hypotenuse multiplied by the sine and divided by the shadow becomes the base. // 13 //
"Multiplied by the shadow" means multiplied by the shadow.
What is multiplied by the shadow? The difference between the tips of the shadows.
The "interval between the tips of the shadows" (*chāyāgravivara*) means the ground situated between the two shadow-tips;
for example, after moving some distance away from a lamp and a measuring-stick of unknown height, a gnomon (*śaṅku*) is placed there.
Its shadow is indeed known.

At a measured distance from the tip of that shadow, there is a second gnomon; the interval between the tip of that shadow and the tip of the shadow of the first gnomon is the "interval between the shadow-tips" (chāyāgravivara).
That [product] is multiplied by the desired first shadow or the second shadow,
and then divided by the difference between the two shadows.
The difference is divided by that [difference];
the result is the "end-limit" (koṭi).
If that is multiplied by the first shadow, then it becomes the distance between the tip of the first shadow and the lamp.
If, by the second shadow, the interval between the tip of that [shadow] and the lamp-pole is the side multiplied by the gnomon— that is,
this side is "gnomon-multiplied" (śaṅkuguṇā), having the gnomon as its multiplier— then [the following applies].
The shadow divided by the base is the arm; the arm is the height of the lamp on its stand.
Both shadows are also established by means of their respective extremities.
The problem:

When the shadows of two gnomons of equal height are seen to be ten and sixteen finger-breadths respectively, and the distance between their tips is observed to be thirty, it is to be stated that the hypotenuse is sixty. (1)
The placement (nyāsa) is as follows:
the drawing (parilekha) is 41; the calculation (karaṇa) is the difference between the shadow-tip and the [reference point], which is 30.
This [number] multiplied by the first shadow is 300; the difference between the two shadows is 6, and by this [division], the result is the hypotenuse (koṭī) 50.
This same hypotenuse (koṭī), multiplied by the sine (śaṅku) of 6, becomes 600; divided by the shadow (chāyā), it is the base (bhuja), 60.
From the second shadow as well, the hypotenuse is 80.
The arm [of the shadow] is that same [value], 60. The problem statement:
It is recorded that the shadows of two men of equal height are five and seven respectively.
When eight is seen as the interval between the extremes, let the base and the perpendicular then be stated. // 2 //
The assignment (nyāsa) is as follows: the diagram (parilekha) is as before; the obtained hypotenuse (koṭi) is 20, and the base (bhuja) is 48.

From the second shadow, the hypotenuse is 28 koṭis and the base (bhuja) is the same, 48. On the day of the equinox, when the sun is situated at the center of the vault of the sky, some determine the yojanas of the interval between the sun and the earth's surface by means of the difference in shadows and the gnomon (śaṅku), measured in yojanas from the interval between the tips of the shadows in equal eastern and western locations.
That is incorrect;
here, even the introduction of the discourse on the two shadows and the movement of a lamp is not tenable.
Why? Because it says: "One should divide the opening of the earth-cavity" [Gola, 39].
The earth is the gnomon; the radius of the sun in yojanas is the distance between the base of the gnomon and its shadow-tip;
and the Blessed Sun himself, the sole lamp of the entire world, is the height of the lamp. Therefore:
It is not possible to calculate the distance in *yojanas* between the sun and the surface of the earth,
because the Siddhas themselves have taught that [the distance] is in terms of *bhūrasivivara-yojanas*.
If it is argued that the sun itself is the height of the lamp and thus the measurement of the sun's diameter is brought forward [as the distance], that too is not the case.

Since he is perceived as illuminating the worlds while seated in the midst of the firmament, joined at a distance of one *yojana* from the earth's horizon and his own zenith, therefore the Sun himself cannot be the height of a lamp.
Now, if the Sun were the height of a lamp, [the following would occur].

The distance between the sun and the earth constitutes the opening of the gnomon, which has a width equal to the entire circumference of the terrestrial sphere; likewise, it is not tenable because there is no standing place for a second such gnomon.
Therefore, it has been well said: "Even the introduction of the operation of the two shadows of a lamp is not possible."
And this earth is taught to be spherical;
therefore, for us who dwell upon its surface, because of its curvature, the calculation of the hypotenuse, the gnomon-shadow, the base, and the perpendicular does not apply here to the circumference.
For it is only on a region made level by water that the configuration of the triangle consisting of the base, the perpendicular, and the hypotenuse exists through the gnomon-shadow.
Furthermore, it is not possible to level this much ground.
Now, if this is cited as a concession: at the equinox in Ujjayinī, when the sun is on the meridian, the shadow is five finger-breadths long;
from that, the latitude is calculated as twenty-two degrees and thirty-seven seconds.
By this latitude, the yojanas between Laṅkā and Ujjayinī are obtained as 207, which is seven times the number of sky (zero) and Yamas (four).
Then, to the north of Ujjayinī, at the very equinox, the midday shadow at Sthāneśvara is seven finger-breadths;
by that, the latitude is obtained as thirty and one-quarter degrees.
By this multiplier, the number of yojanas between the palaces of the lords residing in Laṅkā is obtained as 275, which is the count of arrows (5), mountains (7), and Yamas (12).

Herein, the specific difference between these yojanas is sixty-eight; this is the sixty-eight [difference] increased by two, due to the interval between the two shadows at the gap between the two gnomons.
The difference between the shadow and its tip is seventy.
Here, by the initial operation in the calculation— "the difference between the shadow and its tip multiplied by the shadow"— one obtains *koṭi* yojanas.
And by those being led by a second shadow, they must indeed be situated at a distance of one *yojana* from the palace of the Lord of Laṅkā;
for at that time, the region situated below the sun is Laṅkā.
Whether it be the arm [of the shadow] of the sun, or whatever the height of the sun may be—

Therefore, because the number of yojanas between the peak and the location of the lord of Laṅkā is not established, mathematical calculation does not apply here either. Furthermore, the side (bhuja) that is to be calculated by means of a hypotenuse (koṭi) is itself not yet established; thus, it is illogical to calculate an established side by means of that unestablished hypotenuse. This is another [point].

Furthermore, the claim that "the shadow of a twelve-finger staff, which has been directly perceived by us, is used to perform calculations in *yojanas* by means of that measurement in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)," is not tenable.

Moreover, even if it were said that the shadow of a staff measuring twelve *yojanas* is five *yojanas* or seven *yojanas*, it would be impossible to know the upright position of such a staff by means of its verticality, nor could its raising or setting down be known.
And since the shadow is calculated on level ground, one cannot perceive the irregularities such as depressions, elevations, and rivers over those many *yojanas*; therefore,
the height and diameter of the thousand-rayed sun are established solely through traditional scripture (*āgama*).
Therefore, this snare of the methods of calculation should not be spread here. // 16 //
[The relationship between the sides and the hypotenuse:
To find the hypotenuse, he says:
"The square of the base and the square of the perpendicular are indeed the square of the hypotenuse."
The square of the base and the square of the perpendicular—these two squares combined constitute the square of the hypotenuse.
The problem: [Find the hypotenuse] of those two whose bases and perpendiculars are three and four, and six and eight respectively.
And the ears should be specified in sequence for the groups of twelve and nine. // 1 //
The assignment (nyāsa) is as follows: the diagram (parilekha) 43; the calculation (karaṇa): these are the base (bhuja) and the perpendicular (koṭi), namely 3.
The squares of these two are 9 and 16;
the square of the hypotenuse in one case is 25, and its square root is the hypotenuse, 5.
In this manner, the diagonal (karṇa) is to be applied in a field of one and a half square units or in a rectangular field;
thus, the diagonals for the remaining two fields are obtained as 10 and 15.
[The relationship between the arrow and the half-chord in a circle] To find the chord that penetrates a circular area, he states the second half of the Āryā verse:
"In a circle, the product of two arrows is indeed the square of the half-chord of the two arcs. (17)
In a circle,
the product of the two arrows (śara) is the "arrow-product" (śarasaṃvarga); that becomes the square of the half-chord (ardhajyā).
Indeed, that is the square of the half-chord of those two bows.
The problem (uddeśaka) is as follows:
In a field with a diagonal of ten, two arrows numbering eight were observed by me;
in that very same [field], those measuring nine and one are to be stated respectively as the half-chords. (1)
The assignment (nyāsa) is as follows: drawing (parilekha) 44;
the calculation (karaṇa) is these two arrows: 2 and 8.
The product of these two is the square of the half-chord, which is 16.
Its square root is 4; this is the half-chord.
In the second section as well, the obtained half-chord is 3.
In this very context, they describe the examples of the hawk and the mouse:
namely, the half-chord is the base (bhuja),
and the distance from the center of the circle to the end of the half-chord is the perpendicular (koṭi).
The square root of the sum of those squares is the hypotenuse, which is half the diameter of the circle.
This is now demonstrated:
the arrangement [is as follows].
Diagram 45: This half-chord is the height of the hawk's position;
the interval between the half-chord and the circumference is the ground for the mouse's movement.
Half the diameter is the chord, which is the path of the hawk;
the center of the circle is the place for killing the mouse.
Therein, the height of the hawk’s position is the half-chord (ardhajyā), and its square is as follows:
The ground traversed by the mouse is the arrow (*śara*); by that, it is divided, and the quotient is the second arrow.
Having applied the rule "subtracting the product of the interval" [Śloka 24], the quotient obtained is the ground reached by the mouse's dwelling and the measure of the ear of the hawk's flight.
That which is the second great arrow is itself situated at the point where the bamboo is broken, in the form of a triangular field with three and a half sides;
and that has been demonstrated.
Thus has the calculation been taught as a mere illustration.
[The problem: A hawk is perched atop a wall twelve cubits high.
There, a mouse was seen emerging twenty-four cubits from the base of the wall; and by that mouse, a hawk was also seen.
Thereupon, out of fear of it, the mouse fled very swiftly toward its own dwelling situated within the wall, but on the way, it was killed by the hawk, which pursued it as fast as the wind.
In this regard, we wish to know: how much distance was covered by the mouse, or how much was traversed by the hawk? (2)
The assignment (nyāsa) is as follows:
the drawing (parilekha) is 46; the calculation (karaṇa), namely the square of the height of the hawk (śyenocchrāyavarga), is 144.

Dividing this by the measure of the ground traversed by the mouse (24), one obtains 6; by this interval, the ground traversed by the mouse is added to 30, resulting in 18. Half of these two values are, respectively, the hawk’s flight distance and the distance between the mouse’s dwelling and the point of interception: 15 and 9.
The summary: A hawk perched upon a pillar eighteen cubits high saw a mouse that had emerged from its dwelling;
out of fear, the mouse took refuge at eighty-one cubits' distance.
Then, as he proceeds along the path, having been struck down by the cruel one— the view of the ālayavijñāna—
one should state how much distance he covers before reaching the hole, or whether his gait is like that of a hawk.
The assignment (nyāsa): [as follows]—the diagram (parilekha) 47; the quotient (labdha) from the mouse (ākhu) is the traversed ground (āgatabhūmi) 8 1 2.
The flight of the hawk (śyenagati) [is described] as 42, 1, 2.
In this very manner, the instruction on the breaking of the bamboo (vaṃśabhaṅga) is as follows: a bamboo eighteen units high was felled from its base by the wind.
Having gone six steps, he fell; having formed a triangle, where would it be broken? // 4 //
The placement:
the beam is 15 [units]; the distance from the base is the hypotenuse (apasāra), its measure being 6, which is the half-chord;
its square is 36.
Dividing this by the measure of the bamboo, 18, the quotient obtained is 2.
As before, according to the rule "added to the interval, subtracted from the whole, and halved" [Gaṇitakaumudī 24], the two segments of the bamboo are 10 and 8. The diagram is as follows:
The Instructor: A bamboo sixteen cubits long was felled by the wind from its own root;
having traveled eight [cubits], it fell. At what point did it break? This must be stated regarding the son of Marut. (5)
The assignment:
49. A drawing: having obtained two bamboo segments measuring 10 and 6 [units].
In the case of lotus-designations, the measure of the visible lotus is one arrow (*śara*).
The point of immersion of the lotus is the half-chord (*ardhajyā*).

Here, as before, when the square of the half-chord is divided by the arrow, the great arrow (*mahāśara*) is obtained; from that, by means of the transition to the visible lotus, the measure of the water and the measure of the lotus are determined.
The instructor says:

A lotus, visible above the water, fully blossomed, eight finger-breadths in size, and brought [there] by a windless breeze, sinks quickly when placed in the hand; this is to be declared regarding the lotus and the water. (6)
The placement (nyāsa) and the drawing (parilekha): 50.
The measurement of the visible lotus is 8.
The place of immersion (nimajjanabhūmi) 24.
The operation (karaṇa): the square of the twenty-fourth half-sine (ardhajyā) is 576; that, divided by eight—the visible lotus—yields 72.
This [quantity] together with the visible lotus is 80, and without it is 64.
When these are divided, the measure of the lotus and the measure of the water are 40 and 32 respectively. The problem statement is as follows:
A lotus six finger-breadths deep sinks down two cubits from its base; I wish to understand there the dimensions of both the lotus and the water.
The placement (nyāsa) is as follows: the diagram (parilekha) is 51; the visible portion (dṛśya) is 6; the ground for immersion (nimajjanabhūmi) is 48.
The resulting area of the lotus is 195, as before, and the depth of the water is 189.
In the cases of the problems concerning fish and cranes as well, one side of the rectangular field is likewise the half-chord.
The two arms are like a great arrow; the remainder of the action is as described in the section on the mouse.
The section [on the mouse] is as follows:
There is a pond measuring six by twelve [units]; in its north-eastern quarter stands a fish, and in the north-western corner stands a crane, which quickly flees out of fear of it.
Having pierced the pond, the fish went toward the southern direction by way of Karna;
having approached from the side, he was killed by the crane. This is the account that should be told regarding those two.
The assignment: [this is] the diagram (parilekha) 52.
Regarding the construction of the crane and the fish: the half-chord at the side of the pond; its square is 36.
The two sides are "great arrows" (mahāśara), thus it becomes 18.
By this, the quotient obtained is 2.
By this, through the transition of eighteen, the measure of the movement of the fish and crane, as well as the remainder of the pond's side, is 10 and 8.
When the side-remainder is dropped to the side, the remainder is the attainment of the south-west corner by the fish. The problem statement is as follows:
"In a pond of twelve by ten, there is a crane situated in the southeast; now, where is the fish?"
He who has come from the western direction is slain in the northeast; how much more need be said? 9.
The placement (nyāsa) and the diagram (parilekha) 53: as before, the distance traveled by the crane from the south-west corner is obtained as 3, 3, 11.
The movement of the fish has entered the western arm (8, 8, 11).
All this has been accomplished by means of the reverse-seed operation (*vilomabījakaraṇa*).

And the production of proof (*pratyayakaraṇa*) occurs in all fields indeed: "Whatever is the square of the base (*bhuja*), and the square of the perpendicular (*koṭi*), that is the square of the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). [Gaṇita-sāra-saṃgraha]
17] Thus, by this very [means]. // 17 //
[Knowledge of the diameter,
depth, and arrow] To calculate the diameter, depth, and arrow, he says: One should divide two diameters diminished by the eclipse by the measure of the eclipse separately.
When the *grāsa* (the subtractive quantity) is obtained through conjunction, the *sampāta-śara*s (meeting-arrows) are mutually [subtracted].
"Deficient by a morsel" means lacking one morsel;
what are the two? They are the two circles of the grasped and the grasper.
Regarding "grāsaguṇe" (the two having the morsel as their multiplier): those two for whom the morsel is the multiplier are "grāsaguṇe.
One should divide them separately, that is, one by one. By what? By the quotient obtained from the yoga diminished by the morsel.
The conjunction of the two [quantities] diminished by the divisor is "grāsonayoga";
the sum of those same two quantities when deprived of the divisor is likewise [called] grāsonayoga;
the results obtained by that grāsonayoga are "grāsonayogalabdha."
"Arrows in flight" (sampātaśarau) means arrows that have come into collision; that is to say, arrows that have intercepted one another. From each other.
Mutually;
because, due to the largeness of the circle, the arrow of the great *viṣkambha* is small,
[while that] of the small diameter is large.
The arrow is large; for while even a minute part of a small circle is perceived as being extremely curved,
such is not the case with a large one.

Therefore, those two become "meeting-arrows" (saṃpāta-śarau) with respect to each other. The problem-setter says: When thirty-two [digits] of the Moon are obscured by a shadow having a diameter of eighty, [and] eight [are obscured].
I wish to know that: how many arrows are there for Rāhu and for the Moon, whose tips are fully drawn? (1)
The assignment (nyāsa): the diagram (parilekha) 54;
the calculation (karaṇa): two circles [of diameters] 72 and 24, less the eclipse (grāsa).
In the quotient of the morsels (grāsa-guṇa), 576, divided by 192, the result is 3;
this, added to the morsel (grāsa), gives 96.
By this [division], the two arrows of the moon are obtained as 6.
Of Rāhu, [the result is] two; thus, from each other. // 18 //

[Arithmetic of Series] Now, he speaks for the purpose of calculating the arithmetic of series: "The desired number, diminished by one, halved, together with the preceding term, multiplied by the subsequent term, and added to the first term, is the middle term."
Alternatively, the desired wealth is multiplied by the desired [number], or else the product of the first and last [terms] is divided by half the number of terms. (19)
Desired, sought after;
diminished by one, lessened by one; crushed, halved.

"Sapūrva" means that which is together with what precedes it; those words which were situated prior to the desired word are called "pūrva," and that which exists together with the preceding is "sapūrva.
That which has a subsequent quality is "uttaraguṇa."
*Samukham*: "mouth" (*mukha*) is the beginning; that which exists together with the mouth is *samukham*.
It becomes the middle wealth.
Multiplied by the chosen [number]:
"iṣṭaguṇitam" means multiplied by the chosen [number] (iṣṭena guṇitam).
Desired wealth.
The wealth of the desired group arises;
here, many sūtras are established independently,
and their connection is according to their respective associations.
“*Iṣṭam vyekam dalitam uttaraguṇam samukham*” is the rule for the purpose of calculating the middle term (*madhyadhana*).
“*Madhyam iṣṭaguṇitam iṣṭadhanam*” is for the purpose of calculating the total sum (*gacchadhana*).
“*Iṣṭam vyekam sapūrvam uttaraguṇam samukham*” is for the purpose of calculating the last, penultimate, and other terms.

“Subtract one from the desired number, halve it, add the previous result, multiply by the subsequent multiplier, and then multiply by the desired number; this is the ‘desired wealth’ (*iṣṭadhana*). This [formula] is for the purpose of calculating the number of intermediate terms as desired.
Thus, these [rules] are composed in *āryā* meter with a missing quarter-verse (*pāda*).
We shall explain them in their proper order within the instructional examples (*uddeśaka*) themselves.
The teacher says: "The beginning, the pair, and the subsequent [sum]—they declare these three for the progression (śreḍhī).
The group is explained as five; tell me the middle remainder in the wealth. (1)
The placement (nyāsa) is: Ādi 2, Uttara 3, Gaccha 5.
The operation (karaṇa) is: Ādi 5, Gaccha 5.
Minus one is four; halved is two; the subsequent quality is six.
The face value is 8;
this is the middle wealth.
This very amount, multiplied by the desired divisor (iṣṭagaccha), results in the total wealth, which is 40.
The introductory statement:
"Eight is the first term of which five are said to be the subsequent [terms] of a progression;
eighteen is seen as the sum when the middle remainder of the wealth is to be stated. (2)
The placement (nyāsa) is: first term 8, common difference 5, number of terms 18. As before, the resulting middle term (madhyadhana) is 50 1/2.
909. All the wealth.
Regarding the calculation of the final, penultimate, and other types of wealth, the problem statement is as follows:
twenty-five is the divisor for seven increased by eleven.
In that regard, tell me quickly: what is the value of the penultimate and the last coins, and how much is twenty?
The placement (nyāsa) is: the first term (ādi) is 7, the common difference (uttara) is 11, and the number of terms (gaccha) is 25.
The calculation (karaṇa): the desired [sum] is 25.
The word *pūraṇam* (filling) is one; thus, one form is 1.
This same [number] minus one is zero (0).
This same [zero], with the preceding [one] added to it—that is, added by zero—results in twenty-four (24).
Uttaraguṇa 264,
Samukha 271;
this is the final wealth.
In the calculation of the penultimate amount, there are twenty-three preceding terms here (23).
By means of these preceding terms, the penultimate amount obtained through the previous operation is 260.
However, for twenty, there are nineteen preceding terms.

By these [rules], as before, the value of the twentieth term is 216. Regarding the calculation of the value of any desired intermediate term, here is the problem: In the month of Kārttika, starting from the second day and increasing by three each successive day, [what is the sum] for the entire month?
When fifteen days have passed, the brahmin gives [the gift] to the protector of the earth.
The one most devoted to Brahman arrived, and to him were given ten times the amount of wealth;
to the other, five days' worth was given—tell me, what was the difference in their wealth there? // 4 //
The placement (nyāsa) is: Ādi 2, Uttara 3, Gaccha 30.

Here, when fifteen days had passed, a most learned Brahmin arrived; for him, starting from the sixteenth day, that wealth accumulated over ten days was given—thus, ten (10) is the desired amount (iṣṭa).
"Minus one" results in 9; "halved" results in 4 1/2;
"this with the preceding" results in 19 1/2.
Multiplied by the multiplier (uttaraguṇita) is 58 1/2;
with the face added (samukha) it is 60 1/2; multiplied by the desired number (iṣṭaguṇita), which is the desired amount, being tenfold, the result is 605.
Regarding the second [section] as well: 415. The introductory heading (uddeśaka) begins with the fifteenth; in it, the eighteenth is called the "going" (gaccha).
Let the total sum of wealth for the thirty intermediate periods be calculated quickly. (5)
The placement (nyāsa) is 15 [the first], the subsequent is 18, and the group (gaccha) is 30.

In the ten remaining distinct [factors], there are ten intermediate terms. The result obtained by the previous method is 2,760. Furthermore, he states another method for calculating the total sum with a quarter-verse of an Āryā:
Or else, it is multiplied by half a word from beginning to end.
Or rather, this is another method:
"beginning and end" (ādyanta) refers to both the beginning and the end.
By the word "ādi" (beginning), the initial wealth is included;
by the word "anta" (end), the final wealth [is included].
That is "ādyanta" (from beginning to end).
One goes to a *pada*; half of that is a *padārtha*; multiplied by a *padārtha* is "multiplied by a *padārtha*" (*padārthahata*).
By the continuation of the rule that "the desired sum is the product of the first term and half the number of terms," it becomes the desired sum.
The problem statement is as follows: Let the first conch-shell be five, and let the last one be one less than a hundred.
Tell me what the price of those eleven conch shells is.
The placement (nyāsa) is as follows: the value of the initial conch is 5; that of the final is 95; and the conches are 11.
The operation is as follows: the total capital is 100; half of the principal is 50.
This multiplied by 1.2 gives the total value of all the conch shells as 550. The problem statement is as follows:
For the virtuous have declared that the first wealth is one, while the final wealth is said to be a hundred;
even a single step toward that has been called "all wealth"—how much more, then, is that which is actually seen?
The placement (nyāsa) is as follows:
the initial amount is 1, the final amount is 100,
and the step (gaccha) is also this same value, 100.
All wealth is as before: 5050. // 19 //
Regarding "gacchajñāna" (the knowledge of the *gaccha*): for the purpose of bringing it forth, he says:
"From the *gaccha* multiplied by eight and increased by the square of the specific difference starting from twice one (*dviguṇa*)."
The square root, diminished by twice its predecessor and so forth, divided by its own successor and increased by one-half. // 20 //
By the word "gacchaḥ," the placing of the feet is intended.
"Multiplied by eight plus one" (aṣṭottaraguṇitam) means multiplied by eight and further increased by one;
from that which is thus multiplied by eight plus one.
"From that which is joined with the square of the difference between the double and the subsequent":
"double" (*dviguṇa*) and "initial" (*ādi*) together form "double-initial" (*dviguṇādi*);
the "difference" (*viśeṣa*) between the "subsequent" (*uttara*) and this "double-initial" forms "the difference between the double and the subsequent" (*dviguṇādyuttaraviśeṣa*).
The square of the difference increased by twice [the first term] and so forth is "dviguṇādyuttaraviśeṣavargaḥ"; that which is added to this is "dviguṇādyuttaraviśeṣavargayutam";
from that "dviguṇādyuttaraviśeṣavargayuta" capital sum.

From all the wealth multiplied by eight and one more, the root is that which is diminished by the "twice-the-first" (dviguṇādyūna); and this "twice-the-first" consists of the "twice" (dviguṇa) and the "first" (ādi), thus it is the "twice-the-first.
By that "twice-the-first," it is diminished, hence "diminished by the twice-the-first" (dviguṇādyūna).
"Divided by its own successor" means divided by that which follows it;
"possessing form" (*sarūpa*) means existing together with a form; "halved" (*dalita*) means split in two.
The series (gaccha) is as follows:
the first term (ādi) is said to be five, and the common difference (uttara) is seven; this constitutes an arithmetic progression (śreḍhī).
One should say that the substance consists of one hundred minus five; how much of it is there? // 1 //
The placement is five for the first, seven for the subsequent, and ninety-five for the total sum.
The "wealth of the divisor" (*gacchadhana*) is obtained by multiplying [the divisor] by eight and by the "successor" (*uttara*); thus, it becomes 5,320.
The initial value (*ādi*) is doubled, resulting in 10;
this is specified by the successor as 3.
The square of this is 9; added to that, it becomes 5329; the square root of this is 73.
Sixty-three less than twice [the previous value],
divided by this [value] increased by its own [value] (seven), yields nine;
with the original form added, it becomes ten.
Half [of the total] is the *gaccha* (5).
Now, regarding the section on the nine types of *kāṣṭha*: whatever wealth is proclaimed therein at the beginning of the increase (*vṛddhimukha*), it is presented in successive order.
You must state that the eight arrows of Rāma were seen by you to be the size of a footstep. // 2 //
The placement (nyāsa) is:
the first term (ādi) is 8, the subsequent term (uttara) is 9, and the product of the progression (gacchadhana) is 583.
As before, the obtained measure of the square is 11/20.
Regarding "the knowledge of the dense mass" (*citighanajñāna*),

he says this for the purpose of bringing together the summations and non-summations: "From the accumulation beginning with one, there is a triple product of the sequence and so forth, increasing by one."
That cube-root of the pile, divided by six, is either increased by one unit and cubed, or decreased by its own root. (20)
"Uttara" (subsequent) and "ādi" (beginning) form "uttarādi.
That which has a single "uttarādi" is "ekottarādi. This "ekottarādi" is also an "upaciti" (accumulation); thus, it is "ekottarādyupaciti."
Accumulation (*upaciti*) is qualified by being "increasing by one" (*ekottara*) and so forth; that very accumulation increasing by one and so forth is called "summation" (*saṅkalanā*).

From the "course" (*gaccha*) of that summation—which is designated as accumulation increasing by one and so forth—there is a "threefold multiplication of those increasing by one," meaning the multiplication of three [quantities] starting from the course and so forth, which increase by one.
That is to say: "Come," [and] that which increases by one, and again [that which] increases by one.
The combination of the three, beginning with the *gaccha*: namely, the *gaccha* itself,
which increases by one.
Furthermore, it is "increased by one" (*ekottara*).
This means: go;
that very [number] is increased by one.
That same group is increased by two;
the sum of those three,
divided by six— that is, partitioned by six— [is the result].
"Citighana" means the cube of the "citipada" (the root of the sum); it signifies both the summation and the non-summation.
Now, there is another method for calculation: "saikapadaghana," where "saikapada" refers to that term together with one.

The cube of the square root plus one is "saikapadaghana"; it is "vimūla" (devoid of its root) when divided by six— this phrase carries over from the previous rule— or else, the calculation of the cube of the square root plus one, being devoid of its own root and divided by six, is the "citighana" (the cube of the earth).
There is the instructor:
"The five, the eight, and the fourteen are the layers in their respective order."
The movement, the speed, and the triangularity of the [planets], as well as the determination of their forms, must be explained by me. // 1 //
The assignment (nyāsa) is as follows:
the sequence of values is 5,
8, and 14, in their respective order.
The instrument comes: five (5).
This is the next higher by one (6). Again, this is the next higher by one (7).
The sum of these three is 210.
Divided by six, this becomes the sum of the series, 35. The second method of calculation is: one less than the number of terms, which is 6.
Its cube is 216;
this, being devoid of its square root, is 210 when reduced by six.
Divided by six as before, it results in the sum or non-sum of 35.
The results for the remaining two [parameters] are also obtained in their respective order as 120 and 560. // 21 //

[The cube of a sum of squares and the cube of a sum of cubes]— to find the summation of the cubes of squares, he says: "The sixth part of the triple product of the terms of a sequence, including one, is [the sum]."
That [result] shall be the cube of the sum of the classes, as well as the square of the sum of the cubes and the cube of the sum of the cubes. // 22 //
That which exists together with one is *saika*;
that which exists together with a group (*gaccha*) is *sagaccha*.
The term *saikasagaccha* refers to what has been discussed immediately preceding.
"Going to a place" means going to that single place; "a place with one" (*saika*) and "a place with four" (*sagaccha*); and "places with one and four" (*saikasagacchapadāni*).
Of those "places with one and four," taken in order—that is, sequentially—the product of three is the "triple-product" (*trisaṃvargita*).
Of which three? Of the three previously mentioned [categories], including the one with a single *sagaccha* word. The sixth part.

The sixth part, the sixth portion, of that which has been tripled by the square is the cube of the square; it becomes the cube of the square. The accumulation of the square is the "square-accumulation" (vargaciti); [the cube is] of that square-accumulation.
"Solid" (ghana) refers to the solidification of the collection of squares;

Now, the word *atha* functions here in the sense of taking up the subject matter for thorough knowledge and introducing the subsequent text.
What kind of meaning is established here?
It is said: it is a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*).
And since that convention differs for each subject matter according to worldly usage, it is demonstrated precisely through common worldly application.
For otherwise, the technical definitions would differ for each object, and the objects themselves would be beyond counting;

Therefore, by the word "atha" (now), he sets forth a convention well-known in the world:

[Knowledge of the Time of Conjunction (Yogakālajñāna):
For the purpose of calculating the time of conjunction, he says:
"When the retrograde difference is divided by the sum of the motions, and when the direct difference is divided by two."
The two times of conjunction, past and future, are obtained by means of the other motion. // 31 //
When divided by the quotient,
one moves in the reverse direction while the other returns toward him from that reverse interval; that is the reverse interval (*vilomavivara*).
"Regarding the interval between the forward movement and the reverse movement":
here, it should be understood that the word "forward" (*anuloma*) is mentioned elliptically;
or else, the opening of the reverse movement itself is taken as being of this very nature.
If both [the Sun and the Moon] were to have retrograde motion,
then there would indeed be a direct (anuloma) interval;
in that retrograde interval, when divided [by the daily motion], [the result is obtained].
By what means? He says: by the conjunction of the two movements.
The conjunction of the two movements is "gatiyoga"; by that conjunction of the two movements.
*Anulomavivara* means the interval between the two *anuloma-gatis*. "Two" refers to the two times of the conjunctions of *pratiloma* and *anuloma*; during these, it produces the supreme *aṃśa*.
"By another mode of going" (*gatyantareṇa*): the interval between two modes of going is a "difference in mode of going" (*gaterviśeṣaḥ*); by that difference in mode of going.
The two times of conjunction are obtained;
"conjunction of two" means *dviyoga*,
and the two times of that conjunction are the "two times of conjunction" (*dviyogakāla*).
The past and the future: "atīta" means past, and "eṣya" means that which is to come. "Atītaiṣyau" refers to both the past and the future. "Atīta" is what has passed;
"eṣya" is what will be.
For example: when one planet is situated in the east as retrograde and another is situated in the west, moving according to its course,
the *liptās* between them constitute the retrograde distance (*vilomavivara*).
In that case, since yoga will be achieved in a short time for one who moves in direct order and another who returns in reverse order, their share is deducted by means of the *bhukti-yoga*.
Since their daily enjoyment is exactly that much,
a rule of three (trairāśika) is performed as follows: "If one day is obtained by this daily enjoyment, then what is obtained by this inverse difference?"
Days or *ghaṭikās* are obtained;
that much time has passed when the yoga has elapsed, and it is yet to come when the yoga is to occur.

In that regard, the procedure for applying the correction is as follows: by means of proportionality (*trairāśika*) based on the daily motion, if the true motion of a planet is obtained for sixty *ghaṭikās*, then what is the motion for the *ghaṭikās* produced by the retrograde motion? The result thus obtained is added to the planet if it is in direct motion, and subtracted if it is in retrograde motion.
Thus, those two [planets] become smeared with impurity when they arise at a time of planetary possession (*grahāviṣṭa*).

Now, if the retrograde motion (*vakragati*) occurs behind and the direct motion (*anulomagati*) occurs in front, then the obtained result is added to the retrograde motion because it has already been surpassed.

The motion in direct order (*anuloma*) is purified precisely because it has been transcended. Furthermore, when these two motions are in direct order, then a portion of the direct interval is determined by the specific difference in consumption (*bhukti*), because their daily difference in motion is equal to that specific difference in consumption.
Then, by this specific motion produced [by the planet] in its interval of movement, sixty *nāḍīs* are obtained; at that time, how many *ghaṭikās* are obtained through the direct opening?

And with those, a rule of three (*trairāśika*) is performed together with the true motion of the planet: if by sixty [nāḍīs] the true motion is obtained, [then what is obtained by the given number of *ghaṭikās*]?
What is the purpose of these *ghaṭikās*?
The result obtained in the case of the swift motion (*śīghragati*) is added to both [the true and mean positions] when the swift motion is situated behind;
when the swift motion is situated ahead, both of those are subtracted from both.
In this way, the two periods of conjunction become past and future respectively.
And when both are in retrograde motion, the calculation is exactly the same;
this is the very same procedure.
In our *Karmapradīpa* (Karmanibandha), it was stated: "The distance between two planets should be divided by the sum of their motions when they are moving in opposite or the same directions;

the remainder after being divided by that which is the divisor of the deficient top.

[using] the excess numerator as the divisor.
"Practiced. "The peak of two cuts":

Even though it is obtained as such, it is stated as ninety-seven thousand seven hundred forty-nine (*97,749*), which is the product of nine, four, seven, and nine. (82)
The multipliers for the [sun's] declination are seven, four, and one [347] respectively;
the resulting signs are seen as one, four, and one [141] respectively. // 83 //
The number of intercalary months in a yuga, marked by the figures for sages (7), moon (1), world (3), sky (0), ether (0), and space (0)— that is, 18900317— is observed.
In this case, the multiplier (guṇya) obtained here is five thousand nine hundred and eight (5908), which is always applied to these revolutions (bhagaṇas). // 84 //
The multiplier is equal to the moon (1), the apertures (9), fire (3), sky (0), Śiva (11), the Aśvins (2), and the sun (12);
the quotient obtained here is indeed the quantity produced from the heap. // 85 //
The multiplier (guṇakāra) should be the number 34836, consisting of [the digits] six, three, seven, four, three, two, and one;
and [the divisor] is 8991551, consisting of [the digits] eight, nine, nine, one, five, five, and one.
The result of the calculation for the degrees has been obtained in due order. // 86 //
The multiplier set is seen when multiplied; they declare the quotient to have a measure of [83197819], consisting of nine, one, three, seven, nine, one, and three worlds. // 87 //
When the accomplishment of the qualities of the smeared one is seen,
they declare the gain to be Rudra, mountain, refinement, arrow, woman, serpent, and the moon. (88)
And the numbers for those intent upon the qualities are:

Arrows with perforated feathers were obtained, along with those having vane-like extensions. // 89 //
The heap produced by the multiplier, beginning from the subsequent [terms]— arkakṛtāgninanda (18312)—

The gain here is equal to [440081638531], which is the same as the sky, clouds, Vedas, and oceans. // 90 //
For the asterisms together with their signs, twelve (12) is indeed the divisor;

Thus ends the Chapter on Calculation in the *Āryabhaṭatantrabhāṣya*, the work of Bhāskara.
The *Kālakriyāpāda* [Auspicious Invocation]:
To those known as the Sun, Moon, Ether, Fire, Wind, Water, and Earth, who have been initiated...
