Homage to that Śiva, the sustainer of the three worlds, who, being himself immeasurable and the very embodiment of compassion, manifested as the eightfold form for the sake of the welfare of all the world.
[The Division of Time and the Division of Space] Now, following arithmetic, the calculation of time (kālakriyā) is introduced.
What, then, is time, and what is action?
On this point, some say: "Time is distinct from action";
others say: "Action is time.
Whether time be distinct from action or [action itself], what does it matter?
For us, however, the maximum distance between the sun and the moon constitutes a half-month; their closest approach constitutes a month.
Thus, twelve months constitute a year, and so forth—this is time.
Action (*kriyā*) is activity (*vyāpāra*).
The action of time is "temporal action" (*kālakriyā*);
that is to say, it is an action for the purpose of fully understanding time.
And that action is motion;
it will be demonstrated that time is known by means of that action. For example:
A year consists of twelve months; a month consists of thirty days.
A day consists of sixty nāḍīs, and a nāḍī consists of sixty vināḍikās. (1)
*Varṣa*, *abda*, *samā*, and *saṃvatsara* are synonyms. This word *varṣa* is neuter in gender when it refers to a year;
the measure of that year is twelve months.
Twelve months— two and ten—
are the branches of the year;
that month, moreover, consists of thirty days.
"Thirty" is the number.
"Days," "dināni," and "ahāni" are synonyms.
"Bhavet" means "it would be" or "it should be."
That month which has been mentioned consists of thirty days; this is the meaning.
There are sixty *nāḍīs* in a day;
the measure of that single day is sixty *nāḍīs*.
The *nāḍīs* are *ghaṭikās*. Sixty *vināḍikās* constitute one *nāḍī*;
the measure of that *nāḍī* is sixty *vināḍīs*.
The *vināḍīs* are the *vighaṭikās*.
To this it is said: the statement beginning with "a year consists of twelve months" and so forth need not be undertaken, because it is already well-known in the world.

This principle must be accepted in all cases through what is well-known in the world and the Veda. For instance, even without a formal definition, people in the world understand that "a year consists of twelve months," and likewise, they pay wages to laborers for work performed.
If even that which is well-known in the world were to be explicitly stated, then much would have to be said here; thus [it is said]:
"In humans, a yojana" (Gītikā).
7] Regarding the statement, “A *hasta* is not less than twenty-four *aṅgulas*” [Gītikā,

8], the measurements of the barley grain (*yava*), mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), louse egg (*yūka*), nit (*likṣā*), hair-tip (*vālāgra*), chariot-dust (*rathareṇu*), mote (*trasareṇu*), and the coarse and subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) must be explained.
Furthermore, in the context of the threefold calculation (*trairāśika*), the technical conventions (*paribhāṣā*) consisting of the various regional usages must be explained.

Now, even if worldly convention (*lokaprasiddhi*) were accepted, nevertheless, in the verse "The syllables of the groups are in the group" [Gītikās, 2], the description of the groups, the syllables of the groups, and the vowels must indeed be stated.
Why? Because they are not established in the world.
If this is so, then the analysis of consonant groups, individual consonants, and vowels in grammar would be useless.
This is not a fault; for it is the world and the former teachers who [rely on] non-Buddhist treatises.
It has been stated that they are the authors.

Regarding the statement, “The syllables of the groups are in the group” [Gītikā 2], here, in the determination of the groups, the syllables of the groups, and the vowels, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is a non-external science (*abāhyaśāstra*).
Regarding the statement, "Sixty long syllables constitute a *vināḍikā*" (*Kālakriyā*,
2), the definition of a long syllable must be stated here.
If the passage beginning with "A year consists of twelve months" were not commenced, then all of this would be established through worldly convention alone.
Therefore, let there simply be no communication [of the distinction].
This is not a fault;
for if this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) were not undertaken, these divisions would apply only to the *sāvana* (lunar) month, and not to the solar, lunar, or sidereal months.
Since the solar month alone is the single measure well-known in the world,
and not the solar, lunar, or sidereal ones,
this aphorism must be commenced so that this very convention may apply to all measures.
Otherwise, in the verse "Those lunar [days] which are in excess of the solar months" (*Kālakriyā*, 6), the multiplier of twelve for the solar revolutions would not be obtained;
and [in the verse] "The lunar days are to be known as the days of the earth minus the destructions of the lunar dates" (*Kālakriyā*...).

6] In this context, a multiplier of thirty for lunar days would not be obtained; furthermore, regarding the statement "sixty *nāḍīs* constitute a day," sixty *nāḍīs* have been postulated here as well so as not to contradict the science of *horās*.
Otherwise, indeed, the division of a day could be postulated according to one's own desire.
If a division [of the day] is conceived according to one's desire, what contradiction with the *Horā-śāstra* is there?
It is said: "The duration of the rising of the first and last signs is invariably prescribed as two *muhūrtas* each."
Thus, here a *muhūrta* consisting of two *nāḍikās* is explained; and that *nāḍikā* is a sixtieth part of the day. If it were conceived otherwise, this meaning would be different.

Furthermore, as for how the sixtyth part of a day is calculated, it is explained here: some say that a "ghaṭikā" is a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, shaped like a half-circle, with a capacity of sixty palas of water, which may be filled or emptied.
This is not a fixed rule;
the duration of a *nāḍikā* is not necessarily that amount of time during which sixty *palas* of water flow out or fill [the vessel].
The wise, however, do not think so.
How then?
A rough calculation is that sixty parts of water flowing in a day and night constitute the measure of one ghaṭikā.

However, on level ground, one should mark the shadow of a ghaṭikā at a gnomon (śaṅku) of the specified form; thus the ghaṭikā is calculated, and the hole for the ghaṭikā should be joined according to the stated method based on the time of the shadow. // 1 //
Sixty long syllables constitute one *vināḍikā* of the asterisms, or likewise six breaths (*prāṇas*).
Thus is the division of time; the division of space is likewise derived from the zodiacal circle (*bhagaṇa*). // 2 //
Sixty long syllables constitute one *vināḍikā* of the asterisms; "long syllables" (*gurvakṣarāṇi*) means those which are both long (*guru*) and syllables (*akṣara*),
and sixty such [syllables] make one *vināḍikā* of the asterisms.
The duration of time in which sixty long syllables (*gurvakṣara*) are recited is designated as a *vināḍī*.

By the statement, "Sixty long syllables are a *vināḍikā*," it might follow that all measures—solar (*saura*), civil (*sāvana*), sidereal (*nākṣatra*), and lunar (*cāndra*)—are equal in their duration of *vināḍikās*. To define the specific scope of each, [the author] says: "The sidereal (*ārkṣī*)."
What is a *vināḍikā* consisting of sixty long syllables?
It is the *ārkṣī*, not the others. The *ṛkṣas* are the constellations (*nakṣatras*).
By the word *nakṣatra*, the lunar measurement is intended;
this is the time of the stars (*ṛkṣa*), hence it is called *ārṣa*.
And this time, designated as a *vināḍikā*, attains femininity; thus it is expressed with a feminine gender designation as "vināḍikā.
Or rather, there are exactly six breaths (*prāṇa*); "breaths" refers to inhalations and exhalations (*ucchvāsa*).
The measure of an *ārkṣya-vināḍikā* is the duration of one revolution of the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*). For it is said: "By means of the breath, it traverses a minute of the zodiac" (Gītikā, 6).
In the time of one breath, the wheel of the asterisms—
that is, the circle of stars—
traverses one *kalā*; here, six *vināḍikās* of the asterisms are equal to six *prāṇas*.

One degree consists of ten *vināḍikās* of the *arkṣī* type; therefore, the breaths (*prāṇas*) related to the circle of light (*jyotiścakra*) are measured by the number of *liptās*. By means of these breaths, the operations of the sine (*jyā*) and so forth proceed.
Otherwise, indeed, there would be no basis for the statement: “The sines of half the minutes (*kalā*) [beginning with] *pha* and *cha*.”
Because it has been stated [in the *Gītikā*, verse 12], "by means of breaths," the grasping of the bowstring would not be possible [if measured by breaths alone].
Furthermore, if it were stated generally that "six breaths are a *vināḍikā*," it would follow as a logical consequence that the duration of a *vināḍikā* would be identical for all measures of time.
For the remaining measures, the measure of a *vināḍikā* is simply one-sixtieth of a *nāḍikā*.
No statement regarding the measurement of the constituent parts of that *vināḍikā* is made, due to the absence of necessity;
among heavy syllables (*gurvakṣara*), the medium tempo (*madhyamavṛtti*) is to be understood.
Regarding the statement, "Sixty long syllables [constitute a *vināḍikā*]," it should be understood that in the medium (*madhyamā*) tempo, sixty long syllables constitute the duration of a *vināḍikā*.
Otherwise, there would result an indistinct application across all three tempos.
For instance, in the rapid (*drutā*) tempo, sixty long syllables are recited in a short amount of time.
In the case of the slow [progression], it is by a long time;
in the case of the middling, however, it is neither by a short nor by a long time.
In that case, then, the mention of the "middle pace" (madhyamavṛtti) ought to be made. How is it understood even when it is not explicitly stated?
From common worldly usage.

Just as in the world there is the attainment of a middle course regarding actions that have not been specifically prescribed, so too here: at the end of the month or the end of the fortnight, he indeed [sees] his own mixed, curved, lovely, circular, and full moon in the region of the sky; by day, due to its essence, those [beings] emaciated by hunger perish, while by night, the white one is abundant and fierce.
Therefore, at the end of the palace, while one is sleeping in a secluded spot,
these sixty long syllables constitute the duration of a *vināḍikā*,
or else they are simply six breaths (*prāṇas*).
The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are exhalations;
they are six in number, and this is the duration of one *vināḍikā* of that very *arkṣi*.
This also applies to a healthy, unwearied, and disease-free yogin.
The vital breaths are fully grasped;
even here, one who is healthy does not breathe for a long time,
nor likewise when free from fatigue.
The yogin, moreover, does not breathe for a long time due to the power of the *vyāna* [vital energy].
Why are the divisions of time such as *truṭi*, *truṭya*, and *avayava* not mentioned here?
They think thus: because there is no practical usage (*vyavahāra*) with respect to them.
And the apprehension of the divisions of time is for the sake of conventional usage;
thus is the division of time.
Thus, years, months, days, ghaṭikās, and prāṇas constitute the division of time.
For what purpose is this stated, namely, "Thus is the division of time"?
Is it not already the case that the division of time has been indicated? Indeed, the phrase "Thus is the division of time" is a reference to that very division which has already been indicated.
Since this has not been explicitly stated, one might think that the division of time is such that its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has not been elaborated upon.
This is not a fault;
for the meaning is: "the division of time is thus," that is to say, the division of time is of such a kind.
But when it is explained in the sense of "variety," other divisions of time are also included;
for example: five years constitute a *yuga*, and twelve months constitute a year (*saṃvatsara*).
Two months constitute a season (*ṛtu*), and these are known as spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season; three seasons make a solstice (*ayana*);
a fortnight (*pakṣa*) consists of half a month, namely the bright and the dark.
A watch (yāma) is one-fourth of a day and night;
a moment (muhūrta) consists of two nāḍikās; and so forth.
The division of the field is likewise derived from the sphere of asterisms (bhagaṇa).
The field is the stellar sphere (bhagola);
it is the division of that field.
In that same manner,
just as there is a division of time, so too is there a division of space from the celestial sphere.

The division of time has been stated starting from the year, whereas that of the sphere (kṣetra) proceeds starting from the zodiacal revolution (bhagaṇa). For example: twelve signs constitute one zodiacal revolution.
A zodiac sign (rāśi) consists of thirty degrees (bhāga); one degree consists of sixty minutes (liptā);
and one minute consists of sixty seconds (viliptā).

Sixty *tatparas* are called *viliptās*; such is the enumeration: the circle (*bhagaṇa*), the sign (*rāśi*), the degree (*bhāga*), the minute (*kalā*), the second (*vikalā*), and the *tatpara*. These designations for the spatial [zodiac] should be equivalent to those for the divisions of time.
[The thorough knowledge of the conjunctions of two planets:
For the sake of thoroughly knowing the conjunctions of two planets, the first half of the Āryā verse says:
"Those remainders of the difference between each pair of planetary revolutions (bhagaṇas) in a yuga are the conjunctions of two planets."
The revolutions of the planets have indeed been specified in the Gītikās.
The inclusion of the distributive repetition "of each pair" is for the purpose of excluding three or more.
As for those remaining particulars:

The number of revolutions remaining as the difference between the revolutions of each pair of planets is equal to the number of conjunctions of those two [planets] that have occurred or will occur in a yuga.
Here, how is it determined that the conjunctions of the two are simply the differences of their revolutions, and not rather their multiplication or their sum? It is said in reply:
For example, suppose two horses are equipped with circular saddles;
there, one has a girth of sixty bows, while the other has thirty.
Those two follow the movement of five staffs:
as far as one-fourth of a large mandala, so far does he go in a small mandala;
as far as half of a large mandala, so far does he traverse the entire small mandala.
Thus, as there is one revolution in the great mandala,
there are two revolutions in the small mandala,
and in that same duration, there is one conjunction of those two.
The same should be applied to the planets as well.
This is logical if the planets have equal velocities;
he will demonstrate that the planets indeed have equal velocities.
The questioner asks: "In the yuga of the preceptor and Mars, how many conjunctions are there? The result is:
1,932,600 conjunctions.
This applies to all [the planets] as well.
What, then, is the application of the conjunctions (dviyoga) here? It is said:

if the conjunctions of two desired planets are obtained by means of the day-count (ahargaṇa) of four yugas, then how many are obtained by means of the Kali-era elapsed day-count? That which is thus obtained are the conjunctions already elapsed.
Having converted the remainder into elapsed and remaining [units], one should divide by the *yuga*-separations. The quotient is the days elapsed and remaining; this is one application.
[The remainder, multiplied by sixty and divided by the *yuga*-separations, gives the result in *ghaṭī*s and so forth.]

If, by means of the day-count (ahargaṇa) of four yugas, the number of double-conjunctions (dviyoga) of two desired planets is obtained, then how many are there by means of the elapsed Kali-day-count? The result is the number of double-conjunctions already passed. When the remainder is multiplied by twelve and so forth, the quotient is in signs (rāśi) and so on.
The slow-moving planet, when added to those signs and so forth of the double-conjunctions, becomes the fast-moving planet.

Furthermore, there is another application: the fast-moving planet, when diminished by twice the difference in signs and so forth, becomes the slow-moving planet. Having calculated the signs and so forth using those differences, one should also determine the signs and so forth contained within the sum of their revolutions; then, according to the rule "that which is joined with the difference is subtracted" (*Gaṇitapāda* 24), one should add it in one case and subtract it in the other.
Half of those two, which have been subtracted and purified, are the elapsed revolutions, signs, degrees, and minutes; this is another application.
As for the application regarding the pulverizer (*kuṭṭākāra*), it has already been demonstrated. [The number of Vyatīpātas in a Yuga.]
To explain the knowledge of the *vyatīpāta* [yoga], he states the latter half of the verse: "The groups of suns, moons, and stars, when combined, constitute the *vyatīpātas*. (3)
The groups of constellations are the "nakṣatragaṇas";
the constellations are those beginning with Aśvinī;
and the sun and the moon are "raviśaśī."
The "groups of stars of the sun and moon" means the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) belonging to the cycles of the moon and sun;
These are the *vyatīpāta* yogas.
And the *vyatīpāta* [yogas] are combined;
"combined" means unified. Combined with what?
Because nothing else has been heard [of], the revolutions of the sun and moon are by means of the constellations alone;
the meaning is that those very [revolutions] doubled constitute the *vyatīpātas*.
And these two have sounds imitated by the cries of peacocks (*dviśailarasa*).
Now, these two *vyatīpāta*s are said to consist of twelve and six zodiac signs (*rāśi*) respectively.
Regarding this, it must be asked: is this an illustration of the two *vyatīpāta*s, or rather their definition (*lakṣaṇa*)?
If this is the illustrative example, then everything desired will be established; let it be taken as the example.
For instance: when the moon and the sun are made manifest together in one place within the twelve zodiacal signs, that is *vyatīpāta*.
But is it not well known in the world that the *vaidhṛta* yoga consists of the twelve zodiac signs?
This is not a fault;
the distinction is based on nomenclature and does not affect the result.
Since the venerable Garga and others have taught that the results of Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti are equal,
if those same two, the sun and the moon, are clearly together in one place at six signs [of the zodiac], then that too is Vyatīpāta.

Now, for the purpose of determining the elapsed and remaining time of a *vyatīpāta*, there is a rule of three (*trairāśika*): if sixty *ghaṭikās* are obtained by the sum of the true daily motions of the sun and the moon, then how many [ghaṭikās and vighaṭikās] are obtained by this elapsed or remaining time?
Or, if one wishes to know the positions of the sun and the moon at the time of the elapsed or remaining *vyatīpāta*:

Then, by means of a rule of three proportions involving the past and future [motions]: "If, by the sum of the true daily motions of the sun and moon, the motion of the sun or the motion of the moon is obtained, then what motion is obtained by this sum of the past and future motions of the sun and moon?
By that [result], the sun and moon—either subtracted from or added to [the mean positions]—are [determined] as they stand at the time of the *vyatīpāta* yoga.
Thus has the gross occurrence of *vyatīpāta* been explained;
now it is demonstrated how it occurs in its subtle form. And it has been said:
"The *vyatīpāta* occurs at the solstices (*ayana*) when those two have equal declinations (*apakrama*)."
Its extent is half a wheel, and its width is more or less than that.
[Mahābhāskarīya, 4.36] Thus:
when the sun and the moon are at different solstices (nānāyana) yet have equal declinations (apakrama), that is the Vyatīpāta yoga;
it is the declination of the moon, either increased by or decreased from its latitude (vikṣepa).
It is said that during this Vyatīpāta conjunction, the branches of the milk-tree became devoid of their milky sap.
[The revolutions of the planets' nodes and apogees in a yuga.
To explain the knowledge of the cycles of nodes and apogees, he says:
"The revolutions of one's own apogee, when multiplied by one's own revolutions, are the revolutions of one's own node and apogee."
The revolutions of its own apogee, multiplied by its own revolutions, are the "revolutions of its own apogee" (*svoccabhagaṇāḥ*).
One's own apogee is *svoccam*; the revolutions of that apogee are *svoccabhagaṇāḥ*.
In this context, there are two types of apogees for the planets:
the slow apogee (mandocca) and the fast apogee (śīghrocca).
Which of these apogees is to be understood here?
He says "the apogee" (śīghrocca).

Although the motion of the apogee of the slow [motion] is accepted, nevertheless, because there is no practical application for its revolutions in a yuga, only the revolutions of the apogee of the fast [motion] are taken;
these revolutions of the apogees and perigees are specified by their own respective revolutions.
The difference between the maximum number of revolutions and the natural number of revolutions is the revolution of the apogee and perigee.

Since [the planets] undergo rising, setting, retrogression, and direct motion from one state of being partless (nairaṃśya) to another state of being partless, the revolution of the apogee is thus postulated.
Those days which lie between two such states of being partless are the days of that revolution.
The revolutions and the planets began at the start of the Yuga from Aries;
the completion of the fast revolution occurs at the end of Pisces.
The fast motion is conceived as being greater than the actual planetary motion.
The revolutions of the apogee and perigee:
there are exactly as many revolutions of the apogee as there are of the perigee,
because within one complete revolution of the planet, the attainment of both apogee and perigee occurs at two distinct points.
Now, what then is high and what is low?
That region of space where the planets are perceived as small due to the great distance from the ear is designated as "high."
Where that very planet is observed as a large disc due to its proximity to the ear, that region of space is designated as "low" (nīca).
Now, the apogee or perigee is also brought forward by means of revolutions.
How so? If these revolutions of apogee and perigee are obtained by the number of days in four yugas, [then...]
Then, by means of the *kaliyuga* day-count (*ahargaṇa*), the quotient obtained indicates the number of revolutions already elapsed;
the remainder, multiplied by twelve and so forth, is the planetary position (*parivartabhoga*) in signs and so on.
The planet minus its revolution-position, or the planet plus its revolution-position, is the position of the apogee (*uccabhoga*).

The planetary period (*graha-bhoga*) consists of either a high-enjoyment period accompanied by a revolution-period (*parivarta-bhoga*), or a high-enjoyment period devoid of a revolution-period. The revolution-period itself is the quadrant-period (*kendra-bhoga*).
And the remainder is stated by means of the conjunction of two.
It is the same.

Now, regarding the verse: "The differences between each pair of bhagaṇas are the double conjunctions in a yuga" (Kālakriyā, 3)—has this meaning not already been established in this very verse? What, then, is being stated here?
This undertaking is for the purpose of establishing the notion of the revolution of high and low;
therein, only the conjunction of two [planets] has been explained,
and yet that is stated to be the specific difference in the number of revolutions (bhagaṇa) between each pair of planets.
There is no difference from the revolutions of the planets' apogees; thus it is stated separately.
To define the Jupiter-year (*guru-varṣa*), beginning with the month of Āśvayuja, he says:
The number of Jupiter's revolutions multiplied by the signs [twelve] gives the years of Jupiter beginning from the month of Āśvayuja. (4)
"Jupiter's revolutions multiplied by the signs": Jupiter's revolutions are "gurubhagaṇāḥ";
that is to say, the revolutions of Bṛhaspati.
The qualities of the zodiac signs (rāśiguṇāḥ) mean twelvefold qualities;
these are the years of Jupiter beginning with Aśvayuja.
The year [beginning with] Aśvayuja—
That which occurs at the beginning is "initial" (*ādya*); those for whom Aśvayuja is initial are "those beginning with Aśvayuja.
The meaning is that these are the years of the Guru, the years of the Preceptor.
And these are known as Aśvayuja, Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Māgha, Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Prauṣṭhapada.

Herein is a rule of three proportions (*trairāśika*): if by the total number of days of four *yugas* these years of Jupiter—calculated as eight, eight, eight, zero, seven, seven, and one [4,370,688]—are obtained, [then...]

Then, by means of the *kaliyātā* day-count (*ahargaṇa*), how many [years] are there? The years obtained are those already elapsed. When the obtained years are divided by twelve, [the result is the number of months].
The remaining months, beginning with Āśvayuja, are equal [in length].
How is this understood—that the months beginning with Āśvayuja are equal?
It is said: because of the statement, "The years of the Guru begin with Āśvayuja."
Is it not true that this very statement was urged by us, and a rebuttal is also being stated by us?
Because at the beginning of the Yuga, the preceptor of the gods ascended the peak of the mountain of sunrise while Aśvinī was in the ascendant; therefore, the years of Jupiter begin with Āśvayuja.
And it has been said:
The year in which the Aṅgiras [Jupiter] enters upon his journey at the rising of a particular lunar mansion is reckoned as the Bārhaspatya year beginning with that constellation.
Thus it is said.

Now, Jupiter (*bṛhaspati*) is also brought forth by means of the rule of three (*trairāśika*), using the number formed by the Vasus (8), Vasus (8), Rasas (6), Ākāśa (0), Munis (7), and Dahanas (3) [i.e., 370688].
How so? If, by the total number of days of the four *yugas*, the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*) of Jupiter consisting of the Vasus, Vasus, and so forth are obtained, [then...]
Then, the signs obtained by dividing the accumulated days of the Kali era by [the divisor] are the signs;
the remainder, when multiplied by thirty and so forth, yields the degrees, minutes, and so on.
In this way, the following meaning is established by implication:
Those zodiacal signs of Jupiter that have been passed over are the years of Jupiter beginning with Āśvayuja that have elapsed; and that which remains is the current year.
Now, the years of Jupiter are designated as Vasuvasu and so forth.
But must these not be equal to the *yuga* years? No, he says:
those which are *yuga* years are seen by the solar measure (*saurya-māna*), whereas those which are the years of Jupiter (*guru-abda*) are by the Jupiter-measure (*gurumāna*).
That very *yuga*, when inferred by the solar calculation, has the number 4,320,000, being the product of the fire (three), the sky (zero), the waters (four), and the drops (two) and clouds (one).
That same period, when calculated by the Jovian system, has the number 4,370,688, consisting of the treasures (eight), the treasures (eight), and so forth.
Since a Jovian year is the time taken by Jupiter to traverse one zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), the solar and Jovian systems are not identical. // 4 //
[The Solar, Lunar, Civil, and Sidereal Measures] To demonstrate the solar, lunar, civil, and sidereal measures, he says:
the revolutions of the sun are solar years; the conjunctions of the sun and moon are lunar months.
The days resulting from the conjunction with the Sun, as well as those of the lunar mansions, are revolutions of the asterisms. // 5 //
The revolutions of the sun are solar years;
the revolutions of the sun are "ravibhagaṇāḥ."
"Solar years" (ravyabdāḥ) means solar years;
those which are the revolutions of the sun are themselves the solar years.
Likewise, even though this is not explicitly stated, it is understood that the sun's signs, degrees, and minutes correspond to the sun's months, days, and nāḍīs;
for twelve signs constitute a bhagaṇa, and thirty degrees constitute a sign.
A sixtieth part of a degree is a *liptā*;
six signs constitute a solstice (*ayana*), which is either northern or southern, beginning from Capricorn and Cancer respectively.
How is it determined that this begins from Capricorn and Cancer, and not rather from Dhaniṣṭhā or from the midpoint of Āśleṣā?

For it has been said: "From the half-conjunction of Śraviṣṭhā and the others, when the southern and northern courses of the sun's heat have begun, they are known as the periods of security, good harvests, and abundance."
To this it is replied: the two scriptural passages constitute distinct sentences;
indeed, that can be asserted, because their purpose is transcendental (adṛṣṭārtha).
“The ritual action is one and the same, as understood from all the Vedic branches, being the fruit of the performance of what is taught in the revelation.
Furthermore, when there is a discrepancy between Śruti and Smṛti, that Smṛti which is not contradicted by direct perception is accepted;
this Smṛti of ours is non-deviating from direct perception.
For it is by direct perception alone that the movement toward the north and south is observed, starting precisely from Capricorn, Cancer, and so forth.

How so? Because when the Blessed Sun, having dispelled the entire mass of darkness, is situated at the end of Sagittarius (Dhanus) and has reached the meridian, a greater midday shadow is observed than all other midday shadows.
And that [shadow] decreases gradually starting precisely from Capricorn and so forth,
not from Śraviṣṭhā and so forth;
and because, in Cancer and so forth, the midday shadow is smaller than all other midday shadows.
And since that [precession] increases gradually starting from Karkaṭa and so forth,
and not from the midpoint of Aśleṣā, the precession is thus established by direct perception;
or else, this passage is intended for another purpose altogether.
It is stated precisely because of the acceptance that the southern solstice begins with Cancer and the northern solstice begins with Capricorn:

"When the venerable Sun, having proceeded half-way along the southern path from the conjunction [of the equinox], abandons the fourth part of the *punarvasu* constellation [meaning Cancer and so forth], then there will be security, abundant crops, and plenty."
And when, having abandoned the path beginning with Capricorn (makara) and so forth, it enters the northern course beginning with Śraviṣṭhā, then it possesses that specific fruit.
Now, how does this Vivasvat proceed in this manner?
It is said: the motion of the planets is twofold.
It is both numerical and occasional.
When the occasional course (*autpātikī gati*) occurs in such a manner, then the two solstices (*ayana*) known as "secure," "abounding in grain," and "plentiful" occur.

However, when the commencement and cessation of the southern and northern courses occur without even reaching Cancer or Capricorn, this demonstrates that there will be insecurity, lack of grain, and scarcity.
Furthermore, regarding this matter, the Romakas—who do not know the ultimate truth—recite:
"The sages declared the solstice (ayana) to begin from the midpoint of Libra through the beginning of Taurus; yet how could that be observed without [a change in] motion?"
Thus,
by means of the opening passage and through the sequence of presenting the "scattering of the petty," they state the number of *yuga*-revolutions to be 1,894,110;
therefore, in this context, a *yuga* consists of [the digits] sky, Rudra, Kṛta, Nanda, and Dhṛti (1,894,110).
"From the asterisms known as twenty-seven and the Ādityas, [the solstices occur] in reverse and direct order from the end.
Here, how is this consistent if, whether in reverse or direct order, the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) begins from Aries and the other signs, rather than starting specifically from Cancer?
And likewise, the rainy season would begin from Aries, and spring from Capricorn.
And in that case, a reversal of the proper time would result;
thus, the meaning of the Vedic injunction would not be carried out, as in:
"One should sacrifice in the spring."
Caitra and Vaiśākha constitute spring;
as it is said, "Madhu and Mādhava are the two seasons of spring" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.4.11).
And likewise: "One should sacrifice with the Vājapeya in autumn."
The months of Aśvayuja and Kārttika constitute the autumn (śarad),
according to the passage: "Iṣa and Ūrja are the two autumnal seasons" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.4.11).
And this *ayana* of the luminaries is a limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda;
therefore, there is no movement of the *ayana* itself.
The term *ayana* refers to [the period] beginning with Capricorn and Cancer.
The teacher Lāṭadeva, the preceptor of all established doctrines, said: "The northern solstice begins with Capricorn, and the southern solstice begins with the sign of the Moon."

To determine the seasons, he said: The seasons— namely the dewy season (śiśira), spring (vasanta), summer (grīṣma), the arrival of clouds (ghanāgama), autumn (śarad), and the arrival of winter (himāgamana)—
are equal to the duration of the Sun’s transit through two zodiac signs starting from Capricorn (makara).
Thus it is said;
and furthermore: "The increase of departure [of the sun] occurs at the end of Dhanus and Mithuna alone.
The great increase of night and day occurs precisely at the beginning of Makara and Karkata.
It is not from any other source alone;
this is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, the calculation of the revolutions of the yugas is futile.
Now this must be asked: are they grasped by a swift motion or by a medium motion?
If it is by a medium motion, then those purposes which were stated for the solar mansions (sauryamāna) would be attained through a medium motion.
They are sought by means of their apparent motion.
What, then, are those purposes? It is said:
the modulation of the wind, the arising of clouds, and the strength of the eyes.
The occurrence of cold, heat, and rain, as well as the clarity of the water and its vegetation.
There shall be intoxication for living beings, as well as the seasonal menses for women;
there shall likewise be the emergence of fruits and flowers, and the growth of leaves and sprouts.
The observation of the solstices, the seasons, and the muhūrtas; likewise, the appearance of halos and the encircling of the sacrificial frames.
And likewise of cities of the Gandharvas,
as well as of rainbows, meteors, thunderbolts, and lightning during the two twilights.
[He knows] the earth, the roar of clouds, the falling of celestial hearths,
the differentiation of the colors of the luminaries, and the movements of the planets.
One should understand that the solar measure is the impeller and the restrainer of the dissolution and emergence of fire, heat, and the two powers.
These and others are the purposes [of the calculation].
If these purposes are grasped through the clear motion [of the planets], then this— namely, the apprehension of excesses and deficiencies— is not established.
Since the measurement of the greater and lesser [distances] is by means of the middle measurement,
how then will the statement of the clear meaning serve for the realization of the middle motion? Or, if it is for the realization of the middle motion, how is it a statement of the clear meaning?
This is not a fault:
"Canals are dug for the sake of irrigation,
and from them water is drunk."
And it is established by the rule "tāsu ca upaspṛśyate" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.22, Patañjali’s Bhāṣya),
because of the inclusion of both [the word *tāsu* and the word *upaspṛśyate*].
"Both are included here" means by way of both the mean motion (*madhyamagati*) and the true motion (*sphuṭagati*).

By the mean motion, the inclusion of the additive and subtractive corrections (*adhikāvamāna*) is established; and by the true motion, the purposes declared by the author of the *Saṃhitā* are fulfilled.
The conjunctions of the sun and the moon constitute the lunar months;
the conjunctions of the sun and the moon are "raviśaśiyogāḥ";
they become the lunar months.
Those conjunctions of the sun and moon that have been stated for the yugas are the lunar months;
and how those were previously established has already been explained.
By means of the lunar months, the lunar days and ghaṭikās have been explained.
Furthermore, what are the purposes served by the lunar month?

They are: the performance of the New Moon (darśa) and Full Moon (paurṇamāsa) sacrifices, as well as other ritual acts on earth; the thorough knowledge of the lunar nodes (parvan), and likewise the determination of the lunar days (tithi).
The potency of medicinal herbs and the manifestation of tastes,
as well as the waxing and waning of the moon, and likewise the ebb and flow of the salt ocean.
The duration of gestations, as well as the solar and lunar courses, and the occurrence of Rāhu’s approach— all these rely upon the measurement of the moon.
Such are the purposes [for which this is taught].
"Ravibhūyogāḥ" means days;
"ravibhūyogāḥ" refers to the conjunctions (yoga) of the Sun (ravi) and the Earth (bhū).
Those solar conjunctions that occur in a yuga are the terrestrial days (bhūdivasa) of that yuga.
A terrestrial day is defined as the period from one half-rise of the sun until the next half-rise;
it is called a *sāvana* day, or a terrestrial day.
That very day on earth is designated as "the rising of the sun" by means of the hair-pits.
Furthermore, what are the purposes of the solar (sāvana) measure? They are: the precise determination of the time for sacrifices and the performance of the *savanas* within those sacrifices.
The time for initiation into a vow, as well as the tonsure ceremony and the initiation into student life.
The calculation of lifespans, the increase of ritual applications,
the thorough knowledge of planetary movements, the journeys of the deities,
and whatever else is indicated by number— all these indeed [are to be known].
It is certain that they are calculated by means of the solar (sāvana) measurement alone.
These are the purposes;
and furthermore, "bhāvartāḥ" means those that revolve with the lunar mansions (nakṣatra),
for "bhāvartāḥ" are the revolutions of the lunar mansions.
Regarding the revolutions of the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*):
it must be investigated what its starting point (*ādi*) is.
If it were to begin with Aries (*meṣa*), then when the sun is situated in Aries, the sun and the beginning of the stellar sphere would rise simultaneously.

The second [view], however, holds that the rising of the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*) and so forth occurs precisely when the sun has not yet risen; nor is there a duration of sixty *nāḍīs* between the two risings of the stellar sphere and so forth.
And thus it is said: "By means of the breath, one [measures] a *kalā* of the asterism" (*Gītikā*).
Thus, the equality between the *liptās* of the zodiacal circle and the *liptās* that constitute the measure of the *ghaṭikās* of a day and night is not tenable,
because the wheel of the stars and so forth rises even before the day and night are complete.

Furthermore, when the rising of the sun and the like are taken as the revolution of the stellar sphere (bhacakra), then the breaths of a day and night are equal to the breaths of the rising of the zodiacal signs (rāśi) in one's own location;
and these are equal to sixty thousand (khakhaṣaḍghana). It is thus established that the minutes of arc (liptā) of the stellar sphere are also that many.
Furthermore, the rule for the ascendant at sunrise proceeds from the sun itself, and from the sun as it rises.
That [calculation], being considered from the sun’s sign at one's desired time until the next sunrise, does not introduce any discrepancy.
Therefore, the rising of the sun alone constitutes the beginning of the zodiacal circle and so forth,
for the sake of conventional usage.
If this is so, do the signs traversed by the planets not commence precisely from the portion of the sign occupied by the sun?
This is not a fault,
because these [meanings] are defined by [the rule] "from the birth of Budha, from the day, and from the rising of the Sun in Laṅkā" (Gītikāpāda 4).
Furthermore, since the cycles of the Kṛta age (kubhagaṇāḥ) are completed precisely from the sunrise at the beginning and end of the Yuga,
their commencement from Aja (the Unborn) is established.
These very cycles of the wheel of the Yuga are the sidereal days (nākṣatradivasāḥ), which are the terrestrial days (bhūdivasāḥ).
Because of the continuation of the mention of "day" (divasa).
But who are those *bhāvartas*? They are the *kubhagaṇas*.
“Ku ni śi buṇ lṛ ṣ khṛ” [1582237500] is stated in the *Gītikās* [Gītikās, 3]. How are these *kubhagaṇas* said to be *bhāvartas*?
The lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) are bound to the wheel of the stars (*bhacakra*).

Due to the projection of its [the Earth's] eastward motion, the stars reach the western direction; they perceive the Earth as if it were revolving toward the east by its own motion. By this mode of movement, the revolutions of the Earth are indicated; therefore it is said:
"The stellar revolutions are also those of the Earth."
Others, however, read: "And where are the asterismal whirlpools?
For according to their reading, everything is indeed logically consistent.
Now, others again explain it differently:
A lunar month consists of new moon to new moon; a solar month consists of thirty days;
a solar month is the transit through one zodiac sign; and a sidereal month is the period of the moon's revolution through the lunar mansions.
[Composed by Lāṭadeva:
Regarding the term *darśa*, it is lunar; that which is the closest conjunction of the sun and the moon is expressed by the word *darśa*, and that is their conjunction (*yoga*).
“The conjunctions of the sun and moon constitute lunar months”—this definition is the same [for both].
Furthermore, that “thirty days constitute a solar (sāvana) month” is also the same as saying “thirty sunrises.
And that “the solar [month] is the passage through a zodiacal sign by the sun” is the same as saying “the revolutions of the sun’s signs are solar years.”
“The zodiacal signs of the Sun are also solar months”—this is likewise a definition. “And the lunar orb is the sidereal [measure]”: thus, the orb of the Moon is a sidereal month.
In that regard, the daily motion of the Moon is—
That is a constituent part of that month.
The lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) are also divided accordingly:
for instance, one-thirtieth part of the moon’s revolution through the asterisms is a sidereal day (*nākṣatra-divasa*).

Thus, a tenth part of nine lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) constitutes a sidereal day; this is the identical definition. Our teacher has stated, "The rotations of the [zodiacal] signs are also sidereal," for the purpose of demonstrating a system that is not contradicted by other independent treatises. And what is this system of another independent treatise?

Regarding the statement, “By means of the breath (prāṇa), one goes to the sixteenth part (kalā) and the lunar day (bhā)” [Gītikā, 6], it means that one goes to the sixteenth part and the lunar day by means of the breath; thus, when there is an equivalence between the degrees (liptās) of the circle of luminaries and the breaths of the solar revolution (bhāvarta), the rules concerning the bow-strings (jyā) and so forth are established.
"It is not otherwise"— this is the method.
And for those for whom the definition is "the lunar orb is not a constellation," this was stated by them for the sake of accomplishing the purpose expressed by the form of the *saṃhitā*.
In this case, since the purpose is not encompassed by a single definition, these two definitions are accepted.
How so? Therein, "repetition" (āvṛtti) means "retention of one" (ekaśeṣa).
Because of the grammatical explanation [of the term] *bhāvarta* as a *ekaśeṣa* compound— namely, *bhāvartāśca bhāvartāśca* (both whirlpools and whirlpools), [resulting in] *bhāvartāḥ*—
the *bhāni* are the luminaries, Aśvinī and the rest;
their whirlpools are *bhāvartāḥ*.
The meaning is "the revolutions" (paryāya).
And by "revolution," only that which pertains to the moon in relation to the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) is understood,
according to common worldly usage.
For the world indeed conducts its affairs by means of the lunar mansions as occupied by the moon;
or else, what is undertaken for one purpose may also serve another purpose,
just as irrigation channels are constructed for the sake of rice.
And regarding them, it is said: “In those cases, [the action] is touched upon” (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.24;
Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya).

Alternatively, although it would have been established by the singular form "the Bhāvarta and the Nākṣatra," the Teacher’s use of the plural expression "the Bhāvartas and the Nākṣatras" indicates that the Nākṣatra has multiple characteristics.
Or else, the particle *ca* (and) is employed here [for this purpose].
No specific purpose is established here by that [statement],
yet we consider that because it has been employed, the definition of *akṣara* is not manifold;
and since that manifold definition has been explained exactly as it is established, therefore both definitions are established according to our own system (*svasiddhānta*).
Now, what are the purposes of the stellar measurement?
They are for the determination of the completion of years, months, seasons, lunar phases, and likewise all solar transits.
The auspicious and inauspicious [results] for people, as well as measurement (*māna*) and counter-measurement (*unmāna*), and so forth—these are the purposes [of the treatise].

Now, this statement, "of years, months, and seasons," is like a snare of words intended to frighten away the base; it does not appear to have any purpose other than those already demonstrated by the science of asterisms (*nakṣatra*).
For that duration of years, the lunar [reckoning] does not serve as the basis for determining the start of the first day (pratipad),
because in the authoritative treatises (śāstra), the year begins from the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra;
and that beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra is characterized by the lunar [month].

Furthermore, according to the authors of the *Saṃhitās*, regarding the movement of Jupiter (*bṛhaspaticāra*), there is a year which begins from the heliacal rising of Jupiter in a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
As it is said: "In whichever lunar mansion Aṅgiras rises, [that is the beginning of the year] for one who has gone abroad. This [reckoning] does not apply even to months.
The month in which the moon is conjoined with the Kṛttikās— both in that month and in that half-month— is the month of Kārttika.
That specific conjunction of the moon and the lunar mansion is a particular type of lunar month.
The knowledge of the seasons and the solstices by means of solar measurement has already been demonstrated by us;
therefore, this is not the sidereal measurement. For those who follow the statement, "And the sidereal is the lunar disc," [it follows that] "the revolutions of time are sidereal."

Thus, in explaining the meaning of this word, the use of a plural number for a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa-bahuvacana*)— on account of the word "and" (*ca*)— has caused only those wise ones who know the ultimate truth to undergo mental fatigue.
Therefore, that which was stated by our teacher Ācārya Āryabhaṭa, who perceives objects beyond the senses, is indeed the sidereal measure (*nākṣatramāna*).
Consequently, it has been well said: "This statement is a snare of words intended to frighten the ignorant; its true purpose is not perceived by those who have not demonstrated the sidereal measure.
Now, these measures—the solar, the civil (*sāvana*), the lunar, and the sidereal—are established according to mean motion.
It has been taught that for the sake of that purpose, they should be understood according to their true motion (*sphuṭagati*).
However, by the teacher Lāṭadeva, they were explained precisely according to their true motion:
from new moon to new moon is the lunar month, while thirty solar days constitute the civil (*sāvana*) month.
Thus, by the opening passage [of the text].

And here this question arises: "The day-count (dyugaṇa) without the omitted months (avamādhimāsaka). Having converted the elapsed years into months and added the current months, there is a rule of three (trairāśika): if by the solar months of a yuga the lunar months of a yuga are obtained, [then...]
Then, by means of these solar months, how many lunar months are there? The result obtained is the lunar months; these should be multiplied by thirty and joined with the current lunar day (tithi).

Then follows the rule of three proportions (*trairāśika*): if by the lunar days of a *yuga* the *yuga*-day-count (*ahargaṇa*) is obtained, then what is obtained by these [current] lunar days? Thus the day-count is obtained. In that case, there is one additive (*prakṣepa*). Now, what is it?
And is that a single addition?
It is said: that *ahargaṇa* which has been obtained is the past;
the remainder is the present.
One addition is that the *ahargaṇa* (accumulation of days) is produced by means of the current [day];
this will be explained later in the verse beginning with "by that, the sun and moon.
From these two, the observation of the true conjunction (*parva*) occurs.
The calculation of the true lunar day (*sphuṭatithi*) without reference to the moon and sun is as follows:

“If by the number of days in a *yuga* (the *yugāhargaṇa*) lunar years equal to 4,452,778—[that is,] the number of Vasus, Munis, Mountains, Yamas, Viṣayas, Kṛtas, and Vedas—are obtained, then how many years are obtained by this desired number of days?
Thus one calculates the years.
The remainder, when multiplied by twelve and so forth, yields the months, days, ghaṭīs, and vighaṭīs;

thus the mean lunar day (tithi) is obtained. Now, for the revolutions of the Moon’s apogee and perigee, there is a rule of three: if by the number of civil days in a yuga the revolutions of the Moon’s apogee and perigee are obtained, [then...]
Then, by means of this desired *ahargaṇa*, the number of elapsed revolutions is obtained;
in the remainder, when multiplied by twelve and so forth, the signs and other units are obtained.
The kendram of the Moon is subtracted by three signs;
from that, the result and the motion of the Moon are calculated.
By dividing the result by twelve, the nāḍīs and vināḍīs are obtained.
In the meantime, one should duly settle the debt or credit with the middle guest.

For the purpose of calculating the sun, the rule of three is as follows: if by the number of days of the *yuga* (the *yugāhargaṇa*) one obtains additional years equal to 13,27,78 (the sum of the Vasus, Munis, Mountains, Yamas, Fires, and Moons), then how many [additional years] are obtained by the number of days elapsed in the Kali age (*kaliyātāhargaṇa*)?

The years, months, days, and ghaṭikās are obtained. From each of the mean years, lunar days, and so forth, those [corrections] are to be subtracted; the remainder is the solar years and so forth. By subtracting two months and eighteen days from those, the solar apogee (ravikendra) is obtained.
From that, one should calculate the result and the quotient.
The result, divided by twelve, yields the *nāḍīs* and *vināḍīs*. One should apply the reversal of subtraction and addition to the lunar day (*tithi*) itself.
Now, why is this exchange of debt and wealth performed?
It is said: that which is the debt of the sun is the increase of the lunar day (tithi), and that which is its wealth is its decrease.
In this way, the lunar day (tithi) is established.
Then, this is performed: if sixty nāḍīs are obtained by means of the interval of the mean motion, [then...]
[Then], by means of the difference in true motion, how many [nāḍīs] are there?
Thus, the nāḍīs of the difference in motion are obtained.
By means of these, a rule of three (trairāśika) is applied: if sixty nāḍīs are obtained for these nāḍīs of the difference in motion, [then...]

Then, by means of this remainder of the lunar day (tithi), how many tithi-nāḍīs and vināḍīs are obtained? Alternatively, having divided [the calculation] into two proportions (trairāśika), this operation is performed:

the remainder of the lunar day is multiplied by the difference between the mean motions and divided by the difference between the true motions; the result, in ghaṭikās and vighaṭikās, is thus established.

How, then, are the two sets of three proportions (trairāśika) distinct? It is said: first, if sixty nāḍīs are obtained by means of the difference in mean motion, then how many are obtained by means of the difference in true motion? This is the first proportion. Furthermore, if sixty nāḍīs correspond to the result thus obtained, [then...]
[Then] by means of this remainder of the lunar day (*tithi*), how many [degrees] are there?
That which was the multiplier (*guṇakāra*) in the previous three-proportion calculation (*trairāśika*) is here, by implication, the divisor (*bhāgahāra*).
Furthermore, whatever result arises from the specific difference of longitude (*deśāntara*) and the specific difference of latitude (*akṣa*), that too must be applied according to reason. // 5 //

Regarding the intercalary months and omitted days: he spoke for the sake of fully understanding the intercalary months and omitted days— namely, those lunar months which, within a yuga, are in excess of the solar months.
The days of the moon, diminished by the days of the earth, are to be known as the destructions of the lunar dates (tithis). // 6 //
Those lunar months which are in excess of solar months become the intercalary months (adhimāsa) in each yuga;
and those lunar days which are fewer than terrestrial days become the destructions of lunar days (tithipralaya) in each yuga.
"Pralaya" means destruction.
The "destructions of lunar days" (*tithipralaya*) refers to the *avamārātras* (omitted days).
By stating this, it is demonstrated that the difference between the solar and lunar [calendars] constitutes the duration of the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*).
The solar day (*sāvana*) and the lunar measurement (*cāndra*) are both *sāvana* units.
It has been stated that the accumulation of intercalary and expunged days occurs through mean motion;
if it were by true motion, then when the second [lunar day] had commenced, the first would have ceased and the third would have begun.
They do not exist. What is accomplished by means of intercalary months and omissions?
He says: "The group of days (ahargaṇa).
This is not so.
This is not a fault, because the *ahargaṇa* is accomplished even without the intercalary months (*adhimāsa*) and omissions (*avama*),
as it is a different method.

The calculation of the *ahargaṇa* (the accumulated number of days) without the intercalary months (*adhimāsa*) and omissions (*avama*) has been demonstrated. That method by which the *ahargaṇa* is obtained through the intercalary months and omissions must now be shown.
This is not so.
Because there is a single means;
both that [attainment] and this [practice] are one means. How is there a single means?
Those which are lunar months are accompanied by additive days; because they possess these additives, the total of months obtained is likewise accompanied by additives.

Furthermore, because the terrestrial days are diminished by subtractive days, the *ahargana* (the sum of elapsed days) obtained through the rule of three (*trairāśika*) is likewise diminished by subtractive days.

Now, if someone seeking to simplify the calculation were to subtract the divisor from the multiplier, the quotient obtained by multiplying that remainder should be added to the product of the multiplicand and its reciprocal;

however, if there remains a surplus after subtracting from the divisor, the quotient obtained by multiplying that remainder should be subtracted from the product of the multiplicand and its reciprocal—this is the rule of calculation.
In this case, since the multiplier is greater [than the divisor], months are added, and since the divisor is greater [than the multiplicand], days are subtracted; thus, it is a single method.
Therefore, there is no purpose served by this verse;
nevertheless, for the sake of worldly convention,
the instruction regarding intercalary months and omitted days must be given.
And the world conducts its affairs by means of intercalary months and omissions [of days].
And it has been said: "One should calculate the intercalary month based on the *karaṇa*," and "The annual ritual consists of three hundred and fifty-four days and nights."

The rule of three for the purpose of finding intercalary months is as follows: if by the years or months of a yuga the intercalary months of a yuga are obtained, then how many are obtained by the elapsed years and so forth? This is the calculation for obtaining intercalary months.
In the same way, [the calculation] for omissions is performed using lunar days.
And here is this question: "By that [method], the sun and moon [are calculated]"—this refers to the calculation of the moon and sun without a series of elapsed days (*ahargaṇa*).
It is as follows: one should add the elapsed months to the years that have passed multiplied by twelve;

then, having added the days to those multiplied by thirty, there is a rule of three (*trairāśika*): if by [1,555,200,000] *yuga*-solar days—which correspond to the number of full sky, clouds, oceans, Yamas, arrows, and moon-phases—[the following results are obtained...]
The intercalary months of the yugas are obtained;
then, by these days, how many [intercalary months] are there? The result is the intercalary months.

The addition for the remainder is now stated: if by a remainder of omitted days equal to the number of terrestrial days one obtains an increase equal to the number of intercalary months in a yuga— that is, the remainder of the intercalary months—
then how much is obtained by this [given] remainder of omitted days?
Whatever is obtained, having added that to the remainder of the intercalary months (*adhimāsaka*), one divides by the *yuga* lunar months—[which are] 5343336—and the quotient is the degrees;
sixty times the remainder are the minutes (*liptā*).

Having made the heap of days increased by thirtyfold [the remainder], one performs a three-term proportion (*trairāśika*): if by the *yuga* lunar days the *yuga* omitted days (*avamadināni*) are obtained, [then...]
Then, what is obtained by these is subtracted.
The remainder is multiplied by sixty and divided by the terrestrial days, which take the form of 1,577,917,500; the result is the *ghaṭikās*.
Now, for what purpose is the division by lunar months and terrestrial days performed upon the remainders of intercalary months and omitted days?
It is said: that remainder of intercalary months is a fraction of a lunar month;
therefore, one applies the rule of three (trairāśika) with that [remainder] together with its divisor: if the solar revolutions are obtained by means of the lunar months of a yuga, [then...]
Then, [the question arises] how many [revolutions] there are by this fraction of a lunar month.

In that case, there is a reduction (apavartana) by means of the solar revolution together with the division of the lunar month: for the solar revolutions, the multiplier is one by the divisor of the solar revolutions;
for the division, it is three hundred and sixty by that same divisor.
In that context, since it does not yield a quotient among the zodiacal signs (*bhagaṇas*), twelve and thirty are the multipliers;
therein, by means of a divisor of three hundred and sixty, there is one unit (*rūpa*).
The form of the subtraction is likewise by that same proportion;
the lunar months alone are the divisors.

Since the remainder of the omitted days (*avamaśeṣa*) is also a fraction of terrestrial days, the rule of three (*trairāśika*) is as follows: if lunar days are obtained by means of terrestrial days, [then...]

Then, [the question is]: "What [is obtained] by this terrestrial day-part through the division of the lunar day? In that case, because the multiplier and the divisor are equal, they cancel each other out. When the remainder is multiplied by sixty and divided by the terrestrial days, the result is the *ghaṭikās*.
Then, having made the elapsed years the revolutions (bhagaṇas), the months the signs (rāśis),
and the days the degrees (bhāgas).
The ghaṭīs and liptās obtained from the subtraction are [the result];
one should subtract the amount obtained from the greater remainder from these.
The remainder is the mean sun.
From those very [constants] multiplied by thirteen, one should subtract the result of the greater remainder;
the remainder is the mean moon. By means of the intercalary months (*adhimāsaka*), the omissions (*avama*) are also brought forth.

For example: having converted the desired years into days, one applies the rule of three: "If by the solar days of a *yuga* the *adhimāsa*s (intercalary months) of a *yuga* are obtained, then by these desired solar days how many are obtained? Thus, the elapsed *adhimāsa*s are found.
And this is the remainder for the current [cycle].

This is the method of the three sets (*trairāśika*): if by the intercalary months of a *yuga* the omissions (*avamarātra*) of a *yuga* are obtained, then how many are obtained by these desired intercalary months? Having made them homogeneous according to the rules of calculation, one should multiply by the omissions of a *yuga*.

Alternatively, having multiplied both the desired intercalary month-quantity and the degree-quantity separately by the *yuga*-intercalary months, one divides the degree-quantity by the *yuga*-solar days and adds the result to the [intercalary month] above; then, the quotient obtained by dividing by the *yuga*-intercalary months gives the intercalary months for the desired time. Or, they may also be derived by breaking down two proportions (*trairāśika*): if the *yuga*-intercalary months are obtained by means of the *yuga*-solar days, [then...]
Then, there is one rule of three [proportions] to determine how many [intercalary months] correspond to the desired number of days.

Then again: "If by the intercalary months of a yuga the subtractive days (avamāḥ) of a yuga are obtained, then how many are obtained by the intercalary months produced from the quantities established by the method of the rule of three?"
In that case, in the first rule of three, the intercalary months of a yuga are the multiplier; in the second rule of three, they are the divisor.
Therefore, because the multiplier and the divisor are equal, they cancel each other out, and the result for the desired days is the number of omissions (avamas) in a yuga as the multiplier.

The number of solar days in a yuga is the divisor; the quotient obtained is the desired intercalary days (avamās). From these desired intercalary days, the intercalary months (adhimāsakas) are also calculated.

Having added the intercalary months that have arisen during the desired years and months, one multiplies by thirty and performs two proportional calculations (*trairāśika*): first, "If by the lunar days of a *yuga* the *yuga*-omissions (*avamā*) are obtained, then by the desired lunar days how many [omissions]? This constitutes one proportional calculation.

Furthermore, if the intercalary months are obtained by means of the *yuga*-intercalations, then how many [intercalary months] are obtained by the desired *avamās* (lunar days omitted) constructed through the previous rule of three (*trairāśika*)? In that case,
the *yuga*-intercalations are the multiplier (*guṇakāra*) in the previous rule of three.
In this case, there is a division.

Therefore, because the multiplier and the divisor are equal, they cancel each other out; thus, the number of days in a yuga is the divisor, and the number of intercalary months in a yuga is the multiplier.
The result is the desired intercalary months;
alternatively, it may be calculated separately for each by means of the rule of three (trairāśika) as before. Then, by means of those intercalary months, the desired planets are also brought forward.
For example: if the revolutions of the desired planet are obtained by means of the *yuga*-intercalary months, then how many are obtained by means of the desired intercalary months?
Thus, starting from the limit of the time of the occurrence of the intercalary month, the revolutions and other parameters of the desired planet are obtained.
That very [result] is made to correspond to the desired time.
How so? One should multiply the revolutions of the desired planet by the remainder of the intercalary months and divide by the lunar days multiplied by the intercalary months;
therein, the revolutions and so forth are obtained.
When those [values] are added to the previously obtained lunar months and planetary revolutions,
then it becomes the limit of time until the occurrence of the omitted nights (*avamarātra*).
Thereafter, one should again multiply the remainder of the omitted nights by sixty and divide by the lunar days (*śaśidivasa*) alone.
The result obtained is in *ghaṭikās*.
Then: "If the motion of the desired planet is obtained by sixty *ghaṭikās*, then what is obtained by these *ghaṭikās*? [Thus is the proportion set up.]
One should add what has been obtained from the previously established planet;

thus the planet is determined for the limit of the rising time of the desired day. Now, even by means of omitted days (*avamāni*), if the revolutions of the desired planet are obtained through the *yuga*-omitted days, then one calculates how many are obtained by the elapsed omitted days.

The desired revolutions and other parameters of a planet are obtained up to the limit of the time of completion of the omitted day (*avamarātra*); from that, the value for the sunrise of the desired day is calculated.
How so? One should multiply the desired planetary revolutions by the remainder of the omitted days and divide by the product of the number of omitted days in a *yuga*.
The resulting revolutions and so forth should be added to the previously obtained revolutions and so forth;
thus the planet becomes heliacal.
In this regard, there is this question:

"I shall become a disciple of him who calculates the omitted months by means of the omitted days, or who performs [the calculation] by means of the intercalary months, or who has desired the planetary positions through those two. (1)

The calculation of the sun and the moon by means of the accumulated intercalary months and the remainder of omitted lunar days has been stated. Now, the calculation of all the planets shall be explained from the remainder of omitted lunar days alone.
It is as follows: the number of omitted lunar days in a yuga (yugāvamam), divided by sixty, results in the following arrangement: 418043.

Now, regarding the calculation for bringing the sun [into alignment], these reduced *avamāsa* (omission days), multiplied by some factor, are subtracted from the reduced solar revolutions; the remainder should then be divided by the reduced terrestrial days (*bhūdināni*).
Thus, the *kuṭṭākāra* (pulverizer) method is performed.
Therein, the quotient obtained as the *kuṭṭākāra* is 7147, which in figures is also 87617.
Having multiplied this by the remainder of the [current] year,
one should divide it by the reduced number of civil days;
the remainder therein is the solar remainder of the cycle.
By this, the bringing forward of the Ādityas is explained. The indicator [of the remainder] is as follows:
it has the measure of six, seven, five, one, five, seven, zero, and two; it is the remainder of the accumulated omissions (avamajāta).
By this, the remainder [of the revolutions] of the solar orbs is to be stated; and Vivasvat [is to be stated as having] a number ending in the digit six. (2)
The remainder of the divisor is 20,751,576.
The quotient is the remainder of the solar mandala, 49,665, and the sun is 2;24,58 (2 days, 24 ghaṭīs, 58 palas).
The calculation of the pulverizer for the moon is also exactly as before.

By what [multiplier] are the reduced omissions multiplied so that, when subtracted from the reduced lunar revolutions, they yield a quotient with respect to the reduced terrestrial days? By the method of pulverizer (*kuṭṭākāra*), the result obtained is the pulverizer:
2,119,236. This is the calculation for determining the moon using the given remainder of the omissions.

Alternatively, having converted the elapsed revolutions from the mean sun into minutes of arc, one performs a rule of three: "If by the minutes of arc of the sun in a *yuga* the lunar revolutions in a *yuga* are obtained, then by these elapsed solar minutes how many [revolutions] are obtained?
The result is the revolutions.
In the remainder multiplied by twelve and so forth, the mean Moon is obtained.
Alternatively, when the *yuga* solar *liptās* have been reduced by the factor of sixty thousand (*khakhaṣaḍghana*), then the solar revolutions become the divisor,
and the lunar revolutions become the multiplier for the elapsed solar *liptās*.
The result is the minutes of the mean moon.
Thus, by this method, the desired planet is derived from the moon or from any other desired planet.
How so? When the degrees of the desired planet are the multiplier and the known revolutions of that planet in a yuga (or its degrees) are the divisor, the result is the [revolutions or] degrees.
Herein lies this question:
He who, by means of the moon’s position, establishes the stars and planets from the sun,
is called the foremost of those who know time, even though he is devoid of our established system.
Thus [ends section] 6.
[The measures of years for humans, ancestors,
and gods] In order to determine the measure of years for humans, ancestors, and gods, he says: A human year, when multiplied by thirty, becomes a year of the ancestors (pitrya).
Twelve times the paternal year is declared to be one divine year.
The solar year (*ravivarṣa*):
the year of the sun is the solar year.
And the measure of the solar year has been stated: "The revolutions of the sun are the solar years" (*Kālakriyā*, 5).
The revolution of the sun's asterism is a year for humans;
that which is a year for the sun is indeed a year for humans.
That same [year], multiplied by thirty, becomes a year of the ancestors (pitrya).
That human year multiplied by thirty becomes a year of the ancestors (pitrya), because for them a month is a single day and night.
And it has been said: "The ancestors [have their day and night] in half a lunar month" (*Kālakriyā*, 17).
A year of the ancestors multiplied by twelve is declared to be a divine year;
that which is a year of the ancestors, when multiplied by twelve, becomes one year of the gods.
Since a month of the ancestors is a year of the gods, the years of humans, ancestors, and gods are, respectively, thirty-one, sixty, and three hundred times [the solar year]. (7)
[The measure of a yuga and the duration of a day of Brahmā:
In order to explain the four yugas and the day of Brahmā, he says: A thousand divine years constitute a yuga common to all the planets; it is multiplied by twelve.
One thousand and eight [revolutions] of the planetary yugas constitute one divine day.
This divine year, multiplied by twelve thousand, is the *yuga* common to the planets (*grahasāmānya*). "Common to the planets" means shared by the planets;
what is that? It is the *yuga*.
Since all the planets together with their apogees are simultaneously at the junction of Pisces and Aries,
therefore the *yuga* is common to all the planets; and that is 4,320,000— the sky, the ether, space, zero, Yama, Rāma, and the Vedas.
This very [calculation] is the measure of the years of the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages. For us, however, all the quarters of the yuga are equal in duration;
yet by the Paurāṇikas, they have been explained as having different durations.
They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the other three [ages], along with their junctions and sub-junctions,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.
[Manusmṛti, 1.69–70] Thus:
the measure of the Kṛta age is sky, sky, sky, ether, earth, Yama, sage, and moon [1,728,000];
the measure of the Tretā age is sky, sky, sky, taste, nine, sun [1,296,000].
The measure of the Dvāpara age is 8,640,000 (viyad-ambara-ākāśa-veda-rasa-vasu).
The measure of the Kali age is 432,000 (viyad-ambara-ākāśa-yama-rāma-veda). The years elapsed [of the current Kali age] are 4,320,000 (viyad-ambara-ākāśa-śūnya-yama-rāma-veda).

What, then, is correct here: should one understand it as the authors of the Purāṇas have explained—namely, that the Kṛta and other ages possess distinct measures—or rather as our own Teacher has established—that they possess equal measures? He says: "It is just as they are well-known to us."

If the measures of the yugas established by the methods of the Purāṇas were accepted, then at the beginning of the Kali Yuga, the planets would not simultaneously be at the junction of Pisces and Aries by their mean motion.
Why is this so? It is explained as follows.
The measure of three yugas in one place is 8,880,000— namely, viyat (0), ambara (0), ākāśa (0), aṣṭa (8), vasu (8), vasu (8), and rāmā (3)—
and having produced the *ahargaṇa* by these means, the mean planets are not obtained at the junction of Pisces and Aries according to the prescribed procedure for mean planetary calculation.
By this very method, even now, while the motion of the planets is being calculated, the motion of the desired planets is not obtained.
If, however, the measure of the Kṛta and other ages were indeed equal, then the measure of all three yugas together would be: sky, ether, space, void, Kṛta, Yama, and Agni [3,240,000].
By this path, everything desired is established;
therefore, it is well said: "Just as things are well-known to us.
A thousand and eight [years] constitute a day of Brahmā, which is the age of the planetary conjunctions.
Regarding the phrase "the pair of planets" (*grahayugam*), that which is the general period of the planets (*grahasāmānyam yugam*) is here intended.
When that is multiplied by one thousand and eight, it constitutes the measure of one day of Prajāpati. But is this not also in contradiction with the Purāṇas?
How so? By the knowers of ancient lore:
"Those people who know that the day of Brahmā extends for a thousand yugas, and whose night likewise ends after a thousand yugas—they are the ones who truly understand day and night."
Thus, in the Bhagavadgītā (8.17), it is stated that the measure of a day of Brahmā is a thousand yugas;
and here, it is specified as one thousand and eight four-yuga cycles.
In this regard, the following is considered:

after the Purāṇikas have stated, "Those who know that the day of Brahmā extends for a thousand yugas," they themselves have declared that seventy-one cycles of four ages (caturyuga) constitute a Manvantara, and that fourteen Manus comprise a single day of Brahmā.
In this case, seventy-one multiplied by fourteen does not reach the number of one thousand;
yet it is stated that "fourteen manvantaras are a day of Brahmā" and "a thousand cycles of four yugas [constitute a kalpa]," which is a contradiction of one's own statement.
For us, however, a *manvantara* consists of seventy-two *caturyugas*, and one thousand and eight [such periods] constitute a day of Brahmā; this is established by reasoning.
But how is it known that a *manvantara* consists of seventy-two *caturyugas*?
Because it is well-stated in the Gītikās:
"Kāhaḥ are the Manus, and Ḍha are the Manuyugas; Śkha. [Gītikā, 5] // 8 //
[The division of the ages such as the *utsarpiṇī*:
To explain the *utsarpiṇī*, *apasarpiṇī*, *suṣamā*, and *duṣṣamā* [ages], he says:
"The *utsarpiṇī* consists of half a *yuga*, and subsequently the *apasarpiṇī* consists of the other half of a *yuga*."
In the middle of the Yuga there is Suṣamā; at the beginning and at the end, there is Duṣṣamā, [measured] from the apogee of the Moon. // 9 //
That period in which the lifespan, fame, vigor, happiness, and so forth of living beings increase is designated as the *utsarpiṇī*. Its measure is half a *yuga*;
that is, half of a *yuga* is "half-a-yuga" (*yugārdham*).
The *yuga* has indeed already been explained.
Its measure in terms of half-counts is the *utsarpiṇī*: 21,600,000 [years], consisting of zero, sky, space, void, taste, moon, and two;
thereafter follows the *apasarpiṇī*, which is half a *yuga*.
By the word "afterwards" (paścāt), he indicates the period of the aeon of decrease (apasarpiṇī-kāla) following the aeon of increase (utsarpiṇī-kāla).
For the designation "afterwards" applies to that which occurs subsequent to what has previously proceeded;
[it refers] to that in which [the conditions of] living beings [deteriorate].
That period during which lifespan, fame, vigor, happiness, and so forth decline is known as the *apasarpiṇī* (descending) era.
Its measure is the latter half of a *yuga*, namely 2,160,000 years—[expressed as] sky, ether, space, zero, taste, moon, and twins.
And thus, in the middle of the *yuga*, there is the beginning of the *suṣama* (perfectly happy) age, while at the end, there is the *duṣṣama* (misery) age.
In the middle of its first half are the periods of Suṣamā and Duṣṣamā;
at the beginning and at the end [of that half],
there is Suṣamā at the beginning and Duṣṣamā at the end.
The measure of the *suṣamā* and *duḥṣamā* periods is one-fourth of a *yuga*.
How so? Because of the statement "in the middle";
half of a *yugārdha* is one-fourth of a *yuga*.
Regarding the division of the *yugas* for the purpose of calculation, he says: "From the Moon's apogee.
This means that these periods of *utsarpiṇī*, *apasarpiṇī*, *suṣamā*, and *duṣṣamā* are to be understood from the *yuga* produced from the Moon's apogee.
Now, why is it said "from the Moon's apogee"?
But has it not been stated that "yuga" refers to the generality of the planets?
True.
It is thus:
there is a difference in the *yugas* due to the specific reduction of the *pratigrahas*.
For example: the orbs of the sun are six, seven, and five [576].
The *yuga* of the Moon is 9, 8, 3, 0, 1, and 2 by the measure of its days;
the *yuga* of the Sun is 5, 3, 4, 6, 5, 5, 2, and 5 by the measure of its days.
The same applies to the others as well.
Now, what is the definition of a *yuga*?

It is said: from the moment the planet begins its course at Laṅkā on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra when the sun has half-risen, at the junction of Pisces and Aries, until it reaches that same junction of Pisces and Aries on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra when the sun has half-risen at Laṅkā—by that much [time]...
