One attains it at the proper time; that time is called a *yuga*. And it has been said: "When the sun is at the equinox and half-risen at the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra, there is the attainment of the [solar year] starting from Aries and ending in Pisces, in exactly such a manner."

Thus, in eras with differing beginnings, the method for achieving one-pointed concentration has been stated by means of the *kuṭṭākāra* (pulverizer) method, beginning with: "Someone is one-pointed by two [units] and two-pointed by three," and so forth.
Alternatively, from the cause that is the lunar apogee (*indūcca*), the elapsed and remaining portions of the *utsarpiṇī*, *apasarpiṇī*, *suṣamā*, and *duṣṣamā* ages are to be understood.
But how is it understood that the thorough knowledge of what has been traversed and what remains to be traversed has the apogee of the Moon as its cause?

It is said: by means of the *kuṭṭākāra* (pulverizer) calculation, because the revolutions of the lunar apogee, the years of a *yuga*, or the days of a *yuga*, assume the roles of the dividend and the divisor for the remainder of the lunar apogee's attainment.
For example, in this matter,
it is conceptualized by the teacher as follows:
when the three zodiacal signs beginning with Aries have passed for the lord of the nights (the Moon).
Then, let it be quickly calculated for me how much of the age has passed, as well as the total number of years and days remaining.

The elapsed period of the year (*varṣāgra*) is zero, sky, sky, void, one, four, three, one, and three [32,400,000]; and the elapsed number of days (*dināgra*) is five, arrows, sun, Vasus, fire, Vedas, Rāmas, Vasus, and Rudras [1,183,438,125].
Alternatively, there is this other method: the *utsarpiṇī* is half a *yuga*.
It is called *utsarpiṇī* because it rises upward;
the meaning is that it increases.
What is this *utsarpiṇī*?
The term "planetary motion" (grahabhuktiḥ) is to be supplied [as the subject]. Furthermore, for how long a period is that [motion] progressive (utsarpiṇī)? He says: "for half a yuga" (yugārdham).
A *yuga* is so called because the planets are joined together (*yujyante*) within it.
And by that, the circle of constellations itself is intended,
because within a single mandala the conjunction of a planet with other planets is possible;
half of that yuga is a *yugārdha*.
Six *rāśis*;
thereafter, the descending eon (*apasarpiṇī*) for half a *yuga*;
and thereafter again, the descending eon for half a *yuga*.
"Thus" means "the six groups.
"In the middle of the age" (yugasya madhye) means "in the interval within that age."

"Suṣamā," when reckoned from the beginning and from the end, means "perfectly auspicious"; that is to say, it is auspicious at the beginning of one quarter and at the end of the other. [At the beginning and at the end] Duṣṣamā is observed.
"In another manner" is the completion of the sentence.

How, then, are these—the periods of increase (utsarpiṇī), decrease (apasarpiṇī), the age of perfect happiness (suṣamā), the age of misery (duṣṣamā), and the period of intense suffering (agrahabhukti)—to be understood? To this he says: "From the Moon's apogee," meaning from the center of the Moon.
For example, when the center of the moon is at three signs, two degrees, and twenty-eight minutes,
from that point onward the mean motion increases until the center has become six signs.

Therefore, from that point, there is a decrease in the accumulated traversed portions of the six signs starting from the center in reverse order, until the center amounts to eight signs, twenty-seven degrees, and thirty-two *liptās*. These very same [portions], when calculated in reverse order from the end of the second quadrant, are equal; thus, there is equality at both the beginning and the end.
Alternatively, at the beginning and at the end,

the traversed portions (bhukti) starting from the center indicated by the second quadrant in direct order are equal to those traversed portions starting from the center indicated by the third quadrant in reverse order;
the same applies to the fourth and first quadrants as well.
Thus, there is the *suṣamā* (golden age) at the beginning and at the end;
otherwise, it is the *duṣṣamā* (age of strife).
Here, with reference to Indu and Indra, the teacher has demonstrated the *utsarpiṇī*, *apasarpiṇī*, *suṣamā*, and *duṣṣamā* eras.
This procedure is to be applied to the other planets as well.
For example: when the center of the Sun is at three signs plus fifty-four minutes of arc, then the hypotenuse (karṇa) of the Sun is equal to its semi-diameter.
And the mean motion is as follows:
when eight signs, twenty-nine degrees, and six minutes have elapsed, then too the hypotenuse is equal to the radius, and the motion is mean.

For Mars and the others as well, the distance between the earth and the planet is equal to half the circumference of their orbit; this will be stated in the verse: "[Those moving in the concentric circles and eccentric orbits] [Kālakriyā, 17]. // 9 //
[The time of Āryabhaṭa’s birth: To inform us of the time of his own birth, the teacher Āryabhaṭa says: "When sixty times sixty years and three quarters of a yuga have elapsed..."
At that time, twenty-three years had passed here since my birth. // 10 //
Sixty times sixty years;
the meaning is that sixty years multiplied by sixty have passed.
When [they] have elapsed.
When— at which time—
the three *yuga-pādas* have passed, that is, have elapsed.
The "feet of the yuga" (yugapāda) are the quarters of the yuga;
and when those have passed, numbering three—
that is, twenty increased by three— years.
Twenty increased by three is twenty-three years;
"then" means at that time.
The years elapsed since my birth are these very same ones that the teacher Āryabhaṭa proclaimed to Pāṇḍuraṅgasvāmin, Lāṭadeva, Niśaṅku, and others at the time of explaining this treatise.
Now, it must be asked here: what benefit does its explanation provide?
It is said: by means of this past time being fully understood, the time of the sun and other celestial bodies—whether past or future—is easily recited;
and yet, because the tradition has not been interrupted, the elapsed time is recognized.
This is not so.
Much is to be remembered here regarding the non-mentioning [of the Kali age]:
the number of years for the three yugas taken together is zero, sky, space, ether, Vedas, Yama, fire, and fire [3,240,000]; and this is the time elapsed of the Kali age.
When one [name] is mentioned, no *ara* (intercalary period) need be made for so many [years], because the continuity of the tradition (*sampradāya*) has lasted that long.
However, the continuity of this very tradition must be understood to extend through the time subsequent to the limit of the Teacher’s birth.
Furthermore, the purpose for mentioning "sixty times sixty years" will be explained later.
This is his intention: the sum of days (*ahargaṇa*) must be calculated from the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga;
otherwise, an additive correction (*kṣepa*) arises for the Moon’s apogee and node.
However, when the sum of days is calculated from the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, there is no additive correction at all for the Moon’s apogee and node.
“From the sunrise on Wednesday in Laṅkā” [Gītikāpāda 4];
thus, the day-count (ahargaṇa) begins from Wednesday and determines the weekday.
Now, however, for the sake of practical application in abbreviated calculation (laghugaṇita), the day-count of the Kali Yuga is computed.
The day of the week begins with Venus;
the Moon's apogee consists of three signs, and [the Sun's] six signs.
And the latitude of Rāhu is subtracted from the orb of Tamas because it is contrary [to the direction];

or else, the Tamas as obtained from the astronomical manual (karaṇa) itself is added to the desired true moon, and the calculation of the latitude is performed according to the rule for the south and north directions.

Now, when the *ahargaṇa* has been determined, the calculation of planetary motion is as follows: if by the *yuga-ahargaṇa* the revolutions (*bhagaṇas*) of the planets as stated in the *Gītikā* are obtained, then by this [present] *ahargaṇa*, how many are obtained?
The quotient is the revolutions already completed.
When the remainder is multiplied by twelve and so forth, the mean planet in signs and other units is established.
Now, here the Romakas calculate the sun by means of annual corrections,
and from that sun they derive all the other planets;
this [method] is also to be demonstrated here.

For instance, that which is called the annual correction (*pratyabda-śodhana*) begins from the half-rising (*ardhodaya*) on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra and extends until the time of the sun's transit across the solar disc at sunrise. At the end of a *yuga*, the number of days is determined by the solar revolutions (*ravibhagaṇa*) of the *yuga*, which serve as the standard for the desired calculation. Just as a rule of three (*trairāśika*) is performed using the desired solar revolutions, so too is it done here.

For example: "If by the number of solar revolutions in a yuga the count of terrestrial days is obtained, then by the desired solar revolutions how much [of that] is obtained?"—thus the *ahargaṇa* (accumulated day-count) is obtained;
when the remainder is multiplied by sixty and so forth, the *ghaṭikās* and so on are obtained. Thus, the *ahargaṇa* is obtained with the limit being the time of the completion of a solar revolution.

Therefore, the *ahargaṇa* completed at the end of the year [starting] from the white fortnight of Caitra is subtracted; henceforth, from the beginning of the white fortnight of Caitra, there will be the time limits for the completion of the solar revolutions (*ravibhagaṇa*).

Alternatively, by means of the *ahargaṇa* ending with the end of the year, one applies the rule of three (*trairāśika*): if by the *ahargaṇa* of four *yugas* the solar revolutions equal to "sky-flower" (*khughṛ*) are obtained, [then...]
By this *kalpīkṛta* day-count (*ahargaṇa*), the number of revolutions (*bhagaṇas*) is obtained as the quotient.
From the remainder, having determined the elapsed and remaining portions, the days are obtained by dividing the elapsed and remaining *rāśis* by the solar revolutions of a *yuga*.
When the remainder is multiplied by sixty and so forth, the *ghaṭikās* and subsequent units are obtained.

The days and so forth, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, constitute the periods until the completion of the solar revolution (bhagaṇa), whether reckoned above or below [the starting point]. This very method of annual correction has been explained by us in an even more concise manner in our *Karmapaddhati*. It is as follows:
Having multiplied by the Rudras (eleven), the thousand-fold six parts (six thousand),
and having added years equal in number to the cavities (nine), the Vasus (eight), and fire (three),
one should always calculate by dividing by thirty.
The months and days remaining after the subtraction are as follows.

Having combined [the result] with the deficiencies and impurities, one should divide by the portion of Rāma (3); then, having multiplied by fire, Vedas, and qualities (343), one should again divide by sky, void, sky, and twice the sages (70000).
These are the *pralayas* of the lunar days (*tithis*).
Having combined [them], divide by the number of days in a year (360), which is the product of the elements (5), Yama (2), and Rudra (11).
When the years are multiplied by the moon [one] and the intercalary months [nine],
and divided by six, seven, and five, the result is obtained in days and so forth;
these, when added to the years multiplied by ten, constitute the designation.
It is my firm conviction that the sons of the Sun attain this.
The omitted days (avamāḥ) obtained here should always be added to the Sundays; one should subtract from them the intercalary months multiplied by thirty.
Whatever remains is what must be subtracted from the year.
"If that [remainder] is greater than the [maximum] correction, it must indeed be subtracted"— thus it is taught.
[Mahābhāskarīya, 1.22–23,
27–28] Having thus brought forth the annual correction, the sun is then calculated from that.
How so? This too has been stated therein:

"From the day of Madhu (Caitra), whichever group of days is progressively diminished, the remainder taken by the celestial bodies (the planets) constitutes the weekday, the lunar day, the year, and so forth."
Therefore, this too must be purified;
that which falls short or exceeds the equal [measure] is to be corrected, and nothing else is accepted here.
"The days and so forth are increased by seventy and divided by five; the resulting vighaṭikās are doubled.
The body of the planet, as well as the Sun, Mercury, and Venus, are declared to be diminished by that amount.
[Mahābhāskarīya, 1.30–31]
Thus the sun is established.
Therefore, the signs traversed by the sun are added to the revolutions multiplied by twelve;
then, the degrees are added to those multiplied by thirty.
Thus the solar day-count (sūryāhargaṇa) is established.
The Sun traverses a degree equal to that solar day-count.
Now follows the calculation of the daily motion of all the planets in solar days.
The solar years of a *yuga* multiplied by three hundred and sixty are the solar days of a *yuga*.

If, by these [days], the revolutions of the desired planet are obtained, then how many [revolutions] are there in one solar day? By this method of the rule of three (*trairāśika*), [the result is] the planetary motion expressed in revolutions.
In the calculation of signs, degrees, and minutes, the multipliers are twelve, thirty, and sixty;
their product is one followed by six zeros (khakhaṣaḍghana).
Therefore, when the product of one followed by six zeros is divided by another one followed by six zeros, the result is one.
By dividing the days of the *yuga* (the product of the sun and days) by the portion of sixty thousand multiplied by six hundred, one obtains seventy-two thousand;

thus, by dividing the respective planetary revolutions by these seventy-two thousand, the daily motions of the planets in terms of solar days are obtained, and they are written down as found: for the Moon, [the motion] is twenty-two *liptās* and eight hundred and ninety-four parts of three thousand *liptās*.
For Mars, the *liptās* are thirty-one; the parts of three thousand *liptās* are fifty-seven. For Jupiter, the *liptās* are five; the parts of three hundred and seventy-five *liptās* are twenty-two.
For Saturn, the slow-moving planet, the *liptās* are two; the parts of eighteen thousand *liptās* are one hundred and sixty-one.
The minutes of Mercury’s exaltation are nine; its six-thousandth parts are one hundred thirty-four.
Those of Venus are thirty-seven; its six-thousandth parts are three thousand nine hundred nineteen.
In this manner, one should multiply the solar day-count (*ahargaṇa*) by the recorded daily motions of the sun and the planets;
then, having added the result obtained through the rule of three (*trairāśika*) using the sun's motion in *liptās*, one should divide by sixty thousand (khakhaṣaḍghana).
The remainder is the *liptās* traversed by the planet.

In this regard, the specific distinction is as follows: for the Moon, the additive correction (kṣepa) for the Sun is thirteenfold; for the exaltation of Mercury, it is fourfold; and for the exaltation of Venus, it is multiplied by one.
This calculation for determining all the planets without exception has been demonstrated in an even more concise manner in the *Karmanibandha*;
it should be understood from that very source. // 10 //
[The exposition on the infinity of time beginning with the Yugas:
To demonstrate the infinity of the progression of time, he says:
"The Yugas, years, months, and days began simultaneously from the start of the bright fortnight of Caitra."
This time, which is without beginning or end, is inferred by means of the planets within the field.
The *yuga*, the year, the month, and the day—these are the *yuga-varṣa-māsa-divasāḥ*;
the meaning is that these commenced simultaneously, or began at one and the same time.
To the question "Why?", he says: "From the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra."
The month of Caitra; its bright fortnight; the beginning of that bright fortnight.
The meaning is that it is "half-risen" (*ardhodaya*);
therefore, those "beginnings of the ages" (*yugādi*) which start from the white fortnight of Caitra and so forth have commenced simultaneously.
But surely, when the beginning of the age proceeds from the white fortnight of Caitra and so forth, all [the beginnings of the ages] would likewise proceed simultaneously?
Therefore, let it be that the yuga commenced from the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra;
to this he says "no," because in another treatise the commencement of the year and so forth is stated to be from another [point].
In the first part belongs Vāsava; in the second part, however, belongs Aja;
in the third part belong the Revatīs; and in the fourth part belongs Yama.
In the first portion of Saumya, in the second portion of Vasu,
in the third portion of Sārpa, and in the fourth portion of Bhaga.
In the first portion of Tvāṣṭra, in the second portion of Viśākhā,
in the third portion of Aindra, and in the fourth portion of Āpya.
"When Bṛhaspati, the lord of the Samānas, has risen from there,
or when he rises at the end of his own portion (aṃśaka), the first revolution (paryaya) occurs.
Thus, the commencement of the years is exceedingly different [from the solar year].
And when that commencement of the year has been divided, the commencements of the month and the day likewise become divided.
Or rather, it might be thus: this commencement of the years has been taught in various ways by the authors of the Saṃhitās for the sake of [specific] results;
it is not well-known in the world.
It does not apply to dependent phenomena (*paratantra*).
Therefore, [the opponent argues] that what is intended will be the apprehension of that activity which is well-known in the world and among dependent phenomena;
but this too is not correct.

For example, in Surāṣṭra, the commencement of the months, days, and years occurs on the first day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, and their cessation occurs on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvayuja; likewise, in Magadha, the commencement of the months, days, and years occurs on the first day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha.
The cessation occurs on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha.
Accordingly, it is also stated in the *Arthaśāstra*: "The annual work period consists of three hundred and fifty-four days;
one should pay this [wage] at the conclusion of the month of Āṣāḍha, whether it be deficient or complete."
It was composed by Siṃharāja in the Sahasrākṣara [script] at the rising of the sun in Laṅkā on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, on a Monday;
it marks the beginning of the Yuga, calculated from the time of Śakendra when one thousand years had elapsed.

Thus, it is already established that the commencement of the beginning of the yugas and so forth occurs at the start of the bright fortnight of Caitra; however, what must now be asked is this: was the month ending with the bright fortnight not established by Siṃharāja in his independent treatise?

And likewise, in common worldly usage, it is well known as ending with the bright fortnight; even in the *Horā* [astrological] system, the month from the ninth division conjoined with the Moon is named after the end of the bright fortnight.

To this it is replied: As for that which was stated by Siṃharāja, it was conceived according to his own intention as follows: because the intercalary months and the omitted months proceed simultaneously, the year is defined as having its beginning from the full moon of Āṣāḍha and its conclusion at the fourteenth day [of the following month].
Even if it is said that "the month ending with the bright fortnight (śuklānta) is well-known in the world," that is not so;
for there are indeed months in all regions,
and there exist countries such as Surāṣṭra and others where the conventional usage of the month ending with the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇānta) prevails.

As for what is also said— "The month [is determined] from the ninth part associated with the moon, and its name is the same as that of the end of the bright fortnight"— this too has quite another meaning.
From the ninth division conjoined with the Moon, the month of the querent should be declared;
it is similar to the name [of the querent],
for the name of the month is indeed known by its ending in the bright fortnight (*śuklānta*).
"When the moon is conjoined with the Kṛttikās, this being so, it is the month of Kārttika," and so forth.
Furthermore, by means of a month ending with the bright fortnight (śuklānta), the planets would never be at the junction of Pisces and Aries at the end of the month or the year.
Regarding this, the Lord of the Yavanas says:
When the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipat) has begun in the month, the moon possesses weak strength for ten days;
thus, the month begins with the bright fortnight (śuklādi).
When, moreover, the month begins with the bright fortnight, then the meaning of the Vedic revelation (śruti) is duly observed.
For it is recited thus in the Śruti:
"This indeed is the first night of the year, namely the full moon of Phālguna which is the later one. [If] the month were to begin with the first day of the dark fortnight, [this would not be so].
In that case, how could this Uttarā Paurṇamāsī be Phālgunī,
such that it would be the month of Caitra?
Why?

On the full moon day of Phālguna, the month of Phālguna is complete; at that time, it is the full moon of the following month, Caitra, because the month begins with the first day of the dark fortnight.
Therefore, we consider that even now the month of Phālguna has not yet come to an end; for he said:
"The full moon day of Phālguna which is the later one."
And furthermore: on that new moon day of Vaiśākha, one should establish the sacred fires;
it coincides with the asterism Rohiṇī.
[Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa, 11.1.1.7].
If the month is reckoned as ending with the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa), then there is no conjunction of the moon with the Rohiṇī asterism on the new-moon day (amāvāsyā) of Vaiśākha.
Because the moon is joined with the constellation Citrā on the full moon day of Caitra,
when that Caitrī full moon has passed, it is the first day (pratipad) of Vaiśākha; and from then on,
as the first day and subsequent days are counted through the constellations beginning with Svāti, the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is joined with the constellation Bharaṇī, not Rohiṇī.
If it is argued that this is due to a specific movement of the moon, [we say] no;
for the decrease and increase occur in the entirety of one lunar mansion,
not in two lunar mansions.
Furthermore, when the bright fortnight of the month has begun and the full moon of Vaiśākha has passed, there will be the new moon of Vaiśākha itself.
Then, as the days beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight are counted through the asterisms starting with Anurādhā, the conjunction of Rohiṇī with the new moon becomes possible.
And furthermore:
"In the dark fortnight, he enters the waters and the plants.
Thus it is said.
The *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* [11.1.5.3] reads as follows:
"In that context, the latter fortnight is the dark one (*kṛṣṇa*), not the bright one (*śukla*).
And there is another statement from the *Smṛti*:

"One should perform the śrāddha in the latter fortnight, or after the fourth [lunar day]. In this context, because it refers to a month beginning with the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇādimāsa), the "former" fortnight is the dark one,
and the "latter" is the bright one.

Because the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) comes first, the rule for the ancestral rites (śrāddha) would apply only to the bright fortnight and not to the dark one; yet it is desired that they be performed during both.
Therefore, the month begins with the bright fortnight.

Then, regarding the statement: "The yugas, years, months, and days began simultaneously from the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra," one should observe that this presents a hypothetical objection (*pūrvapakṣa*). Since the yugas and so forth would begin from the start of the bright fortnight of Caitra, it would follow that time has a beginning; therefore, he says: "This time is without beginning or end."
This time has been described by us as the beginning of the Yuga, having commenced from the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra;
yet it has neither end nor beginning.
The beginning and the end are conceptually constructed for the sake of conventional usage.
If time had a beginning, what would follow? He says: it would follow that saṃsāra has a beginning.
And it is accepted that saṃsāra is beginningless;
therefore, it is logical to say, "This time is without beginning or end.
But how is its beginning conceptually constructed for the sake of conventional usage? To this he says: [it] is inferred by the planets in the field.
The planets and the lunar mansions are "grahabhāni";
by means of these planets and mansions, the beginning and the end are inferred.
Regarding the verbal root *mā* in the sense of "measuring" (Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha 1143), in the expression "the inference of fire from smoke," this root functions in the sense of measuring (*māne*).
In this case, however, the meaning is precisely that of a means of knowledge (*māna*), as it is inferred by means of weights;
for instance, heaps of rice and the like are inferred by means of *prastha* measures,
or saffron and the like by means of *pala* weights.
"Thus by the planets":
when all the planets together are simultaneously in conjunction with the earth at the junction of Pisces and Aries, then it is the beginning of the Yuga.
What connection can there be between the earth and the planet,
given that the two are so extremely remote from one another? This is not a fault.
Since a primary conjunction is impossible, a secondary conjunction is accepted.
Where a planet appears as if fixed to the earth, that is the conjunction of the earth and the planet;
and since such a thing occurs at both rising and setting, it is accepted as occurring at either rising or setting.
Others, however, describe it differently, saying that [the beginning and end] are inferred by means of the planets (*graha*).
By means of the planets and the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the beginning and the end of time are conceptualized. For example: "The lunar mansion in which Aṅgiras departed on his journey is rising."
"Therefore, let the year [be calculated] from the month [of Māgha], according to the Bārhaspatya system.
Thus, the beginning of time was determined by the movement of Jupiter;
and in the world, people speak in this way: "We shall set out when Svāti has risen," or "The rising [of the asterism]."
“[He] set out when Venus had set,” and “Today, while the Kṛttikās are situated in the meridian, Dāruka has gone,” and so forth;
this refers to the field (*kṣetra*).
The celestial sphere is the field; within that celestial sphere, a beginning and an end are conventionally established by virtue of the movements of the lunar mansions and the planets. // 11 //
[The Equal Motion of the Planets] To demonstrate the equal motion of the planets, he says: "In sixty solar years, the planets complete the revolution of the asterisms."
Moving through the celestial realm like the very horizon of the sky, they circled within their respective orbits.
In sixty solar years—that is, sixty Āditya years—the planets complete the stellar orbit;
the meaning is that they travel through distances in their respective orbits equal to the dimensions of the stellar orbit.
Furthermore, how many *yojanas* do the planets traverse in the stellar orbit in sixty solar years?
It is said: "The Vasu, Viyat, Ambara, Ākāśa, Rasa, Yama, Triśaila, and Candra.
This measurement of the stellar sphere has not been observed by us;
rather, what is this that has been set forth?
It is said: "The sun is in the bhava portion" (Gītikā, 6).
Here, how is it further explained that they travel in *yojanas* equal to the stellar sphere (*nakṣatrakakṣyā*) by this very [statement]?
If the planets consume their respective revolutions in *arkavarṣas* equal to *khyughṛ* (180), then how many are there in sixty solar years?
By a sixtieth part of sixty, one [revolution is obtained];
furthermore, by another sixtieth part of these *arkavarṣas* equal to *khyughṛ*, there are seventy-two thousand.
In this manner, the undestroyed heaps should be established according to their respective portions.

Then again: if one zodiacal circle (bhagaṇa) is obtained for its own respective orbit, then what is obtained for sixty years' duration? Thus, the stellar orbit (nakṣatra-kakṣyā) is obtained from all the planets.
"By the divine [measure] around the sky": "divine" means existing in the sky; the meaning is "a yuga."
But how, again, is a *yuga* denoted by the term "divine" (*divya*)?
Because the conjunction of the planets moving in the sky occurs at one time, therefore it is called a "divine *yuga*"; by that divine [unit], one measures the circumference of the sky.
The "enclosure of the sky" (nabhasaḥ paridhiḥ) means the "sky-enclosure" (nabhaḥparidhiḥ), that is to say, the celestial orbit (ākāśakakṣyā).
How is this stated?
But surely it is heard that the sky (*viyat*) has an immeasurable extent of *yojana*s;
how then could there be a boundary (*kakṣyā*) for it with a measured extent of *yojana*s? It is said: the sky, as far as it extends for us...
"It illuminates the sky as far as it is the repository of the rays of the sun;
beyond that, space is immeasurable. Here, by the expression "the sphere of the void" (*khakakṣyā*), he demonstrates this.
"To this extent the rays of the sun reach into the sky" means that they revolve equally;
"revolving with equal motion" is the meaning.

As many *yojanas* as the moon traverses in its own orbit, so many *yojanas* does Saturn (*ārki*) also traverse in its own orbit. For example: if one complete revolution (*bhagaṇa*) results in the acquisition of its own orbit, then what is obtained by the revolutions of a *yuga*? Thus, the celestial orbit (*khakakṣyā*) is obtained. Alternatively: if the orbit of the asterisms (*nakṣatracakṣyā*) is obtained by the motion over sixty years, then what is obtained by its own *yuga*-revolutions? Thus, the celestial orbit is obtained.
Thus, by means of the distance in *yojanas*, the planets have equal velocities.

Regarding the calculation of the mean positions of the planets according to their orbits (*kakṣyā*): if all the planets, revolving with uniform velocity in their respective orbits through the days of a *yuga*, traverse a distance in *yojanas* equal to the celestial orbit (*khakakṣyā*), [then...]

To determine how much [distance] is covered in one day, the daily motion of all the planets in *yojanas* is obtained by dividing the celestial sphere (*khakakṣyā*) by the number of terrestrial days (*bhūdina*). Having obtained the daily motion of the planets in *yojanas*, the mean planets are derived through a threefold proportion (*trairāśika*): "If a complete revolution (*bhagaṇa*) is obtained by means of the *yojanas* of their own orbit, then what is obtained by means of the *yojanas* of their daily motion?"—thus the daily motion is obtained.

Then again: "If enjoyment is obtained in one day, what is obtained by a group of days? Here, in the previous rule of three, one is the multiplier (*guṇakāra*) and the others are the divisor (*bhāgahāra*).

Therefore, because the multiplier and the divisor are equal, they cancel each other out; thus, for the *ahargaṇa*, the daily motion in *yojanas* remains as the multiplier, the *yojanas* of its own orbit remain as the divisor, and the quotient consists of the revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) and so forth. And it has been said:
The celestial sphere's circumference divided by the number of days [in a kalpa] yields the yojanas therein;
when these are multiplied by the elapsed days, they yield the revolutions and so forth of the respective planet's orbit.

Thus; or else, the revolutions and so forth are obtained by multiplying the [mean] anomaly's orbit by the accumulated days and dividing by the product of its own orbit and the terrestrial days. // 12 //
[The arrangement of the orbits due to the uniform motion of the planets]—
in order to demonstrate the arrangement of the planetary orbits as they proceed with uniform motion, he says: "The moon fills its small orbit below in a short time."
Above all of them, it moves slowly with great and mighty power. // 13 //
The mandala below is small;
the moon fills all the small mandalas situated below it in a short time.
By the very mention of "below," the smallness of that mandala is established.
It should not be said that it is "small.
How is the smallness of the mandala understood when only "below" is stated?
It is replied: the enclosures (kakṣyās) are arranged one above the other.
Among those situated one above the other, that which is situated at the bottom is the thinnest of all;
therefore, [the moon] would have to be below that.
But this is not the case.
Regarding the statement, "Move slowly below the stars" (Kālakriyā,
15), he will explain there that the orbits are situated one above the other.
Now, however, others say that the orbit of the moon is above all of them.
[That is incorrect.
He states that the orbit of the moon is below all the planets;
if it were above, then when the moon is eclipsed by a planet or a lunar mansion, the planets, lunar mansions, and stars would be visible upon its clearly marked deer-stain.

If the moon were above by virtue of its distance from the sun, then, because the sun would always be situated at a distance, even the two moons would be seen with their own distant portion unobstructed;
yet that which is situated above is not perceived.
Therefore, for all [beings],...
Below is the moon.
Furthermore, others who rely on the Sugata’s teaching state that the sun and moon share a single orbit:
at half the height of Meru, the moon and sun are fifty-one yojanas [in diameter].
Midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise occur simultaneously. Thus it is said.
This is not logical:
if the moon is fifty yojanas and the sun is fifty-one yojanas, then why is the sun not perceived as large?
Are these two observed as equal when half-risen and half-set on the full moon day?
If it is argued that the sun does not appear large because of its distance, that is not so;
for in that case, the sun would be equally distant from the moon on the side of Mount Mandara.
Furthermore, because they are established as being on an equal footing, there would be no solar eclipse at all;
nor is there any Rāhu other than the moon by which the sun could be obscured,
even if the moon were below it.
Even so, because the solar disc is so vast, the sun is not entirely obscured.
If it is argued that the sun is never fully covered by the moon, that too will be explained later.
The moon fills [the sun] in a short time.
He fills it with a small amount of time;
what is it? That small mandala situated below.
Above all the mandalas, the great mandala, moving slowly, fills it over a long period of time.
These two planets are specified as having small and large orbital dimensions respectively;
the orbits of the others are to be understood by one's own intelligence.
For example, the moon traverses one orbit in twenty-seven and a half days.
Mercury, Venus, and the Sun [complete their revolutions] in slightly less than one year;
Mars [completes its revolution] in slightly less than two years.
Jupiter, however, [completes its revolution] in twelve years slightly less [than that],
while Saturn does so in thirty years slightly less [than that].
Thus, these planets, though situated in different orbits, are explained as having equal velocities in terms of the distance traveled in *yojanas*.

Now, if those situated in the same orbit were indeed equal in their motion in *yojanas*, then there would never be a separation among these planets once they have begun their course from the start of the Yuga.

On the other hand, if they were different in their motion in *yojanas*, then when calculating their degrees of motion, the well-known degrees of motion in *liptās* would not be obtained by means of *yojanas* according to their respective values.
Therefore, even though the planets are situated in different orbits, they are indeed equal in their motion in *yojanas*. // 13 //
[The relative smallness and greatness of signs and so forth across different levels:
Because the levels (kakṣyā) vary in size, there arises the doubt as to whether the signs, degrees, and minutes are many or few; to resolve this, he says:
"For when the orbit (maṇḍala) is small, the signs are few, and when it is large, they are great."
The degrees, as well as the minutes, are likewise equal in their respective divisions within their own classes. // 14 //
In a small mandala the zodiacal signs (rāśis) are small, and in a large mandala they are large;
likewise for the degrees (aṃśas) and minutes (kalās),
which are similar only in their proportional division.
For example: in both small and large circles, a zodiac sign (*rāśi*) is one-twelfth of the circle,
a degree (*bhāga*) is one three-hundred-and-sixtieth part,
and a minute (*liptā*) is one sixty-thousandth part.
Because the wheel of light is equal in each of its respective enclosures. // 14 //
[The Order of the Planets' Orbits] To fully understand the order of their positions from above to below within the orbits, he says:
Below the sun are Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.
And beneath these, the earth stands as a pillar, situated in the midst of space.
The *bhāni* are the luminaries,
beginning with Aśvinī; beneath them is Śanaiścara (Saturn).
Below that is Bṛhaspati, then Aṅgāraka, and so forth;
and below these is the earth.
The earth is below these [elements], such as the lunar mansions;
it serves as their sacrificial post (medhī).
In this context, the word *bhūta*, although applicable to many meanings, should be understood in the sense of "like" (*iva*).
Standing like a sacrificial post;
situated in the middle of space.
Space is the sky (ākāśa); the middle of that is the "middle of space."
"Abiding in that, she stands in the midst of the sky;
and the earth is beneath these. To this it is said: when [she] is visible...
When the planets and constellations are in the half-circle [of the zodiac],
then the earth is beneath them;
but when the planets and constellations are in other positions— namely, the fifth, seventh, ninth, eleventh, or second houses— how can the earth be beneath them?
If it were above,
it would not be understood in this way;
for the earth is below all of us, such as ourselves.
And above is space;
therefore, the planets are always above, and the earth is below.
And he will say:
"Just as a cluster of kadamba flowers is covered on all sides with blossoms,
so too is the terrestrial globe filled with all beings, both aquatic and terrestrial.
[Gola, 7]
Others, however, consider this conception to be far from correct;

they believe that the lunar mansions (*bhagaṇa*), Saturn (*śanaiścara*), Jupiter (*bṛhaspati*), Mars (*kuja*), the Sun (*ravi*), Venus (*sita*), Mercury (*budha*), and the Moon (*niśākara*) are situated one above the other and possess equal velocities.
Thus, as far as the smallest orbit, they revolve through the lunar mansions.

Since Saturn and the other planets are unable to fill such vast mandalas, they appear behind [the moon] according to the sequence of their respective orbital mandalas; the resolution to this has already been shown previously: if [the moon] were above, then during the eclipses of the moon and the distinction of the planets and constellations, the planets, constellations, and stars would appear as distinct from the clear spot and the deer [on the moon].
By the passage beginning with "they would diminish" (kṛśyeran),
others consider that the constellations, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon occupy equal ranks; however,
they possess swifter motions in their respective order.

Therefore, by means of the fast-moving constellations (nakṣatras), that which has a slightly slower speed is overtaken slightly; however, that which has an extremely slow speed is overtaken from afar.
Because its speed is slightly slower, Saturn (Śanaiścara) is overtaken slightly.
Because its motion is exceedingly slow, the moon is said to be "far away.

In this regard also, if the planets and other bodies are facing eastward, then the moon—being overtaken by the stars which face east and possess swift motion—would be seen in Aśvinī and observed in Revatī, but not in Bharaṇī. This occurs during the period of retrograde motion (*vakrakāla*).
Moreover, because they move in retrograde motion, a planet seen in Aśvinī would be observed in Bharaṇī; or,
if these planets and others were imagined to face the opposite direction, even so, one seen in Aśvinī during its period of retrogression would, due to its retrograde motion, be observed in Bharaṇī.
Furthermore, there would be no difference in their eclipses for those situated on the same orbital plane;
moreover, there would be no mutual obscuration of their disks,
and even planetary eclipses (grahoparāga) would be impossible because they are situated on the same orbital plane.
Therefore, it has been well said: "Below the [orbit of] Bhānu is Śanaiścara," and so forth. // 15 //
[Knowledge of the Lords of the Kālahorās, etc.
To explain the knowledge of the lords of the kālahorās and so forth, he says: "These seven lords of the horās, beginning with Saturn, are swift in their sequence."
By means of the rapid calculation, the lords of the day from sunrise become the fourth [from the current lord]. // 16 //
These planets, beginning with Saturn, although possessing equal speeds, are perceived as being progressively swifter due to the progressive diminution of their orbits;
these same planets are the lords of the horas in that respective order.
For example, when the *kālahorā* of Saturn has ceased, there follows the *kālahorā* of Jupiter, then that of Mars, then that of the Sun, and so forth.
Thus, from sunrise until the half-setting of the sun, there are twelve *kālahorās*;
and from that half-setting until the next half-rising, there are again twelve.
In this way, there are twenty-four *kālahorās* in a day and night.
The so-called *kālahorā* is indeed the period of half a rising of the ascendant sign;
and it is to be understood day by day, beginning from the ruler of the day.
And it has been stated by Sphujidhvaja Yavaneśvara:
"The Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars shall be the lords of the horas during the day and night respectively;
these are multiplied by four and six therein according to the sequence beginning with the lord of that day."
Thus, counting from the rising of the sun, who is the lord of the day, up to the half-rising of the very next day’s lord according to the swift sequence, the fourth is reached;
this is the fourth lord of the day, following that swift sequence which was stated as "Saturn is below the [other] planets," and so forth.
For example, the fourth from Saturn is the Sun, the lord of the day.
From the Sun comes the Moon as the fourth, from the Moon comes Mars, and so forth;
in this sequence, the lords of the months and the lords of the years are to be understood.
How so? That which is the lord on the first day of a month or a year is both the lord of the month and the lord of the year. The lords of the days are determined from sunrise;
"sunrise" (sūryodaya) means the rising of the sun.

Even though it was stated by Śeṣa that the Ardhodaya [conjunction] is to be understood as occurring at the remainder of the sunrise, why is this so? Because, even when referring to a portion of the solar disc, it is impossible to determine the time of measurement for the extent of that portion; and since the Ardhodaya possesses a clearly manifest characteristic, the Ardhodaya is adopted because it is easily distinguishable.
Alternatively, regarding things not specifically defined, it begins from the rise of one half of the middle course and proceeds again to the rise of another half.
In this regard, some believe that the commencement of the weekday occurs at midday;
however, that is incorrect.
For it has been said:
"In the beginning, this was indeed enveloped in darkness— unknowable, without defining marks, beyond reasoning, incomprehensible, as if entirely asleep."
[Manusmṛti, 1.5] Here, because of the absence of the sun— the light of the world— no convention regarding the days of the week and so forth had arisen.
From the moment the thousand-rayed one appeared, from that time forward, the convention of the days of the week and so forth came into being.
Therefore, it has been well said that "the lords of the day [begin] from sunrise. // 16 //
[The determination of planetary motion according to the method of the counter-epicycle: It is not known in which mandala these planets revolve; therefore, in order to determine that, he says:
"All planets revolve by their own motion, situated upon the counter-epicycles of their orbits."
From the apogee of the slow motion, it is direct; and from the apogee of the fast motion, it is indeed retrograde.
The compound *kakṣyāpratimaṇḍala* means "the enclosure and the circle"; those who go to that are *kakṣyāpratimaṇḍalagāḥ*.
Alternatively, *kakṣyā* and *pratimaṇḍala* together form the dual compound *kakṣyāpratimaṇḍale*.
"They move" refers to those situated in the concentric circles (*kakṣyā-pratimaṇḍala-gāḥ*).
Here, the "those situated in the circles" (*kakṣyā-gāḥ*) are the mean planets, while the "those situated in the epicycles" (*pratimaṇḍala-gāḥ*) are the true [planets].
Alternatively, the point where the orbit (kakṣyā) and the epicycle (pratimaṇḍala) intersect is designated by the term "orbit-epicycle" (kakṣyāpratimaṇḍala).
Those which go to that [point] are called "orbit-epicycle-goers" (kakṣyāpratimaṇḍalagāḥ).
In this case, because there are multiple possible analyses (vigraha) of the compound, [the specific one is chosen].
To address the doubt as to which compound is being adopted here, it is said: *kakṣyā* and *pratimaṇḍala* form the compound *kakṣyāpratimaṇḍala*;
those who go to these are *kakṣyāpratimaṇḍalagāḥ*.
Thus, this [interpretation] is accepted.
How so? Because it is desired and because it expresses the meaning of the remaining compound;
here it is accepted that the middle planets are those whose latitudes are equal, since they have equal motions.
Since the true planets move within their respective orbs and possess similar velocities,
what then are those that are mean,
and which are the true planets?
But is it not the case that there is only one sun, only one moon, and only one Mars, and so forth?
If the mean-true state were being grasped, it would result in two distinct planets;
it is not understood in this way that "the mean planet is the true planet.
How then?
Is it that by the term *madhyamagraha* (mean planet) the motion of the mean planet is denoted, and by the term *sphuṭagraha* (true planet) the motion of the true planet?
It is just as when someone asks an astrologer, "Who is the Sun? [and the latter replies with its motion].
He said to him: "The heap consists of fifteen parts and thirty *liptās*.
In this case, there arises for both the one who asks and the one who explains a dual intention.
This is not a fault;
that which is the mean motion is the means for calculating the true motion.
Otherwise, because it would be indeterminate, the true motion would be impossible to discern.
In the same way, the [Middle Planet’s] capture (*madhyamagraha*) is conceptually constructed for the purpose of fully understanding the planetary circles (*pratimaṇḍala*).

That interval between this planet and the true node (*bhūtārāgraha*), which is equal to its semi-diameter, causes it to remain either above or below the orbital circle (*kakṣyāmaṇḍala*) starting from that point.
Now, what is this point?

It is said: when, in the third operation, the anomaly of the apsis of Jupiter (mandocca-kendra) is three signs, two degrees, and fifty minutes, then the radius (karṇa) of Jupiter's apsis is equal to the semi-diameter (vyāsārdha).
When, in the fourth operation, the anomaly of the [mean] apsis (śīghrocca-kendra) is three signs, five degrees, and twenty minutes—
At that time, the radius of the epicycle (śīghroccakarṇa) is equal to the radius of the circle.
Here, the distance between the true apogee and the planet is equal to the radius of the circle.
From this point onward, the distance between the true apogee and the planet decreases day by day.
By this same reasoning, the distance between the true apogee and a planet for the remaining planets should also be inferred as being equal to the radius of the circle.
That "all planets move by their own motion" is indeed self-evident.
“Anuloma from the apogee.
The ablative case in “from the apogee” (*mandoccāt*) is used in the sense of cause.
Therefore, it is explained as: “anuloma [occurs] because of the apogee.”
Because there is no knowledge of the retrograde motion when at the apogee of slowness (*mandocca*); and it is indeed retrograde from the apogee of swiftness (*śīghrocca*).
From the cause that is the apogee of swiftness, it is retrograde.
Because the knowledge of retrograde motion occurs at the apogee of the swifter [planet].
But how is the knowledge of retrograde motion at the apogee of the swifter [planet] obtained?
It is said: when the apogee of the swifter [planet] is in the second quadrant, then all the planets become retrograde.

And when the apogee of the anomaly is in the third sign, then the motions are retrograde; as it has been said: "When six and eight signs have been subtracted in order from the swifter planets among the planets."
The gait may be crooked, excessively curved, or likewise slightly bent.
Thus it is said: "And this rule is even more subtle.
It is explained as follows: when the planet of tomorrow is equal to the planet of today, then the commencement of retrogression (*vakraprārambha*) occurs;
or, when the planet of today is equal to the planet of yesterday, then too there is the commencement of retrogression.
When the planet of the following day is greater than the planet of the third step from today, then there is the cessation of retrogression (*vakranivṛtti*).
Or, when the planet of today is greater than the planet of yesterday at the third step, then too there is the cessation of retrogression.
When the planet returns after many *liptās*, then it is a state of extreme retrograde motion (*ativakragati*).
But how does the calculator understand this rule from the *śighrocca* alone, and not from the *mandocca*?
It is said: because it is due to the sun that the planets have their rising, setting, retrograde, and direct motions.
If this is so, how is it that for Mercury and Venus here, the other [parameter] is the swiftest apogee, while the mean [longitude] is the Sun?
Even in this case, the complete knowledge of their rising and setting depends solely upon the Sun.
However, retrograde motion is understood through a single means;
or rather, there is no fixed rule or specific statement regarding the means— such as the calculation of the true motion based on the high, low, or middle epicycles—
for these are merely means that accomplish the goal to be attained.
Therefore, this entire procedure by which the true motion of the planets is calculated is unreal;
and thus, those who desire to know the ultimate truth attain the real by means of an unreal expedient.
For instance, physicians practice cutting and so forth on lotus stalks and the like;
barbers practice shaving and so forth on clay pots and the like; and those learned in the sacrificial treatises practice sacrifices such as the *śuṣkeṣṭi* on [dry offerings].
Grammarians explain words through the processes of base, suffix, modification, augment, elision of phonemes, transposition, and so forth; likewise, here too,
astrologers explain the true motion of the planets through the technical application of mean and true apogees, perigees, their epicycles, sines, the maximum and minimum values, and the hypotenuse.
Therefore, there is no objection to these [conventional] means which, though not ultimately real, are intent on establishing what is real.
Now, for what purpose do these planets revolve every day?
Furthermore, in the world, someone who is wandering does so for a specific cause.
Furthermore, it is said that no other such thing is seen moving incessantly as these stars and planets do; thus, they are cited as an illustrative example.

It is replied: indeed, in the beginning of all things, the Blessed Lord Prajāpati commanded the planets, saying, "O you, move through the groups of signs beginning with Aries for the sake of the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of living beings.
And it has been stated by Sphujidhvaja Yavaneśvara:
It is said that Prajāpati, the creator of all, desiring to bring forth progeny, first observed a vow;
he [then] [offered] his own body, which was the source of the twelve limbs.
Having first created the [primordial] matter, he indeed emitted the celestial sphere.
From them he produced the flocks of sheep and so forth, and from them, through their various subdivisions, others as well;
therefore, he is the all-pervading creator of the world of beings.
"Lordship over the production and non-production of beings," and so forth.
Alternatively, inference is made from words to their meanings;
for words are heard here, and there are others which express the [various] destinies.

For example, while the rule *pathaḥ ṣkan* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.75) is in effect, by the subsequent rule *panthaḥ ṇa nityam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.76), the word *pānthaḥ* is formed in the sense of "one who constantly goes on a path" (*nityaṃ panthānaṃ gacchati*).
In this world, no one is seen traveling along a path without ceasing;
therefore, these very planets are the travelers.
Furthermore, this word is not employed when its referents are non-existent, like the words "hare's horn," "tortoise's hair," or "barren woman's son. Therefore...
It is well said that the meaning is inferred from the word: "the planets are travelers.
Or else, there is this other method:
[the motion] is direct from the apogee of the slowest planet, and retrograde from the apogee of the fastest.
From the apogee—that is, from the apogee-centre (mandoccakendra) by means of the method of the epicycle—the fruit which is brought forth increases day by day.
Where? Since nothing else is mentioned, it is at the apogee itself.
Therefore, [the motion] is direct (anuloma) from that apogee.
And it is in reverse order from the swift apogee (śīghrocca), because the result calculated by the method of the epicycle (pratimaṇḍala) is always diminished;
why? Because nothing else is heard [in the scriptures], it is [calculated] precisely from the swift apogee.
Therefore, it is said: "And in reverse order, from the swift apogee. (17)
[The Procedure for the Sub-mandala] It has been stated that the planets move clearly within the sub-mandala;
therefore, in order to explain that, he says:
Each of their respective secondary orbits (pratimaṇḍala) is equal to its own girdle-circle (kakṣyāmaṇḍala). The center of each secondary orbit extends beyond the center of the dense earth. // 18 //
"Equal to the circle of the girth-band":
that which is equal to the circle of the girth-band is "equal to the circle of the girth-band.
It is the measure of the circle of the girth-band: "the wheel situated in the lunar mansion" (Gītikās).
Thus it is explained in this sūtra:
"Each respective mandala" means each individual mandala belonging to these planets. It exists for each of them.
The center of the mandala is that which is the middle;
that middle, which is the center, extends beyond the center of the solid earth. "Solid earth" (ghanabhū) refers to that which is both solid (ghana) and earth (bhū).
The middle of that dense earth is "ghanabhūmadhyam";
from that "ghanabhūmadhyāt," the meaning is that which has passed beyond, emerged, or is situated above.

To explain: having arranged the circle of the orbit (kakṣyāmaṇḍala), which is conceived according to its dimensions and divided into three hundred and sixty parts, extending from east to west and upwards;

then, another such circle is placed above and below the circle of the orbit at the distance to be described later, where it intersects with the east-west line—that which is bound upon the sphere there is called the *pratimaṇḍala* (counter-circle).
Thus, these two, the Kakṣyā and the Pratimaṇḍala, have been explained. // 18 //
[The demonstration of planetary motion according to the method of the eccentric circle.
To demonstrate the interval between the epicycle and the deferent, he says:
"The semi-diameter of the eccentric circle (svoccanīcavṛtta) is the distance between the epicycle and the earth."
The planets move along the circumference of their orbits in this manner, according to their mean motion. // 19 //

The difference between the epicycle (*pratimaṇḍala*) and the terrestrial circle (*bhūmaṇḍala*) is the "epicycle-terrestrial-circle difference" (*pratimaṇḍalabhūvivara*). This is the semi-diameter (*vyāsārdha*) of the eccentric circle (*uccanīcavṛtta*).
The term *uccanīcavṛtta* refers to both the apogee circle (*uccavṛtta*) and the perigee circle (*nīcavṛtta*).
One's own apogee and perigee orbit is the *svoccanīcavṛtta*; the radius of that *svoccanīcavṛtta* is the distance between the concentric circle (*pratimaṇḍala*) and the earth.
This is as stated under the heading "Half the [mean] motion is the slow orbit" (*jhārdhāni mandavṛttam*), regarding which it says: "Of the moon... (*śaśinaḥ cha*) [Gītikāpāda].
Thus, the seven half-orbits of the Moon constitute its high and low orbit;
the meaning is that it measures thirty-one and a half degrees.
Whatever its semi-diameter may be, that is determined by means of the three-proportion (trairāśika) calculation.

Success! If, according to the rule "one hundred and four multiplied by eight" [Gaṇita, 10], an equatorial circumference (*paridhi*) equal to ten thousand (*ayuta*) is obtained for a radius (*vyāsārdha*) of one unit, then what is obtained for a circumference measuring thirty-one and a half parts? The result is five parts and one *liptā* plus a half.
The sun also has three and a half revolutions of slow motion,
measuring thirteen and a half degrees;
and by means of the rule of three, its own orbital radius is obtained as two degrees.
With half more, there are nine *liptās*.

Alternatively: if a semi-diameter measuring three hundred and sixty-eight *liptās* is obtained for a circumference measuring three hundred and sixty parts, then what is obtained for the circumference at the apogee and perigee? Thus, the semi-diameter of the Moon’s apogee and perigee is found to be three hundred *liptās* plus one and a half.
In this manner, for the sun as well, there are one hundred and twenty-nine [and a half].
Therein, the distance between the center and the edge of the orbital circle (kakṣyā-pratimaṇḍala) should be calculated either by means of the measure of degrees or by the measure of minutes (liptā).
This applies likewise to both the sun and the moon.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of multiple epicycles for other planets due to the distinctions of even and uneven motion and slow and fast apogees; therefore, he will state later: "The difference between the true planet and the [mean] planet" (Kālakriyāpāda 25). This refers to the circumference of the orbit.
The circle of the epicycle;
within that circular circumference, the planets move in their mean motion.
It is understood by implication that they move in their true motion upon the eccentric circles (pratimaṇḍala). // 19 //
[The planetary motion on the circumference of the eccentric circle.

To explain the calculation of planetary velocity and the determination of retrograde and direct motion, he says: "That which has a swift motion moves in a retrograde direction from its own apogee upon its own eccentric orbit."
A planet that moves in direct motion (anuloma) within its orbit has slow motion (mandagati). // 20 //

That which has a swift motion is "swift-motion" (śīghragati); that which is both swift-motion and its own apogee (ucca) is "swift-motion-apogee" (śīghragatisvocca); and that which has a retrograde motion from the swift-motion-apogee is "swift-motion-retrograde" (śīghragatipratilomagati).
By the term "own apogee" (svocca), the motion of one's own swift apogee (śīghrocca) is understood.

If that motion of the swift apogee does not fall short of the mean motion— calculated from the sine of its own central difference (svakendrāntajyā)— then that very same corrected mean motion, as calculated from the sine of its own central difference, is subtracted from the motion of the swift apogee in reverse order.
Then it is called "swift motion" or "motion at its highest point.
And by the word *pratiloma*, the remaining degrees (liptās) that have been subtracted in reverse order are understood.
Thus, this meaning of the compound is established:
"one whose motion is retrograde" (*pratilomagati*) means one who possesses a retrograde motion.
This calculation of the true longitude (*bhukti*) will be explained right from the beginning.
That is to say: one should multiply the sine produced from the interval between the apogee and the center, whether by direct or inverse order, by the minutes of the planet's own mean motion.

Then, having multiplied that by the daily motion for that time and divided by eighteen thousand, one should halve the result according to the quadrant of the center; this is then added to or subtracted from the minutes of the planet's mean motion, and finally subtracted from the minutes of its own swift apogee's motion.

The remainder should be multiplied by the sequential and reverse sine (jyā) of the arc between the planet's own mean anomaly and its apogee; that product should then be multiplied by the epicycle of the planet's swift motion for that time. Divide by eighteen thousand to obtain the quotient; this value, situated within the radius of the circle, should then be divided by the planet's own hypotenuse (karṇa).

One should add or subtract half of the obtained value from the minutes of the mean motion of the planet according to the quadrant it occupies. Then, taking that remainder—either added or subtracted—one should perform the third operation: multiply the sine of the arc between the slow apogee and the center (the anomaly) by the epicycle at that time, and divide by eighteen thousand.
One should add or subtract the obtained value entirely from the minutes of the mean motion of the planet, according to the quadrant of the slow epicycle (mandakendra).
The result, whether added or subtracted, is the true mean motion in minutes; these values are not to be discarded.
One should subtract those from the minutes of the motion of its own swift apogee.

Taking the remainder, one should proceed through the fourth operation: the [sine and versed sine] of the interval between the swift apogee and the center; this should be multiplied by the radius at that time and divided by eighteen thousand.
The result, multiplied by the semi-diameter, should be divided by the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).
In that case, if what has been obtained is to be added, one should add it to the minutes of the true mean motion; the resulting value is the planet's true motion.
Alternatively, if what is to be subtracted does not fall short of the true mean motion, then the planet is in retrograde motion, and the minutes of the true mean motion are simply reversed.
These are to be subtracted; the remainder is the true motion.
Regarding this point, there is this verse:
"That which moves swiftly, when moving retrograde from its own apogee within its own circular orbit..."
"Moving in reverse order" means moving in a retrograde course;
"moving in direct order" occurs in the [normal] revolution, and this constitutes moving in direct order.
When the minutes produced by the arc of the angle between the mean anomaly and the apogee are subtracted from the minutes of the true mean motion,
then that planet is retrograde;
and in that case, the specific minutes are designated by the term *anuloma* (direct).
From this, the following analysis is established: "that whose motion is favorable is 'favorably moving' (anulomagati).
And because it moves slowly, it is designated as "slow-moving" (mandagati). // 20 //
[Another method for the revolution of the eccentric circles:
He states another method for the computation of the true positions of the planets:
"The circles move in direct motion from the slow [mean] planet, and in retrograde motion from the fast [mean] planet."
The planet situated at the center of its own orbit, which is attached to the circle of the epicycle, is the mean [planet]. // 21 //
It moves in direct order (*anuloma*), thus it is "direct motion" (*anulomagati*).
This was stated [in the verse]: "From the slow [node], up to the limit of the slow apogee (*mandocca*)," meaning from the middle point.
Therefore, in this case as well, [the rule] "from the mean [longitude] up to the limit of the swift apogee" should apply by a single method.
To this he says: "No; from the swift [apogee], there is retrograde motion up to the limit of the retrograde [motion].
This means that the revolutions and circumferences of the swift apogee which possess retrograde motions—i.e., contrary motions—are [to be calculated].
In this context, because the term "circle" (*vṛtta*) is applied metaphorically to a portion of the circle, [the phrase] "and the circumferences" is used;
just as, for instance, the arcs [are defined] by the sines of the apogees of the slow and fast motions.
Therefore, those arcs produced from the slow apogee are, in order:
They are accumulated;
those born from the swift apsis are accumulated in reverse order.
Therefore, it is said: "The circles moving with the [mean] motion proceed in direct order from the slow [apsis], and those moving against it proceed in reverse order from the swift [apsis]."

How, then, do the equations for the slow and fast apogees proceed through their respective sine-arches in direct and reverse order? Because "motion" (gati) denotes a state [of being], just as it is said:
"The mind of living beings becomes tender [with the thought] that motion exists."
Like an ox that bears its burden day and night without weariness, he carries his responsibility.
Thus, there are three destinies for wealth: giving, enjoyment, and destruction.
For one who neither gives nor enjoys it, the third destiny occurs.
Therefore, those very same bows and arrows possess both retrograde and forward movements.

Now, this must be asked here: why do the arcs of the manda-eccentricity increase from the manda-apsis, while the arcs of the śighra-eccentricity decrease from the śighra-apsis? This is because the tradition has not been interrupted.
Now, "The specific meaning is understood from the commentary; for there is no lack of definition due to doubt" (Aṣṭādhyāyī,
Śivasūtra 6).
[This refers to] the *Pātañjala-mahābhāṣya*.

Alternatively, because the apogee of the slow motion (*mandocca*) and the apogee of the fast motion (*śīghrocca*) are explicitly mentioned, only these two are understood, since nothing else is heard [in the text].

[The procedure for calculating the true position of a planet according to the method of the *pratimaṇḍala*] This is the meaning of the Noble Sūtra; we shall demonstrate through calculation how it is consistent.
One should subtract that apogee from the desired planet.

The remaining portion, such as the zodiacal sign and so forth, which proceeds from the apogee (mandocca), is produced on the orbital circle (kakṣyāmaṇḍala) and is thus applied to the counter-orbit (pratimaṇḍala), because the true planet moves upon the counter-orbit. Therefore, whatever distance [is traversed] starting from that apogee is small on the great orbit.
“Large and great accumulations are to be known;
likewise, portions and minutes [constitute] the passing of time (kālakriyā).
Thus, in a small mandala, that very same measure of wood is much greater.
It occurs because of the smallness of the measure (*māna*).

Just as rice and other grains, when measured by a large specific measure, become few in number according to the count of *prastha* and so forth, yet those same grains, when measured by a small specific measure, become many according to the count of *prastha* and so forth— so it is here as well.
But how is that wooden gnomon, which has emerged from the circle of the girdle-line (*kakṣyāmaṇḍala*), measured upon the eccentric circle (*pratimaṇḍala*)?

It is said: having calculated the elapsed steps of that gnomon, this operation is performed by means of the sine of the arm (*bhuja*) and the sine of the perpendicular (*koṭi*) of the current step: “The center of the eccentric circle is displaced from the center of the dense earth. [Kālakriyā]
Thus, in each circular diagram (*pratimaṇḍala*), a space of one *koṭi* is added to the first and fourth feet and subtracted from the second and third.
To demonstrate this, having fixed the center of a circle on level ground, one should draw a circle with a compass whose radius is determined by that same measurement.

Having drawn the east-west and north-south lines of that circle, one should place a cord from the center of that circle toward the apogee, measuring the length of the epicycle radius (*antyaphalajyā*), extending it toward the south; there, using a compass with a radius equal to half the diameter of the orbital circle (*kakṣyāmaṇḍala*), one should draw a circle.
That is called the "counter-circle" (*pratimaṇḍala*).
[That [line] stands above the orbital circle in the case of the first and fourth quarters,

and below it in the case of the second and third. Therein, that which is the *koṭijyā* (sine of the co-latitude) is produced from the orbital circle and has a magnitude equal to the distance between the orbital circle and the earth's surface.
Because the extremity of the first and fourth circles does not reach [the corresponding point] by that same distance which is the interval between the centers of the circles, it is added;
whereas for the second and third circles, because the extremity is [already] past that distance from the previous circle, it is subtracted.
In this way, the extremity produced for each circle is established.

Now, if the difference between the earth and the eccentric circle (*pratimaṇḍala*) does not subtract from the *koṭijyā*, then the *koṭijyā* is subtracted from the difference between the earth and the eccentric circle;
that much becomes the *koṭi* of the eccentric circle.
In that case, the square root of the sum of the squares of the thus-produced *koṭi* and the *bhuja-jyā* is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).
This is not distinguished by those seeking precision,
because the visual perception [of the planet] varies due to the increase and decrease of the hypotenuse of the epicycle (*pratimaṇḍala*).

If, by means of a radius of the epicycle equal to the semi-diameter [of the sphere], the aforementioned distance between the earth and the epicycle is obtained, then what is obtained by that same radius of the epicycle?

That which is obtained is either added to or subtracted from the previous koti-sine. Thereafter, the square root of the sum of the squares of its bhujā-sine and [the resulting koti-sine] is the radius [of the circle].
Furthermore, the calculation for bringing [the planet] to the position on the eccentric orbit (*pratimaṇḍala*) is as follows, up to this point there is no distinction.

Then, using the non-distinct hypotenuse (*karṇa*), a reverse rule of three (*vyastatrairāśika*) is performed: "If this sine of the arm (*bhujajyā*) is obtained for the circumference of the orbital circle (*kakṣyāmaṇḍala*) which has a diameter equal to the radius of the universe, then what would it be for that hypotenuse produced by the eccentric orbit?"
Because it is a proportional calculation based on three separate sets of values, the radius is the multiplier,
the hypotenuse is the divisor,
and the quotient is the sine of the arc of the counter-epicycle.
Having added that *kāṣṭha* to the slow apogee (*mandocca*), the true planet (*sphuṭagraha*) is obtained;
for when its slow apogee anomaly (*kendram*) is in the first quadrant (*prathamapada*),
[the correction is applied directly], but in the second quadrant, the sine (*bhuja*) is taken by subtracting from six signs (*ṣaḍbhyaḥ rāśibhyaḥ*), and thus it is subtracted from six.
The remainder is added to the apogee.
In the third quadrant, since the arm is greater than a half-circle, that arc, joined with a half-circle, is added to the apogee.
In the fourth quadrant, since the remainder after being subtracted from twelve is the arm, that degree is subtracted from the full circle and the remainder is added to the apogee.
In this way, there is a clear apprehension for that [planet] for which no swift apogee exists;
however, for those for whom a swift apogee does exist, a specific calculation is stated.

For example, by means of the method of moving the circumference (paridhi), one should multiply the semi-diameter by the clearly established circumference; the result obtained by dividing by eighty is the distance between the earth and the epicycle for both the slow and fast apogees. By means of that, using the previously described operation for the slow apogee, one should calculate the slow apogee correction (*mandocca-phala*). The planet, when corrected by all these [corrections], becomes [the true planet].
Thus, for the mean planet that has been thus produced,
half of the difference between it and the mean apogis is added to the mean planet if it is greater than the mean apogis, and subtracted if it is less;
such is the correction for the apogis.
This very same operation is expressed by the following passage: "When Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are in the sign of the Moon, the previously mentioned debt and wealth become halved" (*Kālakriyā*, 22).
How so? When Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars [are in the sign of the Moon].
The meaning is: "among those who are slow, dull-witted, and middling, having achieved success through middling effort.

Regarding the statement, "Half becomes debt or wealth previously" (*Kālakriyā*, 22), as to whose half becomes debt or wealth, the interval between the slow and the middling achievers is understood here due to the unbroken tradition.
What is its half in the middle of the planet,
whether it be wealth or debt, when the operation for the apogee has already been established previously?
And this operation is generally well-known for both the apogee and the perigee.
Why? Because there is no mention of a specific [correction].
For example: "In this way, one should subtract the middle planet, refined by half the [equation of] center, from the planet's own apogee.

Therein, having taken the sine of the arm (bhuja) and the sine of the perpendicular (koṭi) according to the division of the quadrants of the anomaly (kendrapada), [one multiplies them] by the radius using the corrected circumference of its own apogee."
One should derive the side (karṇa) from the area of the circle obtained by multiplying [the diameter] by eighty and dividing by the same, as refined by the previous operation;
here, because there is no difference [in the result],
the "operation of non-difference" does not proceed.

Then, having multiplied the radius by the sine of the arm (bhujajyā) and divided by the hypotenuse (karṇa), the resulting quotient is subtracted from the apogee of the swift motion (śīghrocca) when the center is in the first quadrant;
in the second quadrant, six signs are subtracted [from the center], and the remainder is subtracted from the apogee of the swift motion;
in the third quadrant, it is added to half the circle (cakrārdha).
In the fourth place, the remainder after subtracting twelve from the [mean] is the corrected [longitude], according to the statement:
"The revolutions are traversed in reverse from the swifter [mean].
Thus, the planet becomes corrected by the entire equation of the apsis of the swifter [mean].

And for that [mean anomaly] established by the apogee, one should, as before, apply half the difference to the mean anomaly established by the apogee as either an addition or a subtraction according to the previous assumption.
Having set down that [result], established both by the slow and the fast motions, without discarding it, one should subtract the apogee from it and calculate the apogee again as before.

One should subtract that entire difference—which exists between the established apogee (mandocca) and the mean [longitude] as corrected twice and as established without destruction—from the mean [longitude] minus the twice-corrected [apogee];
one should add it to the mean [longitude] if it is greater.
[That is to say, if the twice-corrected established apogee is less [than the mean], one should subtract; otherwise, one should add.]

Having subtracted that [equation of center] thus computed from the mean apogee by means of the established operation for the mean apogee, the planet will become clearly manifest as its true [longitude].
This very operation has been stated by us in brief in the *Karmānibandha*:
"The operation of the epicycle should also be applied here by the wise."
One should perform the operation for the apogee as before; that [mean anomaly] is subtracted from the perigee.
That alone is to be subtracted [from the half-circle; that moving [value] is to be subtracted from the half-circle];
the arc joined with the half-circle is subtracted from the full circle for the two remaining [values].
Having divided the sine of the argument by eighty— the radius multiplied by its own square root—
and having either subtracted or added the resulting square roots, the hypotenuse is established as before.
This is then combined with half the difference between that and the mean [longitude] derived from the perfected apogee.
If the mandasiddhi is greater, it is added; if it is less, it is subtracted from the mean planet.
That [mean anomaly] should again be calculated from the swift apogee;
having halved the interval produced between the two [true] positions, one should calculate it once more into the true position as before.
When this has been performed, one should again practice for slow accomplishment;
for one who has achieved slow accomplishment, there is this specific distinction which will be described.
Having placed the difference between the twice-proven and the mandasiddha twice-proven as before into the mean [longitude], the planet becomes the true *śīghrasiddha*.
[From the *Mahābhāskarīya*, 4.45–51] Here,
the mention of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars is for the purpose of explaining the planets in the same manner as the swiftest apogee (*śīghrocca*);
therefore, this calculation is also performed for Mercury and Venus.
"In the center of its own circle, touching the orbital circle":
"touching the orbital circle" means that which touches the orbital circle; what is that? It is the center of its own circle.
The center of its own circle;
and that which is both the center of its own circle and touches the orbital circle—that is the "center of its own circle touching the orbital circle.
In that [point], namely, at the center of its own circle touching the orbital circle.
