The mean planet: that which is the mean planet is situated at the center of its own orbit where it touches the circumference of the epicycle (kakṣyāmaṇḍala).
This is what is meant: the mean planet is located at the point where the deferent (kakṣyā) and the epicycle (pratimaṇḍala) intersect.
"That very [longitude] is the true [longitude]"—thus [it is said].
[In the calculation of the true planet, the presentation of the opinions of others:
Now, others provide a different interpretation.
They go in the forward direction, thus they are "forward-going" (*anulomagāni*).
What are they? The verses; that is to say, the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*).
From the slow apogee (mandocca): those [mean motions] which follow the path of the slow apogee, starting from the slow apogee and proceeding in direct order (anuloma),
because the argument of the slow apogee (mandoccakendra) increases day by day.
"Moving in reverse from the swift [apex]":
starting from the swift apogee, those which are the revolutions of the swift apogee move in reverse, because the center of the swift apogee decreases day by day.
In this regard, the following must be asked: how is the anomaly of the apogee of the slow motion accumulated day by day, and how is the anomaly of the apogee of the fast motion diminished day by day?

It is said: when the apogee of the slow motion (mandocca) falls behind the planet, the movements of the slow epicycle (mandakendra) are accumulated; when the apogee of the fast motion (śīghrocca) falls behind the planet, the movements of the fast epicycle (śīghrakendra) are diminished.
If, because of its great magnitude, the apogee of the fast motion does not fall behind the planet, then the circle is projected and then subtracted.
In that case, revolutions should be subtracted from revolutions,
signs from signs, and degrees from degrees.
The sequence is *liptāḥ*, *liptābhyaḥ*, and so forth;
in that context, the revolutions of the apogee of the swifter planet do not even subtract from the revolutions of the planet itself.
Why is this circle of asterisms (bhagaṇa) added [to the longitude] and then subtracted from the apogee of the swift motion?
Therefore, by the logic of calculation, even those circles of swift motion move only in the direct (anuloma) direction;
however, for the sake of simplifying the manual (karaṇalāghava), the Teacher has stated that "the circles move in the reverse (pratiloma) direction."
What, then, is the simplicity of calculation here? It is the freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*).

If the planet falls behind the mean anomaly of the apogee (*śīghrocca*), then the planet is subtracted from the mean anomaly of the apogee; and when the mean anomaly of the apogee falls behind the planet, then the mean anomaly of the apogee is subtracted from the planet.
This is indeed true; however, the assumption of the bow's circumference deviates when the swifter apogee is ahead of the planet.
In that case, the sine (jyā) is one way and the circumference (paridhi) is another;
at that very time, when the planet is subtracted from the swift apogee (śīghrocca), the sine is different and the circumference is likewise different.
Now, if it is thought that when the planet is subtracted from the swift apogee, what was the first quadrant becomes the fourth quadrant—
That which is the second word is the third word;
that which is the third word is the second word;
and that which is the fourth word is the first word.
In that case, according to the superior conception,
the apogee should be subtracted from the planet,
and the planet from the perigee.
The slow and swift revolutions proceed in direct and reverse order respectively.
"Fixed upon the orbital circle" (*kakṣyāmaṇḍalalagna*):
the circle of the orbit is the *kakṣyāmaṇḍala*.

Alternatively, it is both a girth-band (*kakṣyā*) and a circle (*maṇḍala*), hence a "girth-circle" (*kakṣyāmaṇḍala*). Attached by that girth-circle is the "attached-to-the-girth-circle" (*kakṣyāmaṇḍalalagna*). What is it? It is the planet, namely the mean [planet].
Within its own motion (*svavṛtta*):
"its own motion" means its individual motion;
and that is understood generally as both slow motion (*mandavṛtta*) and fast motion (*śīghravṛtta*).

The center of its own slow orbit and its own fast orbit is the "center of its own orbit. In that place is the mean position of the planet, and it is attached to the circumference of the celestial sphere (kakṣyāmaṇḍala).
One should fix it so that the center lies upon the circumference of its own circle;
one should fix it on that [circle] so that the center likewise lies upon the circumference of the felloe-circle.
In that case, one should observe that the chord remains situated exactly as it does within its own circle of the circumference.
How so? Just as there is a wooden chord consisting of ninety-six parts for the circle of the circumference, so too here a wooden chord consisting of ninety-six parts is to be conceived.

For example: beginning from the apogee, by means of the sine of the arc (bhujajyā) and the cosine (koṭijyā), one performs a rule of three: "If these are the sine and cosine on a circumference of three hundred and sixty [minutes], then what are they on the circumference of the apogee and perigee? Or alternatively: "If these are the sine and cosine with respect to the radius (vyāsārdha)..."

Then, by means of the radius of the eccentric circle (*uccanīcavṛtta*) which is equal to the final result, [the values for] *ke* are obtained; these are the sine of the arm (*bhujajyā*) and the sine of the perpendicular (*koṭijyā*) of the eccentric circle. In that regard, since the calculation of the perpendicular (*koṭi*) is situated above the radius in the first and fourth quadrants, it is added to the radius.
Since the second and third terms have proceeded by being diminished by half the diameter (*vyāsārdha*), they are subtracted from the half-diameter;
thus the *koṭi* is produced,
and the square root of the sum of the squares of the *bhuja* and *koṭi* is the *karṇa*.
Thus is the derivation of the *karṇa* for both the slow and the fast [mean motions]. // 21 //
[The calculation of the true positions of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars according to the method of the low and high eccentricities.
To demonstrate the addition and subtraction for the planets, he says:
"From the apogee of the slowest [motion], there shall be loss, gain, and gain-and-loss; from the apogee of the swiftest, it is the reverse."
In the case of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, from the slower planet [the Sun], there is a debt of half a sign, and in the preceding [case] it becomes wealth.
"Destruction, wealth, and the destruction of wealth" (*kṣayadhanadhanakṣayāḥ*):

[this compound is analyzed as] destruction (*kṣayaḥ*), wealth (*dhanaḥ*), and wealth (*dhanaḥ*) and destruction (*kṣayaḥ*). These—destruction, wealth, and the destruction of wealth—are to be understood as corresponding respectively to the [preceding] terms.
For example: in the first step there is loss;
in the second step there is gain; and in the third step there is indeed gain.
"In the fourth quarter, there is destruction. This is the sequence beginning with destruction.
As for why the sequence of quarters is adopted, he says: "From the planet proceeding from its apogee of slowness (*mandocca*)."
Why? It is said: the word "from the apogee" (*mandoccāt*) here expresses a limit (*maryādā*).
Therefore, by the phrase "from the apogee," the planet proceeding from the apogee is understood.
How is that planet proceeding from the apogee to be known?
It is said: there is nothing at all to be understood here [beyond this].
To whatever extent a planet exceeds its apogee of slowness (*mandocca*), by that much it is to be known as a planet proceeding from its apogee of slowness.
Therefore, for the sake of fully understanding that, the apogee of slowness is subtracted from the planet.

In that case, by means of the remaining [longitude] in signs and so forth, this planet has proceeded from the slow apogee (mandocca). Therefore, the result derived from the sequential sine (kramajyā) in the first quadrant is calculated through the rule of three (trairāśika).

If this is the chord for a circumference of three hundred and sixty [units], then what is it for the circumference of the desired planet? This result is obtained; this is precisely the rule of three (trairāśika).
Of the circumference of three hundred and sixty minus one and a half *dhanus*,
eighty is the divisor for the sine multiplied by that circumference, according to the number of syllables stated for its own parts of the circumference.
The multiplier is the number of syllables in one's own circumference;
the quotient obtained is indeed a debt.
This is because, in the second quadrant, the sines are arranged in reverse order.
The result of the inverse sine (utkramajyā) is additive;
furthermore, since the direct sines (kramajyā) are arranged in order in the third quadrant, the result of the direct sine is additive;
in the fourth quadrant, since the sines are arranged in inverse order, the result of the inverse sine is subtractive.
In that case, when the apogee is in the first quadrant,
the resulting correction itself is subtracted from the planet.
When the apogee is in the second quadrant, then the entire correction produced by the sine of the radius of the first quadrant is subtracted.
The result of the inverse sine (utkramajyā) of the second quadrant is positive.
The third and fourth quadrants are explained by the first and second quadrants respectively.
Alternatively, for the sake of simplifying the calculation, it is done thus: whatever result of the sequential sine (kramajyā) arises in the first quadrant is a decrease.

Regarding the second quarter (pada): that which has arisen and subsequently passed—the zodiacal sign and so forth belonging to the past—is positive in nature, as opposed to the three signs designated as the first quarter which are negative in nature.
Having subtracted from that what has been traversed in the second quarter, the remainder remains as a negative value;
therefore, the resulting fruit is a subtraction from the mean planet.
Thus, at the end of the second term, because the loss and the gain are equal, nothing remains.
Therefore, by implication, this meaning arises: in the first term, the result of the subtracted sine (gatajyāphala) is the loss.
In the second quadrant as well, the attained sine-result (jyāphala) is a decrease.
By this, the slow epicycle-result (mandakendraphala) is a decrease in the case of Aries and so forth;
that very same result, which was designated as the "traversed" sine in the first quadrant, is the "unattained" [sine] in the second quadrant.
That which is designated as "ten million" (*koṭi*) is [unaccounted] in the first term,
but is included in the second term and in the third and fourth terms.
In the third term, the result of the sequential sine (*kramajyāphala*) is positive.

In the fourth quarter, from the three signs constituting the third quarter—which are designated as wealth (dhana) because they are wealth—the signs beginning with the first sign of the fourth quarter, designated as loss (kṣaya), are subtracted;
the remainder remains as wealth alone. Thus, at the end of the fourth quarter, because wealth and loss are equal, nothing remains.
Therefore, here too, the same meaning applies: the result of the arm (bhuja-phala) is positive in the quadrants beginning with Libra.
This is indeed well understood;
however, this would be so only if the circumferences were equal in all the quadrants.
Furthermore, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are not recited as being equal;
and if the enclosing sticks are unequal, the positioning of the circular altar (*pratimaṇḍala*) would also be contradicted.
Why? Because in the first quarter, the enclosing stick of Venus (*śukra*) is four [units].
In that case, when reaching the second position,
the pair of circumferences is reduced by half;
however, as the planet moves, it proceeds gradually.
Not by the leap of a deer;
this is not a fault;
the enclosing sticks are equal.
But was it not said that "the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are not recited as being equal"?
This is not so;
for it is understood thus: these enclosing sticks consist of [variable] increase and decrease.
Because they consist of an increase and decrease equal to that [of the preceding], there is an arrangement of sequential and non-sequential order;
since it is precisely those [factors] that come into being,
they are said to be "equal" to that.

For example: having multiplied the sine of the increment by the difference between the circumferences in the first quadrant, the result is divided by the radius; this is added to the circumference of the odd quadrant if it is deficient, and subtracted if it is excessive.
By means of the first and second quadrants, the third and fourth quadrants are explained.
By inversion from the swift apogee— that is,
from the center of the swift apogee— the result of the sines, according to the sequence of the quarters (padas), is reversed:
it is additive in the first and fourth quarters.

The reversal is that there is destruction in the second and third [houses]. Alternatively, the *bhujāphala* (arm-fruit) brought forward according to the sequence of direct motion is positive in Aries and so on, and negative in Libra and so on.
The entire procedure for moving the periphery and so forth is exactly as before.

Here, the equation of center (śīghraphala) is multiplied by the radius (vyāsārdha); the result obtained by dividing that by the resulting hypotenuse (karṇa) is the fruit, whether positive or negative.
This operation is a rule of three (trairāśika): if this is the fruit on the circle of the radius, [then what is it on the hypotenuse?]

When that is obtained, then by means of inverse proportion (*vyastatrairāśika*), one determines how much [the distance] is in the circle of the swift apogee: the radius (*vyāsārdha*) is the multiplier (*guṇakāra*), and the radius-vector (*karṇa*) is the divisor (*bhāgahāra*).
Why is this an inverse proportion here?

It is said: "In a small circle, the accumulations (*rāśi*) are to be known as small; in a large [circle], they are to be known as large" (Kālakriyā, 14). Now, why is the result of the apogee (*mandocca*) not calculated in this manner?
It is said: even if it were calculated, the result would be exactly the same; therefore, it is not performed.
Why? Because the apogee-distance (mandocca-karṇa) remains unchanged.

And in that case, when the radius of the circle (vyāsārdha) is multiplied by the unmodified fruit and divided by the distance (karṇa), the resulting fruit is exactly the same as that previously obtained.
Why, then, is the [mean] ear (karṇa) not distinguished as being rapid?
Because there is no distinct operation [to differentiate it].
Now, in this regard, this must be asked: just as the radius of the circle of the orbit (kakṣyāmaṇḍala) is its own yojana-ear (yojanakarṇa), which is half the diameter, [so too is the case here].
And that [orbit] being measured by its own smeared [minutes], there are 3438 [minutes]; this very same value is the semi-diameter of the epicycle as well.
There is no need for a rule of three (trairāśika) with respect to the minutes of the sine-result produced from the orbital circle (kakṣyāmaṇḍala).
Because the semi-diameters of the epicycle and the [mean] circle are equal.
Now, if it is thought that the hypotenuse produced by the side and the perpendicular arising at that time is the semi-diameter of the epicycle,
then the justification for the rule of three (trairāśika) follows from that.
If that is so, then the epicycle is not equal to the circle of the orbit.
To this it is replied: from the beginning of the fourth quarter [of the verse], the circle of the orbit and the epicycle are equal;
therefore, the semi-diameter (vyāsārdha) of the circle of the orbit and the epicycle is the same.
From that point onward, the semi-diameter of the epicycle increases gradually.
Thus, as it increases step by step, when the planet reaches its maximum altitude (*svocca*), the semi-diameter of the circle of maximum altitude becomes fully increased.
That same value, decreasing in reverse order starting from the beginning of the first quadrant, returns to the original semi-diameter at the end of the first quadrant.

In this manner, as it gradually diminishes, at the end of the second quadrant, half the diameter of the eccentric circle becomes diminished; and at the end of the third [quadrant], as it increases in reverse order, it becomes equal to the semi-diameter of the circle of the epicycle itself. Because the planet's increase and decrease consist of its movement through the ascending and descending nodes, for this reason the instruction regarding the *pratimaṇḍala* (eccentric circle) is given.

Since the determination of a planet's apogee and perigee occurs precisely from the center of the dense earth, it is the radius [of the epicycle] alone that is increased or decreased by the *koṭiphala*.
Now, if there were an increase or decrease of the radius from the center of the eccentric circle (*pratimaṇḍala*),
then a third circle would have to be postulated.
From the center of the dense earth, there is an increase and decrease [of the distance] up to the ear;
therefore, by means of that ear,
the derivation of the inverse rule of three (vyastatrairāśika) is established.
This is established by the very logic of calculation:
regarding Saturn (śani), Jupiter (guru), and Mars (kuja); Saturn and Jupiter and Mars are "Saturn-Jupiter-Mars" (śanigurukujāḥ).
Therefore, regarding those [planets] Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, whatever result arises starting from their slowest point (mandocca), that becomes half [in magnitude],
whether negative or positive; this is in the previous case, starting from the slowest point.
Furthermore, whatever result arises from the [mean] velocity, half of that is applied to those [equations] in the first case of rapid motion;
in other cases, namely the second operation involving both slow and rapid motions, it is understood by implication that the entire result of the slow and rapid motions is applied.
The degrees resulting from the slow and rapid motions are then assigned as either a debt or a credit.

Since the planet revolves by means of the wooden pin (kāṣṭha), where is that result—where is the debt or where is the wealth? This refers to Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars; here, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are taken as the mean planets themselves.
Why? Because it is the means for clarifying the mean [longitude]. For at that time, these [aspects] become manifest.
If this rite is performed when Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are in their mean [positions], [the result is achieved].
When the half-arc of the fruit of the apogee is added to or subtracted from the mean [longitude], the mean state of that [mean longitude] thus made into a debt or a credit is diminished;
therefore, the addition or subtraction of the half-arc of the fruit of the perigee would apply to the unmodified mean.
This is not so.
It will indeed be increased or decreased by half the arc of the equation of the apsis (mandocca-phala).
Why? Because of the rule: "That which has undergone a modification in one part is not different from the original" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 4.1.83, *Patañjala-Mahābhāṣya*).
Thus, even though it has been modified in one part, it remains the middle term itself.
Just as Devadatta, even when well-adorned, does not abandon his own identity, nor even through the cutting off of his ears and nose;
so it is here as well.
In those respective cases, two operations are performed upon the mean [longitude].
Alternatively, half of the result derived from the apogee of the first [equation] is applied to the mean, because it has arisen from the mean;

however, as for half of the result derived from the apogee of the anomaly, since that half-result has already been brought forth by the single correction, it is applied only after that single correction has been made.
Therefore, that entire result of the apogee (mandocca-phala), derived from the two operations, is applied to the mean planet;
that becomes the true mean.
Now, this must be asked: why is that which is obtained from the apogee as established by the two operations not applied directly to the [mean planet] as it stands after those two operations?
It is said: “The mean [longitude] is corrected by the equation of center from the apsis” (*Kālakriyā*, 23);
thus, it is performed upon the mean [longitude].
But is it not the case that the mean [longitude], even when established through two operations, remains indeed the mean?
Why? Because of the statement: "That which is modified in one part is not different [from the original].
If that is so, then since [the result] is already established, the Teacher, by again employing the term "clear-middle," indicates that it is "one whose middle is unmodified."
Otherwise, the separate mention of the "clear" (sphuṭa) mean planet would be redundant.
Therefore, the second correction (phala),
which has been derived from the apogee, is applied in its entirety to the mean planet.
"The true [mean] should be known from the swift apogee.

Thus, when this is done, the mean [longitude] becomes true through the operation of the swift apogee; therefore, the entire arc of the result of the swift apogee is applied to the mean true [longitude], and it becomes true.

To demonstrate the method for calculating debt and wealth, one should draw a circular diagram on level ground using a compass with a radius equal to the semi-diameter [of the circle], and therein draw the lines for the mother and father [the north-south and east-west axes].
That orbital circle is constructed with lines representing the sines of the zodiacal signs.

Then, from the center of that circle, at a distance equal to the desired number of minutes of the maximum equation (antyaphala) of the planet, one should likewise place the center to the south using a compass with the same semi-diameter.
One should draw a circle of equal circumference;
that is the counter-circle (*pratimaṇḍala*).
With a radius equal to the distance by which the counter-circle extends outward from the [inner] enclosure circle (*kakṣyāmaṇḍala*), one should draw it.

Having made the center at the intersection of the east-west and north-south lines of the orbital circle (kakṣyāmaṇḍala), two circles are drawn on both sides; these are the [low and high] apsis circles (nīcocca-vṛtta).
Just as there is a variation in the sine of the zodiacal signs (rāśijyāvikalpa) in the orbital circle, so it should be performed for those two.

Because the first and fourth positions are situated above the circle of the orbit (*kakṣyāmaṇḍala*), the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is formed by adding the calculation of the *koṭi* to the semi-diameter of the counter-orbit (*pratimaṇḍala*). A cord of that same measure touches the circumference of the counter-orbit at a certain point; at that location is the true planet (*sphuṭagraha*). And the chord of the orbit-circle lies ahead of that—this is the meaning.
In the first and fourth quarters,
that produced fruit is diminished due to the middle [node] being grasped;
in the second and third quarters, because the epicycle is situated below the circle of the orbit.
Having subtracted the calculation of the koti from the semi-diameter, a hypotenuse (karṇa) is formed;

a cord of that same measure, starting from the center of the epicycle (kakṣyāmaṇḍala), touches the circumference of the counter-epicycle (pratimaṇḍala) at a certain point, and there the true planet (sphuṭagraha) is located. Furthermore, it stands ahead of the point on the epicycle where the sine (jyā) was measured.
Therefore, that produced result is accumulated through the middle-term extraction (*madhyamagraha*) of the second and third terms.

For those for whom the loss, gain, gain, and loss occur from the *śīghrocca* (the apogee of anomaly), this is the derivation of debt and credit; likewise, it is the same for the *mandocca* (the apogee of mean motion).
However, for those whose reading is "from the *śīghrocca*" with the [terms] reversed, this very derivation is the opposite.
How so? The planet is clearly visible in the epicycle (*pratimaṇḍala*), while its mean position is on the orbital circle (*kakṣyāmaṇḍala*) for the purpose of calculating the apogee of the anomaly.
Furthermore, the sine of the anomaly (*kendrajyā*) arises from the mean anomaly being drawn back [to the orbit] because it stands behind [the planet] in the first and fourth quadrants.

The result becomes positive wealth because the sine of the anomaly (kendrajyā) is situated in front of the planet in the first and fourth quadrants; however, in the second and third quadrants, because the sine of the anomaly is situated behind the planet, that result is subtracted.
Therefore, this is established through the mutual opposition of the slow and fast motions.

The Master has shown the point where the planet is clearly visible as the location corresponding to the measure of the distance between the tips of the true [mean] planet and the planet itself. Therefore, when a thread equal in length to that measure of the distance between the tips of the true planet and the planet is extended from the center of the circle of the orbit (kakṣyāmaṇḍala) toward the circumference of the counter-orbit (pratimaṇḍala) in divisions of degrees, the planet is clearly visible at the point where it touches.
Others, however, read it differently: "In the case of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, when Saturn is at its maximum altitude (mandocca), half of the result becomes negative or positive, as before.

This means that when Saturn is at its maximum altitude, half of the result is negative or positive; if that [result] for the planet was negative or positive, then it is understood by implication that it becomes positive or negative respectively at the maximum altitude.

In that regard, it is stated as follows: "To what extent does that fruit become a debt when [applied to] the slow apogee (mandocca), and how does it become a credit? Conversely, how does a credit become a debt? It is said: "Because the fruit of the fast apogee (śīghrocca) and the fruit of the slow apogee—these two fruits have the slow apogee as their basis."
The two results are to be superimposed; therefore, the equation of the apsis is calculated first. Because of the inclusion of the four operations, that resulting correction is applied right there.

For example: having first brought the *śīghra* correction and made half of it either a debt or a credit in the *mandocca*, and having corrected that by the *manda* anomaly (*manda-āyata*)—the planet, when corrected by the *mandocca* as refined by those two corrections, becomes the true mean planet; that [true mean] is then made true by the *śīghra* operation. This is another method of calculation. // 22 //
[Another method for the correction of Saturn,
Jupiter, and Mars] He states another method for the correction of the planets:
"From the apogee of the slow motion (mandocca) and from the apogee of the fast motion (śīghrocca), half [the value] is subtracted and added to the planets respectively in the slow and fast motions."
The mean [planets] are to be known as true from the apogee of slow motion, and the true [planets] from the apogee of fast motion. // 23 //

The half-arc of the result that has been obtained from the apogee (mandocca) should be applied as either a subtraction or an addition to the planets; [or rather, it should be applied as a subtraction or an addition to the slow-moving planets].
If this is the case, then the word "ca" (and) must be used.
Without the word "ca," the meaning "to the planets and to the slow-moving planets" would not be obtained.
The letter *ca* need not be employed; even without the letter *ca*, the sense of "and" (*cārtha*) is understood.
[How so? It is thus:
"In the case of the young, the old, the wounded, and the emaciated, one should administer milk with due care"—
here, because the sense of "and" (ca) is understood even without the word being explicitly stated,
so it is in this case as well.
It should also be stated regarding one's own slow [factors],
so that it is performed among one's own middling and one's own slow [factors].
Furthermore, the word "own" (sva) need not even be employed.
Since the accomplishment of the calculation depends precisely upon the mean of one's own planet and its own [maximum] slowness,
it is as when it is said, "One must speak to one's mother" and "One must serve one's father.
In that context, it is not specified, "To one's own mother" or "To one's own father."
Thus it is here as well.

Now, regarding this half-fruit which has arrived at the apogee (mandocca), it is applied as either a credit or a debit to the mean planet according to the sequence of decrease or increase. But how is it applied again in the case of the slow motion (manda)?
Is it because the sequence of debt and credit for the slow motion (*manda*) has not been stated?
It is said: the apogee of slow motion (*mandocca*) is always a debt to the planet.
In that case, whatever is the planet's debt is added to the apogee of slow motion.
Because it is of the nature of a debt:
that which is of the nature of wealth in the planet is subtracted from the apogee,
precisely because the apogee is of the nature of a debt.
And this is the principle of calculation: the subtraction of debts from debts or of assets from assets, and the addition of debts to assets or of assets to debts.
Therefore, by this sequence, the increase and decrease of half the fruit occur at the apogee (mandocca).

And that half-fruit which [results] from the swift apogee (śīghrocca) is likewise applied as either a credit or a debit to the slow [mean planet] (manda), but in the opposite manner to the planet itself;

however, because there is no further purpose regarding the planets themselves, it is not applied to them. The corrected slow apogee (mandocca) is taken as the slow apogee refined by the half-fruit of the slow apogee and the swift apogee.
Why? Because of the slow movement indicated for the two [mean] motions.
Therefore, whatever result is obtained by subtracting that same slow [motion] from the mean, that entire amount—whether debt or credit—is applied to the means;
these are the true means (sphuṭamadhyāḥ).
Because they exist within the clear mean, those which are not clear are "mean" (madhyama) because they produce the result in the mean states that are unmodified;
or else, the means of the clear are the "clear-means" (sphuṭamadhyama).
They are produced by a single karma, by which they depend upon a second, distinct karma;
they should be known as clear because of their rapid emergence.
The result derived from the swiftest apsis (śīghrocca) is applied to them, whereby they become manifest (sphuṭa).
The word "ca" (and) expresses the conjunction of the two results.
They are to be known, understood, and comprehended—this is the meaning. // 23 //
[The correction of Venus and Mercury] He states the operation for Venus and Mercury:
half of [the anomaly] subtracted from the swifter apogee should be applied as a debt or credit to its own slower apogee.
But Venus and Mercury, being [calculated] from the mean positions, become manifestly true when derived from the [mean] apogee. // 24 //
The phrase "from the swift apogee" (śīghroccāt) refers to the result previously obtained from the swift apogee;
that very same result from the swift apogee is used hereafter.
In this context, "half of that" means it is reduced by half.
Debt and wealth must be calculated.
If there is debt in the planet, then it must be treated as wealth;
by implication, it is understood that the debt of wealth must be subtracted.
He asks: "Where? [The answer is: "In its own apogee. Its own apogee is *svamandocca*; in that *svamandocca*.
Venus and Mercury become clearly mean [mean anomaly]. How so? From the established [longitude] of the apogee;
that apogee which has been corrected by half the equation of the apsis is the established one.
Thus it is stated.
Therefore, from the established slow [mean], the true mean [longitude] arises.

This is what is meant: having subtracted that established slow [mean] from the mean planet, the true mean longitudes of those two, Venus and Mercury, are obtained through the addition or subtraction of the remaining result.
From your [text], by the word "but" (*tu*), this is established: "The true [meanings] are to be known from the fast-moving [planet] as well" (Kālakriyā 23). // 24 //
[The interval between the true apogee and the planet.
To calculate the measure of the interval between the true apogee and the planet, he says:
"The product of its own radius and the distance between the true apogee and the planet, divided by the semi-major axis."
The velocity of the planet that exists in the [mean] orbit is the [velocity] at the apogee and perigee of the anomaly.
The method for calculating the distance between the stars and planets and the earth is now stated.
That which is the interval between the earth and a star or planet is the "distance from the earth to the star or planet" (bhūtārāgrahavivara); this is what he will state.
[The formula is: the product of its own radius and the semi-diameter [of the orbit] divided by the radius.
The radius of the circle is the trijyā (triple-chord).
Divided by the trijyā means divided by the radius.
The product of two respective radii is the "svakarṇasaṃvarga" (the product of their own radii).

This is what is meant: the product of the apsis-distance of the slow motion (*manda-uccakarṇa*) and the apsis-distance of the fast motion (*śīghra-uccakarṇa*) is the multiplication of its own distances;
this, divided by the semi-diameter (*vyāsārdha*), is the velocity of the planet in the orbit when it is raised to that extent.
The velocity of a planet produced by the equations of anomaly and apsis exists at the front of its distance from the true star (bhūtārā).
For this very reason, the distance from the true star serves as the divisor in the calculation of the latitudinal displacement (vikṣepa).
Others say that the distance from the true star is not the divisor.

What then? It is the semi-diameter [of the epicycle]. For this is the rule of three here: if by the radius (trijyā) the deviation (vikṣepa) stated for its own planet is obtained, then by this sine of the arc of the interval between the desired planet and its own apsis, which is the sine of the amplitude (bhujajyā), what [is obtained]?
This is not correctly understood;

if this alone were the system of three sets (*trairāśika*), then the conjunctions of the lunar mansions, stars, planets, and the moon would always occur in that same direction with equal deviations and intervals.
Because the stars and constellations lack the possibility of high or low motion,

these planets and constellations are nevertheless seen to undergo various states— such as being distant or near, and their conjunctions involving division, the eclipsing of rays, and moving to the right or left— due to the influence of distance and proximity.

If the semi-diameter [of the epicycle] alone were the divisor, then all [planets] would have equal velocities. Due to the difference between the true apogee and the planet, the deviation (vikṣepa) is found to be small or great in the conjunctions of lunar mansions, stars, and planets.
Whether the displacement is small or great, the conjunctions with the intermediate directions—determined by the power of the southern and northern directions—are logically established.
Therefore, the divisor is precisely the distance between the true planet and the node (*bhūtārāgra*).
This operation also consists of two sets of the rule of three (*trairāśika*).

How so? If, by means of the sine of the arm of the difference between the nodes— which is equal to the semi-diameter— one obtains a latitude (vikṣepa) that is either small or great according to its own [proportion], then what latitude is obtained by this [other] sine of the arm produced from the difference between the nodes?

Furthermore, there is another separate threefold proportion (*trairāśika*): if this displacement (*vikṣepa*) is obtained when the diameter of the epicycle (*kakṣyāmaṇḍala*) is the divisor, then what is it when the true apogee and planet separation at the periphery of the ultimate epicycle (*paramārthapratimaṇḍala*) is the divisor?
In the previous threefold proportion, the semi-diameter was the divisor; [here, however, it is the full diameter].
That very same [value] is the multiplier in the second *trairāśika* because of its inversion;
therefore, when the multiplier and the divisor have been eliminated,
the *vikṣepa* (latitude) of the *bhuja-jyā* of the interval between the eclipses (*pātāntara*) is the multiplier.
The divisor is the difference between the true apogee and the planet; the result is the equation of the center (vikṣepa) of the desired planet.
Thus, when the latitudes of the desired planet and the [mean] planet are in the same direction, they are subtracted;
because both proceed from the apakrama-maṇḍala (the declination circle),
their difference becomes equal to that specific latitude.
In that case as well, due to the influence of their respective lesser or greater latitudes, they are mutually related as being south and north of each other.
When the latitudes are in opposite directions, they are to be added together,
because one is to the south of the ecliptic and the other is to the north.

Therefore, the measure of the interval between them is the application of the deviation; one-fourth of the difference in the minutes of arc of the deviation should be stated as the measure in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Furthermore, when there are no minutes of arc in the interval, [the measure is simply the whole number].
Or, if they are small, then because of their mutual non-overlapping, there is either a complete obscuration or a partial obscuration.

In that case, the calculation of the *sthityardha* (half-duration of the eclipse) in *nāḍikās* is performed through the conjunction with the desired planet's latitude, by means of its half-extent and its declination, or by separation.
[The calculation of the clear *yojanakarṇa* (earth-chord) for the luminous planets.]
Now, this calculation is performed for the purpose of fully understanding the parallax and the equation of center within the conjunctions of the lunar mansions, stars, and planets.

Regarding the statement, "The degrees of the moon are *śa-śi-ṅ-a-ṇa-na-māṃ*," it has been explained therein that the distance from the moon multiplied by the letters beginning with *ṅa* becomes the divisor for Venus and the other planets.
The moon's yojana-distance (karṇa) multiplied by five becomes the yojana-distance of Venus; by ten, that of Jupiter;
by fifteen, that of Mercury;
and by twenty, that of Saturn.
[The orbit] of Mars is twenty-five [yojanas].
If this is so, then would it not contradict the description of the orbits of the planets?
This is not a fault.

Up to that point, the planets remain in their respective orbits; here, however, the correction for parallax (dṛṣṭiparikarma) is performed by those who employ the [parameters] beginning with *nā* as multipliers.

This *yojanakarṇa* (earth-chord), multiplied by the difference between the true distance of the planet and the radius of the earth, and divided by the semi-diameter [of the celestial sphere], becomes the corrected value.

This too is a rule of three proportions (*trairāśika*): if so many *yojanas* are obtained by means of the minutes of arc of the semidiameter, then how many are obtained by means of the minutes of arc of the distance between the true apogee and the planet?

Alternatively, by combining two rules of three proportions, the desired planet's precise distance in *yojanas* (the *sphuṭayojanakarṇa*) is derived. How so? In the calculation of the distance between the true apogee and the planet, the semidiameter was the divisor.
And here, for the product of the mean and true semi-major axes and the true and mean semi-major axes, the divisor is simply the radius of the circle (vyāsārdha).
Therefore, the product of the two divisors is the divisor for the product of the apogee of the slow motion, the apogee of the fast motion, and the true and mean semi-major axes.
The result is the true *yojanakarṇa*.
This is the meaning produced from those two: the mean *yojanakarṇa*, multiplied by the slow [or] swift *karṇa* and divided by the square of the radius (*vyāsārdha*), becomes the true *yojanakarṇa*.
By this method, the slow *karṇa*—which was derived for the slow planet at its apogee or perigee—is rendered true.

[The Special Rule for the Correction of Planets] Now, the specific method of the general calculation for the true positions of all planets, based on the sun’s debt or credit (dhanarṇa) at rising and setting, will be described.

It is as follows: the daily motions of the sun and other planets are multiplied by the sun’s *bhujāphala* (equation of time), divided by sixty thousand (60,000), and the resulting minutes are applied to the planets according to whether the *bhujāphala* is additive or subtractive.
This is now considered: how is it understood that this operation (*karma*) is not explicitly taught?
This is not a fault;
for it is indeed taught in the passage: "From the rising of the sun on the day of the *buddha* in Laṅkā" (*Gītikā*, 4).

Because of the instruction that "the beginnings of these [lunar] months occur at the passage [of the sun] from the limit of sunrise," and because the sun indeed occupies the zenith of its rising only by virtue of the motion understood through precise calculation (*sphuṭagaṇita*), the rising of the *sphuṭa* (true) sun is adopted. Furthermore, since the true motion is simply the mean motion augmented or diminished by the minutes of arc of its own equation of time (*bhujāphala*) and so forth, [the correction is made] by means of those minutes of the equation of time.

The rule of three (trairāśika) is performed with [the minutes] equal to the breaths: "If the true daily motions of the Sun and other planets are obtained by means of breaths equal to sixty thousand times ten thousand (3,600,000) breaths in one day and night, then what [motion] is obtained by means of the arc-correction minutes (bhujāphalaliptā) which are equal to breaths? Thus, these arc-correction minutes are equal to breaths.
To this it is replied: it has been explained that the rising and so forth of the celestial sphere and other such bodies occurs precisely from sunrise.
Therefore, due to the impulsion of the [celestial] revolution, the mean [longitude] is always either increased or decreased by its own equation of time.

When it is greater, then the circle of luminaries (jyotiścakra) is diminished by the sun's motion by an amount equal to the minutes of arc of the *bhujāphala* (if it is less, it is increased by the sun's motion by an amount equal to the minutes of arc of the *bhujāphala*);
by this conceptualization, the minutes of arc of the *bhujāphala* are then related to the circle of luminaries.
The degrees of the zodiacal circle and the breaths (prāṇas) are equal;
therefore, there is an absence of those degrees of arc resulting from the arm (bhujāphala) which are equal to the breaths,
when the complete Sun derived from the day-count (ahargaṇa) is equal to its own exaltation.
Thus it is at sunrise;
otherwise, even there the correction for longitudinal parallax (*bhuja-antara-phala*) is indeed performed,
for the sun occupies the zenith only when determined through the calculation of the true [longitude].

Thus, the true motions (sphuṭagati) of these planets, beginning with Vivasvat, are reckoned from the limit of sunrise; therefore, the result consisting of increase and decrease is produced solely by virtue of the sun. The corrections for longitudinal difference (deśāntara) and the half-day arc (caradalakarma) are also established by this very same reasoning.
[The calculation is] by proportion (trairāśika) from the sun situated at midnight, sunset, or midday: "If, by sixty nāḍīs, [the respective motion is obtained as follows...]"

When the mean motion is obtained, then by the proportion "if fifteen *ghaṭikās* yield thirty and forty-five [minutes], what do thirty [ghaṭikās] yield?", the resulting minutes are subtracted from the planets at sunrise; thereafter, by that [correction], the sun and other planets become their true positions for that specific time.
And for them, the method of calculation has already been explained clearly:
the operation of the half-ascensional difference (*caradalakarma*) does not apply at midday or midnight;
for sunrise and sunset occur precisely at the attainment of and the departure from the terrestrial horizon (*kṣitijamaṇḍala*).
In this way, the planets have the motion of the sun as their limit.

When, however, they are calculated relative to another planet—just as with the sun—one first determines the time of rising by means of the moon’s rising; then, taking that time of rising as the limit, the calculations are performed.
[This results in the precise knowledge of the division of the first lunar day.]
Thus, for the purpose of fully understanding the determination of the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipat*) through the method of calculation as instructed, it is said:
namely, the true sun is subtracted from the true moon;
since the lunar date (*tithi*) occurs by virtue of the lunar month, therefore "the conjunctions of the sun and moon constitute the lunar months" (*Kālakriyā*).
Thus, when the [result] is clearly manifest, the revolutions (bhagaṇas) are subtracted;
since revolutions are not possible here according to the circumstances, only the signs and so forth are subtracted from the signs and so forth.
Alternatively, those solar revolutions that have been traversed from the beginning of the Kalpa are subtracted from the lunar revolutions.
"From the zodiac signs and so forth, the zodiac signs and so forth [are subtracted]. In that case, the remaining [units] are the lunar months and so forth;
since there is no purpose for the months, the months are discarded.
In that regard, those remaining [quantities], such as the *rāśi* and so forth, which constitute parts of the current lunar month, are converted into *liptās*.

By means of these, a threefold proportion (*trairāśika*) is applied: "If a lunar month is obtained by a difference between the sun and the moon equal to sixty thousand, six hundred (60,600), then how many lunar months are obtained by these *liptās* of difference between the moon and the sun? Thus, it does not yield a full month.
Thus the days are calculated.
According to the rule, "Thirty days shall constitute a month" [Kālakriyā, 1], thirty is the multiplier.

In that case, when applying the reduction (*apavartana*) for both multiplication and division: one [unit] is the thirtieth part of thirty; and the thirteenth part of sixty thousand (*khakhaṣaḍghana*) is seven hundred and twenty.
The minutes of arc of the difference between the sun and the moon are divided by seven hundred and twenty.

The elapsed lunar days of the result are those that have commenced from the first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of the current lunar month; therein, the remaining seconds are the portions consumed by the current lunar day, and when these are subtracted from the divisor-seconds, the remainder is the portion yet to be consumed.

Therefore, by means of those [digits] smeared with the consumed and the consumable, a rule of three is applied: "If one lunar day is obtained by the digits of the difference between the true motions of the sun and the moon for that day, then how many [parts] of a lunar day are obtained by these digits of the consumed and the consumable? In this case, since they do not yield a quotient in whole days, they are converted into *nāḍīs* (minutes).

"Sixty *nāḍīs* constitute a day" (*Kālakriyā*, 1). Having multiplied by sixty and divided by the *liptās* of the difference between the true motions, the resulting *nāḍīs*—whether elapsed or yet to come—represent the time of the lunar day (*tithi*) from the limit of sunrise; this is the "equalizing of the *liptās* of the sun and moon."

Alternatively, at the desired time-limit, the rule for equal smeared portions (*samaliptā*) is applied on the *parvan* day. Having determined the elapsed and remaining portions of the *parvan*, one performs a three-proportion calculation (*trairāśika*) using those elapsed and remaining smeared portions.
For example: if, by means of the smeared portions of the difference between the true daily motions of the sun and the moon, [one calculates] the [longitude] of the sun and the moon...

The true motion (*sphuṭabhukti*) is obtained for each [planet] accordingly; then, by means of these *liptās* of the elapsed and yet-to-be-traversed tithis, one calculates how many *liptās* of true motion are obtained. These *liptās* are added to the Sun when the parvan is yet to be traversed, and to the Moon as well. Now, when the parvan has already elapsed, the *liptās* derived from the respective triproportional calculations (*trairāśika*) for those two are subtracted. Thus...

Since it was stated by us briefly in the *Gaṇitapāda*— in this very Āryā verse, "In the reverse difference from the elapsed [longitude]" (*gaṇita, 31*)— that at the time of completion of the *gantavyagataparvan*, the two [meanings] become equal and smeared (i.e., coincident), it has been demonstrated here in detail [concerning the determination of the lunar day,
the nakṣatra, and the division].

Since worldly convention is based on the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) conjoined with the moon, the determination of the specific lunar mansion conjoined with the moon at the beginning of each day is performed. This is as follows: by means of the moon's degrees (liptās), a rule of three (trairāśika) is applied: "If twenty-seven lunar mansions are obtained by means of the degrees of the [lunar] orbit equal to sixty thousand, zero, and six (060000), then what [number of mansions] is obtained by these degrees traversed by the moon?"
In this case, the reduction (apavartana) of both the multiplier and the divisor is performed.
By dividing twenty-seven by twenty-seven, the result is one; likewise, by dividing sixty thousand (khakhaṣaḍghana) by that same factor, the result is eight hundred.
Therefore, there is a division of the lunar minutes (śaśiliptā) by eight hundred.

The number of those lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī that have already passed is obtained. Having calculated the elapsed and remaining portions of the remainder, the elapsed and remaining *nāḍīs* of the currently occurring mansion are determined.
How so? If sixty *nāḍīs* are obtained by means of the true motion (*sphuṭabhukti*), [then...]
By means of these [proportions] involving the elapsed and the remaining [time], the number of elapsed and remaining *nāḍīs* (hours) is obtained;

since the lunar motion is established as having the duration of one day and night (*ahorātra*), and the measure of a day and night is sixty *nāḍīs*, a rule of three (*trairāśika*) is performed by means of sixty. // 25 //
Thus ends the chapter on the calculation of time (*kālakriyāpāda*) in the *Āryabhaṭatantrabhāṣya*, the work of Bhāskara.
Golapāda [Invocation]: Homage to the one who shines as a vessel filled with the true, auspicious knowledge of Maṅgala.
To the Creator, whose footstool is rubbed by the heads of the gods and asuras.

[The Sphere-Binding: After the performance of the funeral rites (kālakriyā), there is the sphere (gola), because it has been stated: "He speaks of three: calculation (gaṇita), the performance of the funeral rites (kālakriyā), and the sphere (gola)."
That from which things are understood or known is called *golam* (the sphere). What, then, is understood from it?
Everything, including the revolution of the planets, the configuration of the earth, and so forth.
Thus, those who desire to know the ultimate truth (paramārtha) attain the truth by means of the unreal.
For example, physicians perform venesection and other procedures on lotus stalks and the like;
and those skilled in sacrificial instruments perform sacrifices and other rites through the "dry sacrifice" (śuṣkeṣṭi).
Just as grammarians arrive at the correct word through the analysis of roots, suffixes, elisions, augmentations, and vowel modifications,
so too here the astronomers arrive at the ultimate celestial sphere through specific calculations of the field, such as the movement of the gnomon and the suspension of the thread.
Therefore, this work is undertaken merely to provide a general indication of the directions.

Because it is impossible to demonstrate [the whole] in its entirety— who indeed, while painting, would paint even the closing and opening of an eye? Therefore, one should produce a single circular form using saws, from either *śrīparṇī* wood or *vañcula* wood, as the nature of a semi-circular wheel.
Then, one should construct a single circle using two well-fitted semi-circles, or by means of three well-fitted circular segments.

In that [circle], there are three points where the joints of the circular segments are severed: the joint at the side of the arrow-feather (*śurapuṅkha*), the joint at the side of the shaft (*pārśva*), and the joint at the half-portion (*avayavārdha*).

There, one should join the circular segments of these [pieces] together with one another by means of copper pins; having thus produced one circle, one should place it from east to west, and a second from south to north, above and below, so as to form a svastika at their intersection; then, having cut two mandalas at the junction of the svastikas by means of a half-cut.
They should be joined in such a way that only a single circle is perceived. Having inserted four svastikas by means of cutting them in half, one should fix them immovably with copper pegs.
Then, outside those two circles, like a surrounding frame, one should likewise insert another set of four svastikas produced in the four directions by cutting them in half, and fix them immovably.
One should cause the eastern and western circles to be marked with sixty figures,
so that there may be fifteen figures in each of the four divisions,
and these represent the ghaṭīs of the day and night.
In this manner, one should also cause the two remaining circles to be marked with three hundred and sixty [degrees] each;
these are the equinoctial circles [of the southern and northern horizons].

Another mandala of equal size, marked with three hundred and sixty [units], should be formed by making a horizontal division into three parts at both the eastern and western *svastikas*; one should then construct two *svastikas* for the mandala area using two of those three parts.
Alternatively, the division should be conceived in such a way that the meeting point of the three mandalas appears as a single point.

Between the eastern, western, southern, and northern mandalas, from the svastika that is below, one should fashion a svastika by cutting it in half on the twenty-fourth division along the northern spoke to the north; likewise above, from the upper svastika, one should fashion a svastika on the twenty-fourth division along the southern spoke to the south.
In all cases, this ensures stability.
With copper pegs,
the position of the zodiacal signs is thus established crosswise;
that very thing is called the ecliptic.

One should fix another circle of that same measure where the conjunction of the moon occurs; then, having turned it back on the part further to the north, one should fasten it at the point of the *pāta* (node) within half a circle, so that there are four and a half parts between that [circle] and the *apakrama-maṇḍala*.
Thus, one should place it to the south of that [point] at the ninetieth part, such that four and a half parts lie between it and the apakrama-maṇḍala;
this is the *vimaṇḍala*,
which is called the *vikṣepamaṇḍala*.
In this way, there are also orbs for the others from their respective degrees of descent.
For Mercury and Venus, [the calculation is] from the two fast apogees.

The orbs of their respective days and nights are also moving; to the north of the equinox, at a distance equal to the limit of Aries's obliquity, there is an orb extending east-west, which is the day-and-night orb of Aries.

In a distance of degrees equal to the oblique ascension (krānti) at the end of Taurus, there is the [ascensional] interval for Taurus; in a distance of degrees equal to the oblique ascension at the end of Gemini, there is the [ascensional] interval for Gemini;
and those same [intervals], in reverse order, belong to Cancer, Leo, and Virgo.

Thus, to the south of the equinox, one should fix the circles of the respective day-and-night [measures] for Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius; those same [circles], in reverse order, are for Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces.
Upon these circles of respective day-and-night measures, one should bind threads extending from south to north.
Half of those [distances] are the apakramajyās (declination-chords).

Having tied one end of a cord at the point where the equinoctial circle intersects the unmaṇḍala (the diurnal circle) of Aries, one should tie the second end at the intersection of the equinoctial and unmaṇḍala of Pisces;
thus, one should fix the cord that pierces the center of the earth together with the equinoctial line.
Wherever there is the intersection of that first line and another, there occurs half of the first line;
likewise for the halves of the other lines.
All of these are the sines of the declination (apakrama) for the respective days and nights.
However, because it is impossible [to show them all], some are demonstrated;
those which were explained as the circles of the day-and-night [paths] during the deviation and departure [from the equator] are not demonstrated here.
Otherwise, the sphere equal to time cannot be rotated.
Because there are many mandalas,

one should then place a very smooth, straight iron rod— shaped like a cow’s tail in its length and circumference, piercing through the north-south and east-west cross-lines, with both ends protruding, and capable of supporting the weight of a cage— in the center.
One should fashion the ground in that middle space into a perfect circle using clay or some other material.
Thus, this is the single cage for all the planets;
because even though the planets occupy different orbits, they are observed as being situated within a single cage, therefore this alone is the one cage.
Alternatively, separate cages for all [the deities] should be displayed, each having a circumference exactly equal to the extent of its own respective enclosure.

Or else, outside the cage, at the two *svastika* marks (southeast and northwest), one should place a smooth, immovable autumn-staff (*śaradaṇḍikā*) three or four finger-breadths long upon an iron rod.
Then, that which is fashioned according to the dimensions of the respective enclosures and pierced on both sides by the interval between the two wheels—
Having placed the mandala extending from south to north, one should cause her to enter a cage in its center and insert that iron rod through both side-piercings,
so that the arrow-shaft becomes immersed within the boundaries of the two cages.
One should place another vṛtta of that same measure, extending both forward and backward, and having produced svastikas above and below as before;
that is the *samamaṇḍala*.

Furthermore, one should again prepare another circle equipped with its accessories, marked with svastikas produced in the four cardinal directions and pierced by the intersection of the north-south and east-west svastikas; having inserted an iron rod at both points, one should fix it immovably.
That is the terrestrial circle (kṣitijamaṇḍala).
Thus, this sphere remains exactly level at the equinox.
To the north of the equinox, one should make a piercing (vedha) above the northern cross-point of the celestial sphere at as many degrees as the obliquity of the ecliptic (akṣa);
and to the south, at that same distance, one should make a piercing below.
Having removed the iron pin from the two previous apertures, one should insert it into the apertures prepared according to the measure of the degrees of the axis of one's own location.
Thus, the sphere remains fixed by the measure of the axis of its own domain; therein, everything indeed becomes visible.

Then, one should insert the tip of an iron rod that has emerged from the north into another circle of the same dimensions as the celestial sphere (khagola), which has been pierced at both ends at a distance of half a circle;
likewise, one should insert the tip of an iron rod that has emerged from the south into the second piercing.
Having fixed it there so that it is immovable,
At the intersection of the eastern and western *svastika*s, one should place that circle fixedly upon the eastern and western *svastika*s by means of a horizontal division as before;
they call that the "outer circle" (*unmaṇḍala*).
One should have all the circles marked with divisions representing three hundred and sixty parts.

Others, however, having dug a pit in level ground to the depth of half the celestial sphere (khagola), place the celestial sphere therein half-submerged such that the terrestrial equator (kṣitijamaṇḍala) lies above; they demonstrate it in this manner, and thus this wooden sphere is constructed.
In the absence of wood, a sphere may be constructed using circular bamboo rods that are well-ripened, small, hollow, and smooth.
Having thus fashioned the sphere, everything remaining is explained in the treatise; [on the terrestrial sphere is the declination circle].
In this regard, first of all, he describes the declination circle (apakrama-maṇḍala): from Aries to Virgo, half of the northern declination circle extends equally to the north;
from Libra to Pisces, the remaining half extends only to the south. // 1 //
"Aries-beginning" (meṣādi) means Aries is the beginning; from that "Aries-beginning," up to the end, which is Virgo.
The end of Virgo is *kanyānta*;
from the beginning of Aries up to the end of Virgo is equal or uniform.
To the north of the water;
half of the apamaṇḍala;
half of the apamaṇḍala, that is, half of the apakrama-maṇḍala.
The half-circle of departure;
"departed" means situated obliquely.
"Taulyādi" refers to the beginning of weighing and so forth, such as the scales.
Therefore, from Libra and so forth,
"the end of Pisces" means *mīnāntam*;
that is, starting from Libra and continuing until the end of Pisces.

"Half of the remainder" (śeṣārdha) means both the remainder and half of that remainder; alternatively, "half of the remainder" refers to half of the remainder of the stellar sphere (jyotiścakra), which is designated as the ecliptic (apamaṇḍala).
To the south of that,
by way of the southern direction, it is half of that.
The word "eva" (indeed) is employed for the purpose of completing the verse.
Alternatively, it shows even half a digit in the southern half;
just as the circle of declination is situated obliquely to the north,
so too here, half of that very same circle of declination remains obliquely to the south.

In this context, even without the word "equal" (*sama*), the equality of the two halves of the northern and southern declination circles is understood from the mention of the measure of six signs; thus, the inclusion of the word "equal" is redundant. It is not redundant: because of the specific difference in latitude (*akṣa*) for each region, the rising times of the signs are observed to be unequal.

Without the word "equal" (*sama*), there would be the inclusion of heaps of unequal measure; consequently, due to the difference in latitude (*akṣa*), the declination-sines (*apakramajyā*) of Aries and the other signs would vary in measure according to each location.
However, when the word "equal" is employed, the inclusion of heaps of equal measure is established.
Because every single zodiacal sign (rāśi) constitutes one-twelfth part of the circle of luminaries (jyotiścakra), and each of those is measured by thirty degrees.
Thus, the apakrama-maṇḍala (the circle of declination) stands obliquely to the north of the equinox, from the beginning of Aries to the end of Virgo;
that same [circle] likewise stands to the south of the equinox, from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces.
How is it understood that this is "from the equinox," even though it is not explicitly stated?
This is not a fault;
by saying "to the north and south," the teacher demonstrates that the equinoctial circle (viṣuvanmaṇḍala) is indeed established.
For otherwise, the expression "to the north and south" would be meaningless;
moreover, the words "north" and "south" denote directions.
The determination of the directions depends [on this];
therefore, having first fixed the equinoctial circle, the solstitial circle is then fixed.
All mandalas indeed are made marked with three hundred and sixty [divisions], because the circle of luminaries (jyotiścakra) consists of three hundred and sixty parts. // 1 //
[Regarding those moving in the apakrama-maṇḍala:
He states which ones revolve in that apakrama-maṇḍala:
"The stars, the planets, the moon, and the *pāta* revolve incessantly in the apamaṇḍala, as does the sun."
For as that [sun] revolves through half the orb from the point of conjunction, the shadow of the earth indeed moves.
The stellar planets— Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn—
and the lunar nodes (the moon and its apogee) revolve incessantly and without interruption upon the ecliptic, that is, the circle of declination.
And not only these—the stars, planets, moon, and nodes—do they revolve in the ecliptic; the sun also does so.
Therein, in that ecliptic, the sun revolves incessantly.
And from the sun, at one half of the circle, and again from the sun, at another half of the circle, at a distance of six signs (180 degrees), [the nodes move].
For the shadow of the earth revolves there within that half-circle;
just as the shadows of pillars and other objects revolve by the power of a lamp, so too does the shadow of the earth revolve by the power of the sun.
It is not only the stars, planets, moon, and *pāta* that are mentioned;
the motion of the *pātas* on the apogee-circle (*apakrama-maṇḍala*) has already been stated.
So why is it now said that the shadow of the earth revolves at half the circle from the sun?
Furthermore, there is no descent of the moon other than its shadow on the earth;
this is not a fault.
For the descents of all the stars and planets move within the apogee-ecliptic (apakramamaṇḍala).

Furthermore, the descent (pāta) of the moon revolves at half a circle from the sun within the apogee-eccentricity circle; it is for this very purpose that [the author] states: "For in that [circle], at half a circle from the sun, the shadow of the earth indeed revolves.
Now, are not the descents of Mercury and the other planets fixed? Indeed they are.
How can it be said that those which are immobile possess a motion in the form of an apakrama-maṇḍala?
They are not immobile;
for it is said: "Having traveled nine rāśis and nine degrees, the first eclipses occur" (Gītikā).
9] Thus, since their motion is taught here by the word "having gone" (*gatvā*),
for what purpose is this Āryā verse beginning with "The stars, planets, moon, and [the lunar] node" (*tārāgrahendupātāḥ*) commenced?
The motion of the stars, planets, and so forth is understood to occur within the eccentric circle (*apakramamaṇḍala*).
And it has been stated: "The declination increments are the degrees of the planets" [Gītikā, 8]; thus, these are the degrees of declination for all those possessing motion.
Furthermore, even that which was stated in the Gītikā is here repeated again.
In that case, there would be much to be said here;
or else, it would have to be demonstrated that the shadow of the earth revolves within half the solar disk, and that has already been shown in another section.
Regarding the statement, "One should divide the opening of the earth-cavity" (Gola,
39), one should here teach the calculation of the shadow of the earth by means of the demonstration of the shadow of a lamp.

This demonstrates that the shadow of the earth revolves within half the orb of the sun; for the shadow of a lamp standing upright follows a straight path. Therefore, this Āryā verse must be commenced. // 2 //
Regarding those that move in the eccentric circles (*vikṣepamaṇḍala*),
he speaks in order to demonstrate the eccentric circles of the planets: "The Moon moves northward from the node (*pāta*) of the epicycle, and southward."
Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn [are thus]; and Mercury and Venus are likewise [calculated] by means of their swiftest apogees.
Of the apamaṇḍala;
the apamaṇḍala is the apakrama-maṇḍala (the declination circle);
and of the apakrama-maṇḍala, the moon.
The moon connected with the apamaṇḍala is called "the moon of the apamaṇḍala";
or, the moon situated upon the apamaṇḍala is "the moon of the apamaṇḍala," just as rice grains are said to belong to a granary.

Alternatively, this genitive case has the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), since there are one hundred and six meanings of the genitive, as in the expression "the moon is in the small circle" (*apamaṇḍale candraḥ*).
That moon, situated within the apamaṇḍala, moves from the pāta;
by the word "pāta," the conjunction of the moon’s vikṣepamaṇḍala and apakramamaṇḍala is denoted.
And because that conjunction possesses motion at every moment,
that motion is designated by the word "fall" (pāta) through metaphorical usage.
Therefore, in whichever zodiac sign and in whichever fractional part that fall— so termed as "motion"— occurs, [the result] is in that same zodiac sign and in that same fractional part.

In that portion, having fixed another circle with the same measurement as the *apakrama-maṇḍala*, one should likewise fix a second half within the interval of the wheel such that its first half remains to the north of the *apakrama-maṇḍala*,
while its second half is observed to the south.
And thus, from the first node,
the eccentric circle lies to the north,
and from the second node, it lies to the south.

In both cases, one should fix the *vikṣepamaṇḍala* (obliquity circle) such that there are four and a half parts within the interval of each quadrant of the circle, and these lie within the interval of that *apakramamaṇḍala* (declination circle).
The moon revolves within that [circle].
That *apakramamaṇḍala* lies to the north or south of the equator (*viṣuvat*).
Therefore, one should demonstrate the circle of deviation (vikṣepamaṇḍala) either to the north or to the south of the circle of apogee (apakramamaṇḍala).
This is the method for calculating the interval between the moon situated on the circle of deviation and the equator (viṣuvat):

a rule of three (trairāśika) using the sine of the amplitude (bhujajyā) of the true moon; namely, if by a sine of amplitude equal to the radius (vyāsārdha), the sine of twenty-four degrees of declination [is obtained].
From that, by means of the sine of the moon's arm,
what is obtained is the sine of the degrees of declination;
from that, he stated that the moon, situated upon the circle of declination, moves either to the south or to the north from the node.
For the sake of determining the node (pāta) up to its apogee, the node of the true moon is subtracted;

there, by means of the sine (jyā) of that difference, a rule of three proportions is applied: "If the sine of the lunar latitude (candravikṣepa) is obtained by the radius (vyāsārdha), then what is obtained by this desired sine?"
The sine of the desired deviation is obtained.
When those two— the sines of deviation and declination— are reduced to their maximum values (kāṣṭhīkṛta) and are of the same direction, their sum is taken,
because the Moon lies beyond the circle of declination.
There is a distinction between those situated in different directions, because from the apakrama-maṇḍala (the declination circle), the moon [is at] the vikṣepa-maṇḍala (the oblique circle);
one should demonstrate this correctly on the celestial globe (gola).
The distance from the equator to the moon is equal to the sine (jyā) of the degrees of separation from the yoga-point;
the measure of the gnomon (kāṣṭha) is stated according to the measure of that sine.
Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—namely, Bhauma, Bṛhaspati, and Śanaiścara—are likewise [calculated].

Just as the moon moves situated on its apogee-circle to the north or south of its own apsis, so too do Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn; the epicycles of deviation for these [planets], along with the specific methods for their conjunctions with the deviation-apogees, are to be understood in the same manner as those of the moon.
The word "ca" (and) collects this very meaning:
Mercury and Venus [are calculated] by means of the swiftness arising from the apsis;
for Mercury and Venus revolve in the epicycles of their respective deviations due to the apsis.
The velocities of the apogees of these two in the apsidal circle (apakrama-maṇḍala) are equal in measure to the degrees of the node (pāta).
One should fix the eccentricity circles (vikṣepa-maṇḍala) at their respective locations according to those degrees of the node.
Thus, the determination of the apsidal distance for these two also proceeds from the apogee itself.
Why? By stating that the deviation (*vikṣepa*) results from the fall from the apogee-circle (*apakramamaṇḍala*), the position of those two apogees on the apogee-circle is demonstrated;
for it is while situated on the apogee-circle that [the body] moves upon the deviation-circle.
Therefore, this is correctly understood: that the apogee of these two is also [calculated] from the fast apogee (*śīghrocca*).
Why [is it] "of the eccentricity alone"?
Because of the statement, "Mercury and Venus [are affected] by the apogee as well," it is taught that the determination of their eccentricity results from the apogee from which the node proceeds,
not the determination of their declination.
Therefore, the calculation of the declination (apakrama) of these two [the Sun and Moon] is derived directly from their own apogees.
Even so, it is entirely logical that these two, while situated on the circle of declination, move along the circle of deviation (vikṣepamaṇḍala).
Why is this so? Because for these two, there is only the knowledge of the deviation itself.
When [the moon] is displaced by another means, it is again taught through direct perception from its own [original] circle;
thus, one conceives of that specific object as being demonstrated by the displacement of the moon.
The displacement of all [planets] occurs to the north and south of the apsidal circle (apakramamaṇḍala).

The degrees of declination (*vikṣepabhāga*) as previously stated within one-fourth of the *pāta* arc are demonstrated here according to how they are situated between the circle of declination (*vikṣepamandala*) and the ecliptic (*apakramamaṇḍala*). Furthermore, the statement in the *Gītikās*, “the Moon moves from the *pāta* along the circle of declination,” should also be understood in accordance with the *pāta*. From the *pāta* located on the circle of declination, the Moon proceeds along that very circle of declination.
This which has not been stated is not understood;
therefore, it must also be said: "Mercury and Venus [are calculated] by means of the swiftest apogee as well."
Therefore, this noble sūtra must necessarily be spoken. // 3 //
[The Time-Parts of the Planets] To fully understand the rising and setting of the planets, he states the degrees of separation from the Sun for each planet:
the Moon, when not eclipsed and situated at a distance of twelve degrees from the Sun, is visible.
Bhṛgu [is formed] from nine of those [vowels], and from Bhṛgu [are formed the others] by adding two more each, in such a way that they become smooth. 4.
The moon [is worshipped] with twelve parts (*aṃśa*).
This word *aṃśa* generally denotes mere division;
therefore, according to the principle that "general injunctions are restricted to specific instances," they are established within specific parts.
Furthermore, there is the distinction of being a portion of time;
these are the divisions of time,
and they are called temporal parts.
It has been stated: "By means of the breath (prāṇa), one goes through a sixteenth part (kalā)" [Gītikā, 6].
By this, the exhalation-breath (ucchvāsaprāṇa) is designated as a *liptā*.
Consequently, twelve parts of seven hundred and twenty [720] breaths are taken.
The meaning is "two *ghaṭikās*";
for there are seven hundred and twenty breaths (*prāṇas*) in two *ghaṭikās*.
Alternatively, since a planet is visible when it is separated from the sun by a period of time—either behind or ahead of it—it is therefore a portion of time (*kālāṃśa*).
Thus, the moon is separated by twelve divisions of time;
it is "undistracted" (*avikṣipta*), meaning it is not distracted (*na vikṣipta*).
"Situated within the sun":
the interval from the sun is "arkāntara"; within that interval, he remains established without being distracted, according to the measure of twelve kālāṃśas.
When that [moon] is visible in a sky free from clouds and darkness,
it is observed again when its displacement (*vikṣipta*) occurs at a time either less than or more than two *ghaṭikās*.
This is because, since the moon is displaced to the north of the sun due to the northern elevation of the celestial sphere (*golasya*), it is seen even when the time is less than two *ghaṭikās*.
And because the sphere is elevated, that which is cast southward is visible for a period exceeding two *ghaṭikās* to the south;
therefore, it is said to be "uncast" (*avikṣipta*).
Consequently, having performed the calculation of the displacement (*vikṣepa-karman*), this interval is considered.
Venus is visible for nine [time-divisions].
Likewise, when situated within the solar sphere and not displaced, Venus is visible for nine time-divisions;
for that which is displaced, the motion of displacement is exactly like that of the Moon.
"Of Bhṛgu, by those [digits].
These are the portions belonging to Bhṛgu, that is, Śukra.

Although the meaning is established simply by saying "by nine," with each [subsequent period] increased by two, the Teacher repeats the mention of "Bhṛgu" in order to indicate: "These nine are the wood-digits (kāṣṭhabhāga) of Bhṛgu."
From those same nine [planets], there is the understanding of the internal divisions beginning with the preceptor (the Sun).

Otherwise, this planet Venus (*Bhṛgu*) would be observed to rise and set while separated by even three or four [other planets] during its period of retrogression; thus, there is this specific mention of the planet Venus.
The inclusion of the distributive repetition "by those [parts] increased by two, increased by two" is for the purpose of including the intervals between the two parts;
otherwise, there would be only nine parts for all of them,
as in the case of the smooth ones.
These planets have been described as smooth and diminishing in size; likewise, they are seen situated at intervals of two [signs] each from the sun, remaining unscattered.
And their sequence of smoothness has been stated:
Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Saturn, Mars, Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Mars, and the Moon—[these are] the forms of the letters *śa*, *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*. (Gītikā, 7)
Thus: Jupiter is seen with two parts more than those of Bhṛgu, which is two ghaṭīs less a sixth part; Mercury with thirteen parts more than those of Jupiter, which is two ghaṭīs plus a sixth part;
