and Saturn with two parts more than those of Mercury, which is two and a half ghaṭīs.
It has been stated that Mars is separated by these same temporal divisions— namely, two degrees more than Saturn's [longitude] and three ghaṭīs less a sixth part— and thus they are seen.
But how is their non-appearance understood?
Some, first of all, say: "By these very portions.
Why? Because there is equality in the *saṃhitā*;
[the sun] situated within another *arka* is both visible and invisible.
How is it that by these very same digits (kalās) the planet is both visible and invisible?
When the planet emerges from the sun, it is visible by those very same digits; when that same planet enters the sun, it is not seen because it is obscured by those very same [digits].
And this [is not so], for as long as this interval is equal to that of a planet exiting or entering,
there must be either a visible planet or an invisible one; yet,
for that duration, it is perceived as being indeed visible through its desired degrees of time.
Therefore, the explanation based on an identical phonetic combination (*saṃhitā*) is incorrect.
How then [should it be]?
It is said: by these many [factors].
Thus, situated within the sun, it is seen either emerging or entering according to these degrees;
from this it is understood by implication that it is seen less when [the degrees] are fewer,
whereas when they are greater, it is seen even more clearly— this even one ignorant of the scriptures knows.
Furthermore, the calculation of time here is determined by means of the longitudinal difference, the ascensional differences, and the measures of the rising times of the zodiacal signs.

For example: if thirty [degrees] are obtained as the time of rising for the signs of one's own locality, then what [time] is obtained now by the degrees of the interval between the computed sun and the planet?
Thus, the time is obtained.
If that [calculated time] is equal to the interval between the desired planets, then that planet is visible;
if it is less, it has set; if it is greater, it is even more clearly visible.

Alternatively, having performed a rule of three (trairāśika) using the ascensional right ascension (rāśyudaya) of one's own country and thirty degrees, the calculation of the intervening degrees for all signs is as follows: "If thirty degrees are obtained by the time of the sign's ascension, then how many are obtained by the time stated for the interval between the desired planet? Thus, the intervening degrees for all signs are obtained.
By means of those intervening degrees, which are established in a single operation, the visibility of the planet in the desired location should be declared.

This operation applies to the eastern rising and setting of the planets. For their western rising and setting, this calculation is made using the time of the rising of the seventh sign from that [western] point; for it is by virtue of the rising sign alone that the signs proceed to their setting. // 4 //
[The cause of illumination for the earth, planets, and so forth:
In order to demonstrate the cause of illumination for the earth, the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars, he says:
"The hemispheres of the earth, planets, and stars are discolored by their own shadows."
The halves shine according to their essential nature, facing toward the sun.
Bhūḥ is the earth;
the grahas are the sun and other celestial bodies;
the bhāni are the luminaries, the constellations.
The earth (bhūḥ), the planets (grahāḥ), and the lunar mansions (bhāni) constitute "earth-planets-mansions" (bhūgrahabhāni);
[the term refers to] the hemispheres of those earth-planets-mansions.
The bodies of the Earth and the other [planets] are denoted by the word "gola" (sphere).
Therefore, "half of those spheres" means half of their spherical bodies.
How do these planets and others come to possess spherical bodies?
Now, some consider the earth to be shaped like a cart or circular like a mirror;
this is not so.
How the earth is established as being spherical in shape, I shall explain further on.
But how, then, are these planets understood here to be spherical in shape?
For the sun and the moon are observed to be circular like mirrors,
and so too are the others.
Furthermore, the process of calculating the half-duration of a station (*sthityardha*) and so forth is not possible for bodies that are spherical in shape;
this is not the case.
For these planets and others, although they possess spherical bodies...
Because they are situated at a great distance, they appear circular like mirrors.
That process of calculating the semi-diameter and so forth pertains to the visual field;
since it belongs to the visual field, the Teacher has stated [the rules] by accepting the shapes of the disks exactly as they appear to sight.
Alternatively, it is possible to explain the calculation of the semi-diameter of the orbit (*sthityardha*) and other parameters even for globular bodies.

This is because, having understood that the [ecliptic] deviation (*vikṣepa*) and other elements proceed from the center of the disk, one observes that the interior of the globe— which is produced by revolving like a circular mirror to form a spherical disk— is itself circular like a mirror-disk.
Therefore, even from the fact that they are spherical in shape, the establishment of the half-duration of their stay and so forth is proven;
thus, they are indeed spherical in form in the ultimate sense.
Otherwise, the waning and waxing of the moon would not correspond to its reflection in a circular mirror.
Therefore, these [luminaries] have globular bodies. And it has been said:
"The sun is a globe consisting of fire; the moon is by nature a globe consisting of water and is transparent."
"Discolored by their own shadow":
one's own shadow is *svacchāyā*;
by that *svacchāyā*, the halves of these [faces] are discolored, meaning they are non-luminous and black.
There is no other cause for the discoloration than that;
just as one side of a jar situated in the sun is discolored by its own shadow,
so it is here as well.
Those halves which shine are those facing the sun; that is,
the halves of those spheres.
As many as remain, distinct from the discolorations of one's own shadow,
according to their substance:
for those that are few, there are few.
The great [fires] of the great ones are directed toward the sun,
facing the Āditya.
They shine and gleam.
[Regarding] the bright portion of the moon:
if half of the planets gleam when facing toward the sun, then why does the half-disk of the moon not always gleam in that same way?

It indeed shines; why is it not perceived? It is said: on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), the sun is above the moon; at that time, it illuminates the entire half-disk of that moon which is situated above it.
From the center of the upper disk of the moon as marked by the new moon (amāvāsyā), as the sun descends further behind, so too does the center of the [moon's] disk descend to the west.
Due to that shift of the center, the moon’s disk is perceived by us only to the extent that its half-disk descends from the limit of the half-circumference of the disk as marked by the new moon.
The remainder is not perceived because it is situated above;
even when facing the sun, it is not seen because it is obscured by the sun's rays.
Therefore, to the extent that the lunar disc hangs down more smoothly than the solar disc, to that same extent the clear white portion of the moon is perceived.
And by that [reflection], these rays of the moon illuminate the expanse of the moonlight;
whereas, on the other hand, the rays of the sun, having coalesced with the lunar disc— which is naturally clear when composed of water— dispel the nocturnal darkness.
Just as the suns, having converged in a mirror or in water, dispel the darkness within a house;
and furthermore: whichever portion of the lunar disc is situated directly along the path of the sun, that alone is perceived in the rising of the horns, and no other.
And thus, those desiring to know that perform the ritual action as follows:

having determined the positions of the sun and the moon at the time of half-setting on the first day of the bright fortnight and subsequent days, the versed sine (*utkramajyā*) of the moon's excess over the sun is taken;
since that [sine] increases day by day, [the calculation proceeds].
The bright portion of the moon increases;

and the versed sine (utkramajyā) is the measure of that which is increasing. Therefore, by means of that versed sine, there is a rule of three (trairāśika): if, by a versed sine equal to the radius, [such and such a result is obtained...]

When the half-disk of the moon is perceived as clearly full, then by means of this inverse sine (utkramajyā), one determines how much [of the diameter] there is; that is obtained as the measure of the moon's phase at that time.

The increase of the bright [fortnight] following the eighth day of the bright fortnight is observed to be accumulating due to the power of the successive chords (*kramajyā*); thus, the successive chord is taken.
Having added those successive chords to the previously accumulated half-chords of the diameter, a threefold proportion (*trairāśika*) is performed.

Alternatively, having performed a threefold proportion with those very same successive chords and the radius of the lunar disc, that which is obtained is added to the radius of the lunar disc to become the measure of the illuminated portion (*sita*).

Just as the white portion of the moon increases from the first day of the bright fortnight onwards, so too the white portion decreases in reverse order starting from the first day of the dark fortnight.
Therefore, having subtracted six zodiacal signs (rāśi) due to the specific difference between the sun and the moon, the ritual action is performed in that very same manner.
[The time of the moon's appearance:

For the time of appearance is as long as the moon remains visible. Regarding the means for calculating the duration of time it takes for it to rise: in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), the motion of the celestial sphere occurs solely by virtue of the zodiacal sign of its rising.
Therefore, as many degrees of lunar *rāśis* as there are from the sun, just so many *prāṇas* of the local *rāśi*-ascensions are taken from the limit of sunrise.

For example, when the sun is at sunset, six *rāśis* are subtracted; it then becomes the seventh *rāśi* from the sun. Likewise, having subtracted six *rāśis* from the moon, one should subtract the degrees of the *rāśi* occupied by the sun from thirty; the remainder is the degree of the *rāśi* reached by the sun.
Multiply that by the duration of the rising sign (lagna) in which the sun currently resides—calculated as being joined with six signs—and divide by thirty; the result is the *prāṇas*.
One should set those aside in one place.

Having added the degrees of the zodiacal sign occupied by the Sun to the Sun increased by six signs, one should accumulate the local rising times (prāṇas) of those signs until the degrees reached by the Moon increased by six signs are attained.
Then, having multiplied the degrees reached by the Moon increased by six signs by the rising times of those respective signs and divided by thirty, the result is the *prāṇas*.
Having added all those previously calculated breaths to the breaths placed together in one location, divide by six;
the result is *vighaṭikās*, and sixty of those are *ghaṭikās*. In this manner, the time of the new moon (*darśanakāla*) is characterized by *ghaṭikās* and so forth.

During that period of time, there is a specific movement of the sun and the moon; thus, the calculation of their specific motion proceeds as follows: if the solar or lunar motion is obtained for sixty *ghaṭikās*, then by this duration of observation, what are their respective motions?
One should add the result of the solar motion to the sun as it is conjoined with six signs (*ṣaḍrāśi*).
One should also add the result obtained from the moon's motion to the moon when it is joined with six signs, and perform this calculation until there is no further difference.
The time at which that difference ceases is the time of the new moon (darśana);
for that duration, [the moon remains] during the night.
The moon is visible.
Whatever portion of the moon is conjoined with six signs [of the zodiac], one should subtract that from half the circle; at that point, the moon sets at the completion of the time of its appearance.
Now, if someone should wish to know by how much time the rising of the moon will occur before the sun has set:
One should perform this operation as follows:
beginning from the solar degrees at the time of sunset when unaltered, one should sum up the breaths (*prāṇa*) until the breaths corresponding to the elapsed degrees of the moon when unaltered.
Having converted those into *ghaṭikās* as before, one should subtract them from the *ghaṭikās* that constitute the measure of the day.
In that case, whatever remains is the remainder of the day;
by that much of the day remaining, the rising of the moon will then occur.
Here too, the non-distinctive activity of the sun and the moon proceeds.

For example, because the sun and the moon are superior by virtue of whichever enjoyment belongs to these channels, they are repeatedly eclipsed by them, and thus a state of non-distinction is produced.
When the time for their appearance is rendered indistinguishable, the rising of the moon occurs precisely at that time when the day is still remaining.
That moon which is undifferentiated is the moon at the time of its rising at the end of that day;
or else, one should multiply the moon's motion by the time of the moon's rising at the end of the day previously brought forward, divide by sixty,
and subtract the result from the moon.
That moon remains for the duration of the remaining part of the day;
then, one should calculate the ascendant at sunrise using the time of the first-mentioned day.
When that ascendant at sunrise is equal to the moon that has risen during the remainder of that day, [then the calculation is complete].
Then, the remainder of the day is the time until moonrise.
Now, if the Moon is less than that ascendant, then it has risen earlier;
[one should calculate] the breaths (prāṇas) in the interval between those two—the ascendant and the Moon—from the previously calculated time remaining of the day.
One should subtract [the result].

From that moon which has risen at the end of the day, as much as the lunar motion of those breaths is obtained through the rule of three (trairāśika), so much is subtracted; that much is the moon risen at the end of the day, and that much is the time remaining of the day.

And when the Moon is greater, then as before, one should add those intervening breaths to the time remaining of the day; one should add the Moon’s motion for that many breaths to the Moon, performing this operation until there is no difference. Alternatively, having subtracted from the Moon at its first setting the Moon’s motion produced during the intervening remaining time of the day, [one proceeds] according to the sequence of the ascendant for that time.
The non-specific operation is performed.

Now, if the Moon is greater than the rising sign, then one should add the breaths (prāṇas) of the interval between them to the remainder of the day previously calculated, in order to determine by how many nāḍīs the Moon will rise.
One should add that motion (bhukti) to the Moon until there is no difference.
In this manner, the ascendant of rising (udayalagna) and the moon are determined, as well as the time of the moonrise remaining after the day has ended.
Thus, one calculates the times of visibility until the full moon (paurṇamāsī).

On the full moon day, if those same internal ghaṭikās should be fewer than the ghaṭikās constituting the duration of the day, then the rising of the moon occurs while the sun has not yet set; if they are greater, then it occurs after the sun has set.

In both cases, the non-specific action is determined by the measure of the intervening period, just like the immediate action. Furthermore, on the first day of the dark fortnight and so forth, having subtracted the ghaṭīs of the day’s duration from the ghaṭīs between the moon and the sun, one moves the sun and the moon by means of the consumption [of time] calculated through the rule of three (trairāśika) using the remaining ghaṭīs; then, from the ghaṭīs between those two...
One should subtract the ghaṭikās of the day-measure.

By means of the remaining ghaṭikās, the moon and sun, as well as the ghaṭikās of the interval between them, are determined; thus the ritual action is performed up to the end of the initial distinction.
In that regard, by an undifferentiated time, the moon rises after sunset. Thus...
In this way, the moonrise occurs at an unqualified time prior to sunrise.
Now, one who desires to know by how much time the moon will set after the sun has not yet set should perform this operation as follows:
having established the moon as it arose at the time of sunrise, one should add six signs (rāśis) to that.
[Then] the moonrise [is to be known] beforehand.

Now, from the heliacal rising of the sun, taking the moon as the limit when it is conjoined with six signs, one calculates how many *ghaṭikās* there are according to the method for the rising of the signs in one's own locality; these are distinguished without further qualification.
How so? By means of the rule of three (*trairāśika*), one should add to the moon that amount which constitutes its motion; therefore, once again, starting from that same sun—
From the starting point of the moon conjoined with six signs, the *ghaṭikās* are calculated as before until there is no further difference.
There, by those unaltered *ghaṭikās*, the moon sets after that many *ghaṭikās* have passed during the day;
having subtracted this from the measure of the day, the remainder is the *ghaṭikās* remaining of the day.
In this context, the moon that is unqualified [by signs] is of such magnitude at that time,
and the moon conjoined with six signs is the ascendant at its rising at that time.
[The southern and northern positions of the moon.]
Now, if someone should desire to know after how much time, following the eighth day of the bright fortnight, the moon enters the center of the sky, or what its size is there,
he should perform this rite.
Then, after that time, having calculated by means of one's own intellect the positions of the meridian ecliptic point (*madhyalagna*) and the moon,
if at that moment the meridian ecliptic point and the moon should be equal, then the moon will ascend to the center of the sky in exactly that much time.
However, if the moon is further [behind], then it has not yet reached the center of the sky even today.

In that case, having added the time interval between the meridian ascendant (*madhyalagna*) and the moon— calculated by one's own intelligence— to the [current] time, one should adjust the meridian ascendant and the moon until they become equal. If, however, the moon is less than the meridian ascendant, then one should subtract that intervening time from the time calculated by one's own intelligence, and thus adjust the meridian ascendant and the moon until the meridian ascendant and the moon [are equal].
The two would be equal.

In this manner, the midday shadow is calculated from the moonlight that has ascended the center of the sky thus established, by means of the declination, the latitude, and the obliquity of the ecliptic. [This is the procedure for the diagrammatic representation of the rising of the lunar horns.]
Now, when the tips of the moon and the moon-gnomon are in the same direction, their sum is taken;
when they are in opposite directions, their difference is taken.
That sum or difference is equal to the [bāhu] of the moon at the desired time.
And that [longitude] is specified as being in the same direction as the tip of the sun from the meridian,
because the moon is calculated from the sun itself, either to the north or to the south, and not from the equator.
Since the conjunction is applied to the two directions, this interval between the sun and the moon should be demonstrated either in a diagram (chedyaka) or on a sphere (gola).
Thus, the side (bhuja), having its magnitude established, is extended from the sun toward the south or north.
The moon’s gnomon is the hypotenuse.
If the moon is to the north of the sun, then the arm is extended from its northern tip, oriented east-west.

When the moon is to the south of the sun, then from the southern tip of that arm, a line extending east-west should be drawn. Having thus laid out the arms and the perpendiculars according to their respective dimensions, one should extend the hypotenuse— which plunges into the tips of the arms and has its end projecting far outward— and having established the center at the intersection of the tips of the perpendiculars and the hypotenuse, one should draw the lunar disc.
From the western side of that lunar disc’s circumference, one should mark a point by measuring the white portion according to the ear-line (karṇa).
The ear-line runs from the eastern to the western center of the lunar disc;
from that, by means of the "fish" construction (matsyavidhāna), [one determines] the south and north.
On the meridian, two points are made at the intersection of the north-south line with the circumference of the moon's disk.

Then, by means of those two points and the previously established point, one should draw a circle according to the prescribed method for constructing diagrams (*chedyakavidhāna*) such that it touches the heads of those three points.
The space between that circle and the circumference of the moon’s disk is the white portion of the moon.

Thus, the rising of the moon's horns is observed in the sky after the eighth day of the bright fortnight. The calculation is performed using the *agrajyā* (sine of the arc) of the ascendant at the time of setting or rising, similar to the method for the sun's *agrā*.
The gnomon (*śaṅku*) is produced from the breath-units (*prāṇas*) corresponding to the interval between the moon's rising and the ascendant.
The other end of the cord is likewise extended.
Therein, the white measurement as it was obtained must be subtracted from the size of the moon's disc; the remainder becomes the black portion.
Following that radius, one should mark a point by taking the black measurement from the eastern edge of the moon's circumference to the edge of the disc.
From those southern and northern points, one should draw a circle as before that touches the heads of the three points;
the space between that circle and the circumference of the lunar disc is black.

And on the first lunar day of the dark fortnight and subsequent days, one should draw the black interior as before in a circle, starting from the western side of the lunar disc— which has its edge extended toward the west and its tip marked at the tip of the ear-line— following the direction of the ear-line. However, at the desired time, having calculated the sine of the ascendant at the moment of rising or setting as it occurs nearest to that time, and having determined the tip of the moon's gnomon (śaṅku) for that time,
the moon should be delineated by means of the perpendicular (koṭi) of the gnomon produced from the breath-units (prāṇas) of the interval between the desired ascendant and the moon.
Thus is the method of delineating the moon as it is situated above the terrestrial plane in all cases. [Observing the elevation of the horns by piercing the roof-plate:

Then, at the tip of an instrument constructed according to the measurements of the gnomon, the base, and the hypotenuse, the elevation of the horns is observed within the interval between the roof-plate and the lunar orb, with a white measurement calculated according to the moon's digits.

For example: having correctly established the interior of the house, one should extend from the east-west line a cord marked by the tip of the sun at a measured distance of finger-breadths to the north or south as previously described, and thus make a point;
that is the "sun-point" (arkabindu).

From the southern and northern ends of the east-west line, one should extend a cord toward the respective directions—measuring as many finger-breadths as the specific *jyā* (sine) of the distance between the tips of the gnomon and the tip of the moon—and mark a point;
that is the lunar point (*śaśibindu*).
The side (*bhuja*) is equal in finger-breadths to the distance between the solar and lunar points.
At that time, the *avalambaka* (plumb line) is equal to the moon’s shadow-stake (*śaṅku*).

Following its alignment—that is, by means of the *avalambaka* positioned according to the lunar disc—one should pierce the ceiling of the house. There, upon the head of the staff extending from the tip of the stake, one should fix the gaze upon the sun’s dot as it corresponds to the elevation of the white horn as drawn in the diagram; then, following the ear-line, the measure of the finger-breadths of the raised *avalambaka* shall be attached to the top.
One sees the moon marked with the hare;
in the very same way, the planets too are to be visualized by those situated within the interior of the house.
[This is the conceptualization of the rising of the lunar horns when the moon has half-risen.]
Because the moon’s disk is half-submerged by the terrestrial horizon, its tip is not visible;
therefore, the elevation of the horn is calculated there at the moon’s tip using the sines of rising and setting.
For example: if the sine of rising is to the south of the moon’s tip and the sine of setting is to the north, then the northern horn of the moon is first seen.
Since the lunar node (bhavṛttacandra) is situated to the south,
the solar rays penetrate the lunar disc by way of the ear-line (karṇagati) following the lunar node.
Furthermore, when the tip of the moon is to the north and the sine of ascension (udayajyā) is to the south, then the southern horn of the moon [is illuminated].
It is seen first because it is situated to the south of the moon; and following the course of the ecliptic, the rays of the sun penetrate the lunar disc.
There is a distinction between the two when they are in the same direction relative to the south:
when the tip of the moon exceeds [the sun], then the northern horn of the moon is first seen;
otherwise, it is the southern horn.
When the moon's tip exceeds [the sun] by the north, then the southern horn is first seen; otherwise, the northern horn.
When, however, there is no difference whatsoever, then both horns are seen simultaneously.
And when the sine of altitude (*udayajyā*) and the sine of the moon's zenith distance (*candrāgra*) are both zero,

then at the time of the moon's setting, the setting of the lunar horn— either in the east or in the west— should be determined by means of the sine of the setting-ascendant (*astalagnajyā*) and the sine of the moon's zenith distance (*candrāgrā*).
[This concerns the cause of the moon's bright and dark portions.]
Thus, the times for the appearance of the white and black horns of the moon and so forth are due solely to the influence of the sun.
And thus it is recited in the *Nirukta*:
"One of its rays shines toward the moon."
For he must not be neglected;
from the sun his brilliance arises.
Suṣumṇa, the ray of the sun, the moon, is the Gandharva.
[Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 18, Maṇḍala 40; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, 3.4.7.1]
Furthermore, there is a Vedic scripture (nigama) to this effect.
Therefore, by this very indicative mark, and because it cannot be otherwise established, the path of the sun is above the path of the moon.
Furthermore, the remaining stars and planets are situated at a great distance above the path of the sun;
therefore, their hemispheres facing away from it always appear entirely full.
This is because the upward-pointing rays of the sun always illuminate the portion that is turned away from it.

Because Mercury and Venus revolve in close proximity [to the sun], the rays of the sun penetrate their disks from all sides, like a sphere situated near a lamp; therefore, even for these two, there is no state of having a non-full disk.
If this is so, how do these planets and others shine when the sun has set, given the absence of the sun's rays?
This is not a fault;
for the path of the sun is far from the earth,
and therefore the earth does not serve as an obstruction for the solar rays directed upward.
Just as a jar situated above, below, or at a distance from a lamp does not act as an obstacle to it;
and because the eastern part of the moon’s orb is close to the sun during the first day of the dark fortnight and so forth, its whiteness is perceived by that [light];
and in the case of gems, it is only the rays of the sun that become the cause of their brilliance—therefore, those [gems]...
Furthermore, they do not possess the nature of light even at night;
and it is said in the *Ratnaparīkṣā*:
"Having encountered the pervasive connection with the rays of the sun, [the gem] reaches far by means of a mass of beams."
For those endowed with virtues, such as crystal and other gems, please all their sides.
As for what is heard in the narratives (*upākhyāna*) and so forth—that jewels indeed dispel darkness—that narrative is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Others, however, think otherwise:
that the observation of the moon as incomplete is due to its own shadow resulting from proximity to the sun.
Thus, the moon is perceived as white by its own shadow;
that whiteness of the moon undergoes a change of color (*vaivarṇya*) due to its proximity to the sun.

Why is this so? If the moon, which is white by nature, were to undergo a change of color due to proximity to the sun, then the far side of the moon would appear discolored during the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipad*) and subsequent days.
Nor is it the front part; for in that case, the lunar disc would be perceived as facing downwards. Therefore, this which is asserted by the Buddhists is merely a false cognition. // 5 //

[The Configuration of the Earth] To demonstrate the configuration of the earth within the orbits beginning with Aries, he says: "In the midst of the spherical frame of the heavens, surrounded by its orbit, situated in the center of space."
The terrestrial globe, composed of earth, water, fire, and air, is circular on all sides. // 5 //
The *bhāni* are the luminaries, the constellations (*nakṣatra*). The cage of those luminaries is the *bhapañjara*.
Because the luminaries are perceived everywhere in the sky as if situated within a cage, it is for this reason that it is described by means of this analogy.

It is circular (*vṛtta*) and it is the cage of the stars (*bhapañjara*); thus, it is the circular cage of the stars (*vṛttabhapañjara*). "In the middle of the circular cage of the stars" means in the center, inside.
Of that circular frame;
there, in the middle of that circular frame,
it is "encircled by zones" (kakṣyāpariveṣṭita), meaning it is surrounded by the zones of the planets.
"Situated in the middle of space": "space" (kha) means the sky (ākāśa); the middle of that is the "middle of space" (khamadhya).
"Situated in the center of space" means situated in the center of the void;
that is to say, abiding in the midst of space.
How does the earth remain in the midst of space without any support?
It is said: because of the predominance of its own nature (*svabhāva*);
just as water, fire, and wind have the natures of moistening, burning, and propelling, respectively.
For them, there is no other agent that causes moisture, burning, or movement;
likewise, this earth is of the nature of supporting,
not of being supported.
Or else, as the earth falls, it says, "Let it fall below.
Now, what is this that is called "below"?
Just as the earth is below us, what is below the earth?
Furthermore, the word "below" (adhas) denotes a direction.
And the directions exist in dependence upon a fixed convention:
for example, where the sun rises is the east, and where it sets is the west.
That direction in which one goes while invisible is the north; the remaining one is the south.
Between these very directions lie the intermediate points.
In this way, "above" and "below" exist only in relation to the earth;
therefore, for that earth, there is nothing above and nothing below.
Therefore, there is no falling of the earth.
And thus, the ocean situated encircling half of the earth does not fall.
Furthermore, if the earth were falling, clods of earth, arrows, and the like, when cast into the sky, would not reach the earth.
If it is argued that the earth falls slowly,
this is also established by those skilled in the art of illusion.
In the sky, there would be a pillar dug in without support.
Alternatively, others think that the earth is supported by Śeṣa or by another;
that has already been addressed.

For Śeṣa and the others as well, some specific substratum must necessarily be postulated; if one substratum were to exist for them, another would be required for that too, resulting in an infinite regress.
If it is argued that they abide by their own power alone, [then...]
Why, then, is that power not postulated as being the earth itself?
Therefore, depending upon the merit and demerit of the world, the earth— the sustainer of all beings— remains motionless in space,
composed of earth, water, fire, and air.
The earth is spherical, as it is perceived through direct observation; it is round on all sides and should be understood to be perfectly circular like a ball made of clay or wood upon an iron rod.
Outside of this, the orbits of the moon and other celestial bodies should be shown. // 6 //
[The existence of living beings on the surface of the terrestrial globe] Regarding the demonstration of the terrestrial globe, he says:
Just as the cluster of a kadamba flower is covered on all sides with blossoms, so too is this earth-globe covered everywhere by mountains and oceans.
For in that same way, the terrestrial globe is [covered] by all beings, both those born in water and those born on land. // 7 //
Just as a cluster of *kadamba* flowers is filled with filaments on all sides— that is, pervaded—
so too is this terrestrial globe surrounded on all sides by creatures born of water and born of land.

Now, as for those living beings established on the earth, such as mountains and so forth—how is their situation? It is said: wherever living beings go, there the earth appears beneath them and the sky above them, just as it does for us. (7)
[The increase and decrease of the earth.
He speaks for the sake of knowing the increase and decrease of the earth:
"By a day of Brahmā, there is an increase of one *yojana* above the earth."
There is a loss of that which has been gradually accumulated over one night, equal to a day. // 8 //
The earth, existing in the form of grass, wood, ash, and so forth, undergoes an increase of one *yojana*.
For this very reason, when houses, trees, ponds, and the like are excavated, parts such as jars and baskets are found layer upon layer.
This occurs through a single night equal to a day, and through a night equal to a day of Brahmā.
There is a loss for that which has been accumulated by means of the soft; "accumulated by means of the soft" means *mṛdupacitā*,
and there is a loss of that which has been so accumulated.

But for what reason is that which has been accumulated on the earth exhausted? At the conclusion of a day of Brahmā, it is said, that which has been accumulated on the earth is exhausted by the water released in continuous streams from the clouds known as Saṃvartaka. // 8 //
[The measurement of the earth]—in order to set forth the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttara-pakṣa*) regarding the rotation of the earth, he says:
Just as one standing on a boat moving with the current perceives the stationary land as moving in the opposite direction; so it is here.
Likewise, the stars situated directly to the west of Laṅkā are immovable. // 9 //
One standing on a boat moving with the current perceives [the shore] as motionless; another standing on a boat moving with the current likewise perceives it as motionless.
A thing that is not moving is not stationary even in terms of its actual state,
just as one standing on both banks of a river and ocean sees trees and other objects on the opposite shore as moving in the reverse direction;
and likewise, when the earth is rotating eastward, people situated above it see the unmoving stars fixed in the sky as moving westward in the reverse direction.
For instance, those residing in Laṅkā see the stars situated directly behind them;
Laṅkā is merely an illustration, and others likewise perceive things in this way.
Therefore, it is this very earth that rotates toward the east,
while the stellar sphere remains motionless.
Due to the motion of the earth, that portion of the stellar sphere situated above it appears as if rising in the east.
That which is in the middle appears as if situated in the center of the sky,
while that which is far away appears as if setting;
for otherwise, there would be no possibility of rising or setting for the fixed wheel of the stars.
This is his view:
that while the earth-sphere is spinning, the world would be submerged by the ocean,
and trees, treetops, palaces, and so forth, being cast down by the winds generated by the momentum of the terrestrial globe, would be shattered.
Even birds, though flying in the sky, would not fail to reach their own nests;
therefore, there is no evidence whatsoever for the rotation of the earth.
Consequently, this Sūtra must be explained otherwise.
Just as a person on a boat moving with the current perceives moving objects as moving in the opposite direction,

so too do they perceive the moving stars— driven by the Pravaha wind— as moving in the opposite direction relative to the objects in Laṅkā due to the force of that velocity; and they perceive the earth situated below as if it were stationary while it is actually revolving.
Even though they are visible, the stars that have risen in the east reach toward the western direction.
[The cause of the earth's rotation] He states the cause of its rotation:
it is constantly impelled by the Pravaḥa wind for the purpose of its rising and setting.
The stellar cage, together with the planets, revolves, situated at the western edge of Laṅkā. // 10 //
Regarding rising and setting (*udayāstamayau*):
the cause of these two, rising and setting, is that the stellar sphere (*bhapañjara*) is constantly impelled by the wind known as the "current" (*pravaha*),
and the stellar sphere itself is indeed in constant motion.
The region of space that is most western in Laṅkā is "the most western part of Laṅkā" (laṅkāsamapaścima);
one who goes there is "one who goes to the most western part of Laṅkā" (laṅkāsamapaścimagaḥ);
and that which exists together with the planets is "with the planets" (sagrahaḥ).
It revolves and does not remain stationary even for a moment;
although the planets move toward the east, they nevertheless move toward the western direction relative to the stellar sphere (*bhapañjara*),
appearing as if they are being carried away by the great motion of the stellar sphere.
Like insects situated upon a potter's wheel. // 10 //
[Description of Meru] He states the measurement of Meru:
Meru is one *yojana* in height, the maker of light, and is encircled by the Himavat mountain.
In the midst of the Nandana grove, there is a circular structure made entirely of jewels. // 11 //
That whose measure is one *yojana* is "one-yojana-measured" (*yojanamātra*); the suffix *mātra* is used here to denote measurement.
[He is] Prabhākara.
It is called Prabhākara because it produces light;
it is encircled by the Himavat,
meaning it is surrounded on all sides by the Himavat mountain.
In the middle of the Nandana grove;
the Nandana grove is the place of recreation for the gods who are surrounded by hosts of apsarases,
and it is in the center of that.
"Consisting of jewels" means made of jewels— such as gold, silver, pearls, coral, rubies, emeralds, and so forth;
that which is fashioned from these is "consisting of jewels."
"From all sides" means "all around"; it is circular, meaning it has the shape of a sphere.
Now, as for the claim by the Paurāṇikas that Mount Meru measures one hundred thousand *yojanas*, that is devoid of logical justification.
From Laṅkā to the center of Meru, there is not even a thousand *yojana*s;
how then could it exist in a single part of that?
If, on the other hand, the earth itself is conceived as being of vast proportions, [then...]
That is incorrect.
That measurement of the earth's diameter as fifty-one thousand yojanas, established by means of the elevation of the axle-pole, is supported by logical proof;
for, setting aside what is proven by the rising and setting of the planets, by midday shadows, by the descent of shadows, by parallax, and so forth, what else could be perceived?
Furthermore, it is stated in the Purāṇas that Vivasvat, situated above Puṣkaradvīpa, causes midday; indeed,
Jambūdvīpa is said to be one hundred thousand yojanas [in extent],
and there are seven oceans and seven continents, each double the size of the preceding one.
And the seventh is Puṣkaradvīpa;
it is situated at an interval of many thousands of yojanas from that [previous continent].
If it were midday for the sun there, because we would be situated in the northern hemisphere, there would be no disappearance of the shadow of the gnomon.
The disappearance of its shadow is observed;
therefore, it is established that at the equinox, the sun passes through the center of Laṅkā. [At the equinox, the sun passes through the center of Laṅkā]
It was stated by them that "the sun does not go," and that is untenable because of its extreme distance;
however, if it were to go by leaping like a bird, then it would be logical.
And that is impossible to conceive, because it contradicts direct perception.
Therefore, it is established that the measurement of the earth is indeed brought about by its constant elevation.
In that case, there would be no standing at all for Meru of such great magnitude.
[If Meru, being of such great magnitude, were somehow to remain present, why is it not seen by us?
Meru is not seen by us because of its distance.
Alternatively, it is not seen because it lacks luster; in that case, however, it would not be made of jewels.
Furthermore, if Mount Meru were of immense size, the stars to the north would not be visible because they would be obscured by the peaks of Meru.
Therefore, it is precisely on the uppermost peak region of that Golden Mountain (Kanaka-giri) that the one consisting of all jewels is designated by the name Meru. // 11 //
Regarding the locations of Meru and the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha): in which part of the earth is Meru situated, and where is the Mare’s Mouth? To this he says:

In the midst of the Meru plateau there is hell, and in the midst of the waters is the submarine fire; situated below, the immortals and the gods certainly regard one another as being beneath them. 12.
Svaḥ is that which is characterized by heaven,
and Meru is in the middle of the land.
Hell and the submarine fire (baḍavāmukha) are in the midst of the waters;
"immortals" (amara) refers to the gods,
while "mortals" (mara) refers to those dwelling in hell.
They consider each other to be situated below;
since the earth is below for everyone,
they therefore consider one another to be standing beneath them.
Where the iron rod emerges from the earth to the north, in that region is heaven and Mount Meru;
where it emerges to the south, there are the hells and the Mare’s Mouth (Baḍavāmukha). 12.
[The Determination of Rising and so forth] He states the regions situated at a great distance from one another:
that which is sunrise in Laṅkā is sunset for the sun in Siddhapura.
It would be midday at Yamakoṭi and midnight in the region of Romaka. // 13 //
That which is sunrise for the inhabitants of Laṅkā is sunset for the inhabitants of Siddhapura,
because Siddhapura is situated below the region of Laṅkā;
it is midday at Yamakoṭi.
That which is sunrise for the inhabitants of Laṅkāpura is midday for the inhabitants of Yamakoṭi,
because Yamakoṭi lies to the east of the region of Laṅkā at one-fourth of the earth's circumference.
That which is sunrise for the inhabitants of Laṅkā is midnight for the inhabitants of Romaka.

Since Romaka is located four quarters of the earth's circumference west of Laṅkā, these regions situated within intervals of one-fourth of the earth’s circumference— lying at the junctions of land and sea— must be shown to have a measure of longitudinal difference (deśāntara) equal to one-fourth of a day and night for each other. // 13 //
Regarding the two cities situated on the same meridian,
he says for the purpose of demonstrating other regions:
"From the middle of the land and water, Laṅkā shall be at the fourth part of the terrestrial circle."
Ujjayinī is located at the fourth part of Laṅkā, exactly to the north.
Starting from Meru at the center of the land and from the submarine fire (Vaḍavāmukha) at the center of the water, Laṅkā is situated in the fourth part of the terrestrial circumference.
The terrestrial circumference is 3,298;17,25 [yojanas], and its fourth part is 824;67.
100. Situated at this distance, Ujjayinī is located exactly to the north of Laṅkā, which lies at the junction of land and water;
it is situated at one-fourth of that [distance].
In the fourth part of that fourth part of the earth;
that is, one-sixteenth part of the circumference of the earth, which is 206; 67; 400 [yojanas]. At this distance from Laṅkā lies Ujjayinī.
Along the equatorial line passing through Laṅkā and Ujjayinī, there are situated places such as Vātsya-gulma and Cakra-pura.
To the north of Ujjayinī, starting from Daśapura, Mālava-nagara, Caṭṭa-śiva, Sthāneśvara, and so forth,
extending as far as Meru, all the planets, according to the *Karaṇa* system, are situated upon the equatorial line that passes through the center of the earth.
Those situated in the eastern part see the sun first of all;
therefore, the correction for longitudinal difference (*deśāntara-phala*) is subtracted.
Those situated in the western part see it later.

Therefore, the result for another location is added there. A rule of three (trairāśika) is performed using the degrees of the difference between the latitudes of one's own location and the equatorial meridian: "If 3298;17,25 yojanas of the earth's circumference are obtained by means of the degrees of the zodiacal circle, then what is obtained by means of the degrees of the difference in latitudes?"
The yojanas between the points where the meridians of the eastern and western hemispheres intersect are in the form of ten million (*koṭi*).
From one's own location, the distance in yojanas to a place such as Ujjayinī situated transversely is known from common experience; this constitutes the *karṇa* (the hypotenuse).
The square root of the difference between the squares of the two ears (karṇas) is the distance in yojanas between the two arms.
Then, if the circumference of the earth corresponds to a vertical drop equal to the radius of the earth, what would it be for a desired vertical drop?
This is the true circumference of the earth.

Furthermore, if the planetary motion is obtained by means of the clearly determined circumference of the earth, then what is the motion corresponding to the *deśāntara* (longitude) *yojanas*? Thus, the *deśāntara* correction is obtained; as before, it is additive or subtractive. // 14 //

[The visible and invisible portions of the stellar sphere (bhagola): To explain the visible and invisible parts of the stellar sphere, he says: From an equidistant location, half of the stellar sphere is visible, diminished by the radius of the earth.
Half is covered by the earth, and it is indeed greater than half the diameter of the earth. // 15 //
The diameter of the earth is *bhūvyāsa*; half of that is *bhūvyāsārdha*, which is 525 [yojanas].
The visible half of the lunar sphere (*bhagola*) is observed to be diminished by that amount.
Why? From an equidistant location.
"Uninterrupted and level" means that the region is devoid of high objects such as great mountains and trees; it is "level.
Half of it is covered by the earth and is not seen; more than half the diameter of the earth remains invisible.

One desiring to understand this should extend a thread reaching down to the surface of the earth and fix it at the eastern horizon and the western horizon. The vision of an observer situated on the earth's surface follows the extended thread;
there, in the eastern region, he sees the luminaries half-risen.
Afterwards, one observes those that have half-set.
Thus, the visible hemisphere is situated within the interval of the celestial equator (gola-sūtra) and is diminished by half the diameter of the earth;
whereas that invisible hemisphere of the globe situated within the interval of the celestial equator is increased by half the diameter of the earth.
On level ground such as this,
however, for one who is a spectator on the summit of a lofty mountain, that [ground] becomes invisible to him, exceeding the measure of the mountain itself.
Vidyādharas and others, situated far in the sky, perceive a vast circle of light,
because their vision has an unobstructed range when directed toward what is situated high above and far away;
Brahmā, situated at an extreme distance, perceives the sun at all times.
For those situated on the surface of the earth, who see only half of the celestial vault due to half the earth's diameter, the day constantly diminishes from its own measure and the night increases.
To that end, there is a rule of three: if sixty *nāḍīs* are obtained at the solar orbit, then how many are obtained by the *yojanas* of half the earth’s diameter, which is 525?
By the obtained [measure] doubled, the day is always deficient and the night is greater. // 15 //
[The observation of the rotation of the stellar sphere by those residing on Mount Meru and at the mouth of the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha):
To explain the view of those dwelling on Mount Meru and at the mouth of the submarine fire, he says:
"The gods situated on Meru see the northern half of the stellar sphere moving to the right."
But half, situated in the southward direction, are the pretas in the Mare’s Mouth (Baḍavāmukha). // 16 //
The gods situated on Mount Meru to the north see the northern half of the stellar sphere as being on their left, moving in a clockwise direction;
the *pretas* situated at the Mare’s Mouth see the second half, the southern one, as being on their right, moving in a counter-clockwise direction.
Standing at the junction of land and water, the Teacher explains this.
For it is in relation to that [sun] that Meru and the Mare’s Mouth (Badavāmukha) have their status as north and south;
there is no fixed determination of directions for those situated on Meru or at the Mare’s Mouth.
The conventional usage of "east" and so forth is based on the movement of the sun.
Where the sun rises is the east;
[where it sets is the west].
It is not so for those situated on Mount Meru or in the Mare’s Mouth (the submarine fire).
Because the rising and setting of the sun occur everywhere on all sides,
the appearance of half the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*) is otherwise due to the intervention of different locations.
When a person travels toward the north and reaches another location, he perceives the Pole Star (*dhruva*) as having ascended higher above him.
For one who has gradually reached Mount Meru, Dhruva is situated above;
to the north and south of Meru, Dhruva hangs down.
This should be demonstrated by placing the svastika at the tip of the northern iron rod above, and placing the svastika at the tip of the southern iron rod below, facing downward.
Likewise, that region of the equatorial path which appears as east and west to those situated in Laṅkā is, for those situated on Meru, attached to the horizon.
In this same way, to those situated at the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha), the sun also appears [to move] like a wheel. // 16 //
[The duration of the day for gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans]—
He states how long those situated on Mount Meru and at the mouth of the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha) behold the sun: "For half a solar year, the gods behold the risen sun, and likewise the pretas."
The ancestors, moving through the moon, [complete their cycle] in half a lunar month;
here on earth, humans [complete theirs] in half a *kudina*.

The meaning is that the gods dwelling on Meru see the sun, which has risen during the six signs beginning with Aries, for half a solar year— that is, for six months— until it circles clockwise like a wheel, touching the horizon and gradually reaching twenty-four degrees of declination before leaving the horizon. In the same way, the pretas also see the sun, having risen once, for exactly half a solar year while it is in the six signs of the southern hemisphere.
The ancestors, moving with the moon— meaning those who go with the moon—
are the ancestors residing in the lunar world; they behold the moon for half a month, that is, for as long as these fifteen lunar days (tithis) last.
On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), the sun is above the ancestors;
that is their midday. Thereafter, as the sun descends further from the first lunar day (pratipad) onwards, so too does it become the period following midday for the ancestors.
Separated by three zodiac signs, it sets;
having set, separated by six signs, it rises in the east after a fortnight.
Therefore, for them, a fortnight is a day.
A "pakṣa" is a night;
here, humans [reckon] half a *kudinam* as a day,
and a *kudinam* as a terrestrial day (*bhūdinam*), from sunrise to sunrise.
Humans here see only half of that;
one should demonstrate everything as it truly exists within the sphere. // 17 //

[The Celestial Sphere and the Horizon Circle] To demonstrate the horizon circle within the celestial sphere, he says: "Then there is the east-west and the up-down circle, as well as the south-north circle."
The horizon is situated at equal sides, where the rising and setting of the stars occur.
That east-west circle here is the measure of the celestial sphere;
it alone extends upward, above and below, through all the frames of the zodiacal signs.
Likewise, there is another north-south circle of the same measure.

The southern and northern [halves] penetrate the southern and northern mandalas respectively, while above and below they produce svastikas. The terrestrial plane (kṣitija) stands with equal sides; likewise, another mandala of the same size is situated with equal sides penetrating [the center], producing svastikas in the four directions like a surrounding frame—this is called the terrestrial plane.
Where the rising and setting of the sun occurs;
that is, the mandala in which the rising and setting of the sun are observed— some call this "born of Hari."
This celestial sphere stands outside of all the cages of the planets. // 18 //
[The Unmaṇḍala]:
To demonstrate the unmaṇḍala, he says: "That which is fixed between the eastern and western directions, and which touches the two tips of the gnomon above the horizon."
That would be the equinoctial circle (unmaṇḍala), where there is neither decrease nor increase in the length of day and night.

From the *svastika* at the southern and northern points of the horizon, one should make two perforations at an interval equal to the degrees of the latitude (*akṣabhāga*) of one's own location on the southern and northern circles respectively, insert iron needles into them, and place the sphere upon them. Thereafter,
one should show the *unmaṇḍala*,
which touches the eastern and western directions— that is, it is fixed at the eastern and western points.
The intersection of the horizon and the two lines of the poles—
that which is formed above and below the eastern and western points of the horizon at a distance equal to the degrees of the latitude of one's own location—
is the unmaṇḍala (prime vertical).
The *udaya-maṇḍala* is the *unmaṇḍala*,
that circle upon which the decrease and increase of day and night are observed.
At the equinox (*viṣuvat*), because the *unmaṇḍala* and the horizon (*kṣitija*) coincide, there is neither decrease nor increase of day and night.
To the north of the equinox, the [sun] stands above the horizon on the prime vertical circle (unmaṇḍala) and below it to the south.
Therefore, in the northern hemisphere, the [Savitṛ] rises before reaching the prime vertical circle by a measure of ghaṭikās equal to the caradalas;
subsequently, having passed beyond the prime vertical circle, he sets.
Therefore, the day increases in the northern hemisphere.
In the southern hemisphere, having passed beyond the horizon (unmaṇḍala), it rises from the terrestrial horizon (kṣitija) and sets even before reaching it.
Therefore, in the southern hemisphere, the night increases;
consequently, the decrease and increase of day and night are equal to that. For this purpose, there is a rule of three: if by sixty [nāḍīs] the planetary motion is obtained, [then...]
Then, [to determine] how many ghaṭīs the cara-arc amounts to:
the result obtained should be subtracted from the sunrise in the northern hemisphere;
in the southern hemisphere, it is the reverse.
Thus, for those situated in the northern direction, there occur great decreases and increases of day and night respectively;
in that region where the sun, situated at the end of Gemini, does not set,
the day consists of sixty nāḍīs.
In that case, thirty ghaṭikās are the *cara*,
and fifteen ghaṭikās are the *carārdha*.
The sine (*jyā*) of that *kāṣṭha* is the *carajyā*.

By that inverse operation, the *kṣitijyā* (zenith distance sine) is obtained: if this *carajyā* (ascensional difference sine), equal to the radius (*vyāsārdha*), corresponds to the equatorial semi-diameter, then what will it be for the semi-diameter of the day-night circle at the end of Gemini? Thus, the *kṣitijyā* equal to the semi-diameter of the day-night circle at the end of Gemini is found.
The square root of the sum of the squares of that *kṣitijyā* and the declination sine (*apakramajyā*) at the end of Gemini is the *arkāgrā* (shadow-tip sine) equal to the radius (*trijyā*).

Therefore, in that region, having entered the celestial equator (*sama-maṇḍala*) from the horizon by forty-two degrees to the south of the zenith in the southern direction, it likewise reaches the horizon again at its first rising after having traversed the north-south line.
In that context, sixty *nāḍīs* constitute a day; from the sine of the sun’s amplitude, the terrestrial sine is derived—
for this purpose, there is a rule of three.
If by the *arka-agrā* (the sine of the sun's amplitude) equal to the desired [latitude] the terrestrial sine (*kṣitijyā*) is obtained, what would it be by means of the radius (*vyāsārdha*)?
Since the multiplier and the divisor are equal, they both vanish; thus the *akṣajyā* (the sine of the latitude) becomes the measure of the terrestrial sine.
How so? The *akṣa* (latitude) is sixty-six degrees.
In that region, the movement of the planets deviates;
therefore, this fixed rule does not apply to the north. // 19 //
[The observer's position relative to the celestial sphere]—
in order to establish the arrangement of the directions such as east and so forth, he says:
"The line of the eastern and western directions, and the lines below, above, and situated south and north."
In whatever place the convergence of these [lights] may be seen by the observer... // 20 //
The line from east to west, the line from bottom to top, and that which stands from south to north.
The word *ca* (and) denotes conjunction. The "conjunction" (*sampāta*) of these lines is their meeting at a single point;
that is, wherever the observer is located, there is the meeting of those lines at that very spot.
Therefore, the determination of the directions depends on the observer:
where the observer sees the sun rising, that is the east;
where [the sun] reaches midday, that is the south.
Where the sun sets is the southern [direction],
where it is midnight is the northern;
for all, Mount Meru is to the north.
When it is midday for those dwelling in Laṅkā, it is sunrise for those dwelling in Romaka;
thus, in that region of Laṅkā, the east lies toward them,
and in relation to that, Mount Meru appears to the north of their own location.
When it is midday at Romaka, it is sunrise for the inhabitants of Siddhapura; [therefore, in that region of Romaka, they face the east].
Relative to them, Mount Meru lies to the north of their own location.
In the same way, at Yamakoṭi as well,
one should draw a circle on the ground with a radius equal to the length of the gnomon, and observe the shadow during both the forenoon and the afternoon.
That direction in which the shadow of the gnomon enters the circle is the west.
The direction in which it exits is the east.
Having produced a fish at the two tips of that [line], one should stretch out a thread touching its mouth and tail;
that becomes the south-north direction.
Alternatively, the intersection of two lines—one touching the tips of the three shadows and the other touching the mouth and tail of the two fish—is the northern and southern direction;
or else, the directions are to be established by means of Citrā and Svātī. (20)
[The Zenith-Nadir Circle and the Diurnal Circle] [He states the nature of the zenith-nadir circle and the diurnal circle:
The zenith-nadir circle should be known as being above and below the observer, facing toward the planet.
The ascendant of the oblique horizon (dṛkkṣepamaṇḍala) should also be the eastern ascendant minus three signs.
The visual circle [of the observer] is directed upward and downward toward the planet;
where the observer is, there is its center,
and where the planet is, there is its circumference.
The visible horizon-circle (dṛṅmaṇḍala) is seen with a radius equal to the distance between the observer and the planet;
that very circle becomes the declination-circle (dṛkkṣepamaṇḍala) when the planet is situated at midday. The declination-circle is also [defined as follows].

From the center of the equatorial circle (samamaṇḍala), toward the south or north, wherever the displacement of the vision (dṛṣṭeḥ kṣepaḥ) is directed facing the planet, there the planet with a larger orbital radius is displaced by a smaller amount, while the one with a smaller orbital radius is displaced by a greater amount.
This should be fixed from the center of the equatorial circle at midday using the radius equal to the measure of the sagitta (dṛgjyā).
The method for its calculation is as follows: the eastern ascendant (prāglagna) shall be diminished by three signs.
One should subtract the ghaṭīs of the time of the lunar node from half the day in the forenoon.
The remaining breaths (prāṇas) should be diminished by the breaths of the Laṅkā-ascendants obtained through the rule of three (trairāśika).
From the remaining [units], as many breaths as are required for the rising of Laṅkā are to be subtracted;
the zodiacal signs (rāśis) are subtracted only to that extent.
One should multiply the remaining breaths by thirty.
One should divide by the impure *laṅka*-rise; the resulting quotient and so forth should be subtracted from those very values previously subtracted.
In the forenoon, it becomes the midday ascendant.
In the afternoon, because of the sun's increased [declination], as many Laṅkā-suns as are cleared away are added, and thus the ascendant is calculated.
According to the coarse method of the Teacher, having computed the eastern ascendant by the desired ghaṭīs according to the rule for the ascendant, it is then diminished by three signs.

It becomes the midheaven (*madhyalagna*). Since the signs enter the meridian by means of the Laṅkā-rising times (*laṅkodaya*), that midheaven which is calculated by means of the Laṅkā-rising times is the subtle one.

Its declination limit (*apakramakāṣṭha*), increased by the degrees of latitude (*akṣabhāga*) of one's own location when they are of the same direction, and diminished when they are of different directions, [is the result].
The interval between the center of the sky and the solar orbit constitutes the equinoctial shadow;
its sine is called the "middle sine" (madhyajyā).
To the moon's declination-limit, the [ecliptic] latitude is added or subtracted.
Since the moon is at its apogee (vimaṇḍala), the sine of the [longitude] increased or decreased by the degrees of latitude (akṣabhāga) becomes the middle sine (madhyajyā) of the moon;
by this, the middle sine here is explained. // 21 //
[The Self-Moving Sphere Instrument] To explain the self-moving sphere instrument, he says:
A wooden sphere that is perfectly circular, equal in weight on all sides, and light.
One should stir that [substance] with ghee, oil, and water, using one's own intelligence, for a duration equal to the time [prescribed]. // 22 //
"Made of wood" means consisting of wood, such as *śrīparṇī* and other materials, as previously described;
"perfectly round" means equal in all parts.
"Not inferior or superior" means that one should maintain equal respect toward all teachers; the gravity [of one's conduct] must be uniform in every respect.
If it were excessively heavy, it would be as motionless as a stone;

[it rotates only after a long time]. Therefore, it must have an even number of syllables and all syllables must be heavy. Here too, the word "even" (*sama*) should be understood to mean "light" (*laghu*).
How should one cause this sphere, distinguished by these qualities, to revolve? With mercury, oil, and water;
and with one's own intellect—that is, with one's own wisdom—one should cause it to revolve.
"Equal to time" means equal with time;
"equal to time" means that one should cause it to revolve just as it revolves, being equal to the day and night.
For example, one should fashion a single peg slightly elevated at the junction of Virgo and Libra within the circle of one's own day-and-night marked by sixty *ghaṭikās*.
One should place a water-vessel in a location previously established as fixed in the east, west, south, and north.

Having prepared the vessel—level, circular, long, and with a fine hole placed in the middle of its base—such that it becomes empty when filled with water in sixty *ghaṭikās*, according to one's own intelligence, then...
Action is performed:
as long as water flows from the bowl, the gourd, descending downward by the force of the water due to its weight, draws the ball along with it.
In this way, the sphere (gola), once joined, revolves during the day and night just like the ultimate stellar sphere (bhagola).

First, having tied one end of a cord with a loop to a copper pin, one should wrap the sphere-instrument starting from the bottom and bring the cord back to that same location; such is the procedure for the axis-field (akṣakṣetra).
To demonstrate the location of the equinoctial chord, he says:

"One should divide the hemisphere of the celestial sphere by means of the half-chord; the equatorial circle is its base, while the equinoctial sine is its side, and the altitude is its perpendicular. (23)
Because the visible hemisphere of the celestial sphere (dṛggola) is situated like the half-shell of a jar, it is called the "hemisphere-jar" (dṛggolārdhakapāla).
Only the visible hemisphere of the ecliptic (bhagola) is seen;
by means of this, the visible [world] is conventionally designated.
The term *bhagolārdha* is used in the singular because it refers to two [halves] born as one.
One should calculate by means of the half-chord (*jyārdha*).
Having drawn a circle on the ground and marked the directions of east, west, south, and north, one should mark three zodiac signs (*rāśi*) in each of the four quarters.
Furthermore, each individual heap should be divided eightfold; there, threads should be stretched out,
and these are the chord-threads (*jyāsūtra*).
The half-chords are half of those;
or else, there is another method of calculation:
the equinoctial chord and the sine of latitude.
Because it is situated at a distance equal to the *akṣa* to the north of the equatorial circle (*viṣuvat*), it is called the *akṣa*.
The sine of that *akṣa*-staff,
the *akṣajyā*, and the equinoctial sine (*viṣuvajyā*) are synonyms.
The radius is the hypotenuse;
the square root of the difference between the squares of the side and the hypotenuse is the perpendicular;
that is the upright.
One should demonstrate this on the sphere (*gola*).
Having tied one end of a thread at a distance equal to the latitude-sine (*ākṣajyā*) to the south of the center of the equatorial circle (*samamaṇḍala*), one should extend it to reach the planet;
that is the plummet (*avalambaka*).
The square root of the sum of the squares of the sine (bhuja) and cosine (koṭi) is the hypotenuse (karṇa), which is the radius (vyāsārdha).
In this same manner, in other cases as well, the arrangement of sine, cosine, and hypotenuse should be conceived for the assumed half-chords within the visible hemisphere of the sphere. // 23 //
[The diameter of the half-svāhorātra circle:

He states the construction of the *bhuja* and other sides by means of the declination (*apakrama*) and so forth: "Having subtracted the square of the desired declination from the square of the radius, that which is the square root [is the *bhuja*]."
At the equinox, to the north and south, that is the diameter of half a day and night. // 24 //

The square of the desired declination-chord of the sun and the square of the desired declination-chord of the moon constitute the "square of the desired declination. Subtracting that from the square of the radius, the square root of the remainder is the diameter of the day-and-night circle (ahorātra-viṣkambha) to the north or south of the equator.
The declination-chord is the side (bhuja).
The radius is half the diameter.
The square root of the difference between the squares of those two is the diameter of the midday shadow-circle (svāhorātrārdhaviṣkambha).
According to the previous rule, that [shadow] is to the north in the northern hemisphere.
In the southern hemisphere, one should demonstrate it toward the south. // 24 //
[The ascensions at Laṅkā for Aries and the other signs] He states the calculation of the breaths of the Laṅkā-ascensions:
the radius of the equinoctial day-circle (ahorātravyāsārdha), multiplied by the desired sine (iṣṭajyā), is indeed the final degree (kāṣṭhāntyam).
The square root of that result, divided by half of one's own day-and-night, yields the sines of the ascensional differences for Laṅkā and the eastern region.

The term *iṣṭajyā* refers to the sines (*jyā*) at the ends of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini; by these [sines] multiplied, the radius of one's own day-and-night circle (*svāhorātrārdhaviṣkambha*) is obtained. *Kāṣṭhānta* means the end of the quarter (*kāṣṭha*).
In that context, "belonging to that" (*tatra bhavam*) means belonging to the end of the final degree (*kāṣṭhāntyam*).

That which belongs to the end of a degree in which there are ninety parts—that is, half of its own day-and-night (*svahorātrārdha*)—is multiplied by the desired sines (*iṣṭajyābhiḥ*) and divided by half of its own day-and-night; that is, divided by its respective half-day.
The resulting quotient is the desired sines of the eastern ascensional differences (*iṣṭalaṅkodayaprāgjyāḥ*).
"From Aries onwards, it becomes wood"— thus it is made into wood (*kāṣṭhīkriyate*).
One should subtract the initial degree of the sign of Taurus from the initial degree of the sign of Gemini.
The remainder is the breaths of the *laṅkodaya* for Gemini.
[In this manner: from the eastern limit of the amplitude at the end of Taurus, one should subtract the eastern limit of the amplitude at the end of Aries;
the remainder is the breaths of the *laṅkodaya* for Taurus.
By their very nature, they become the life-breaths of the rising [signs] such as Aries and Libra. // 25 //
To demonstrate the decrease and increase of day and night, he says:
"The sine of latitude multiplied by the desired declination, divided by the sine of colatitude..."
In one's own day and night, that [sine] is the sine of decrease and increase for the day and night of the terrestrial sphere.
The sine of the desired amplitude (akṣajyā) multiplied by the desired amplitude (iṣṭāpakrama),
and then divided by the sine of the colatitude (lambaka), results in the terrestrial sine (kṣitijyā) on the equatorial circle (svāhorātramaṇḍala).
In this context, the sine of the desired amplitude is the hypotenuse (koṭi).
The sine of latitude (kṣitijyā) is the base (bhuja); the square root of the sum of its squares is the hypotenuse (karṇa), which becomes the sun's amplitude (arkāgrā).
Having tied a cord between the two sun-amplitudes at the eastern and western gnomon-marks (svastika), the derivation of the base and the perpendicular (koṭi) should be demonstrated.
The interval between the horizon and the celestial equator is called the *kṣitijā*.
By means of that, there is the decrease and increase of day and night;
it is like a sine (*jyā*) situated between the upper and lower horizons relative to the eastern horizon.
It is demonstrated. // 26 //
[The risings at their own latitudes:
To explain the time of the rising of the zodiacal signs, he says:
"For a quarter of the circle rises with a quarter of the day diminished by the [local] ascensional difference."
The first and the last, as well as the other two, together with that [central one], are [to be applied] in direct and reverse order. // 27 //
The rising is seen;
half of the wheel's rim is above, and there are three signs [of the zodiac].
By the phrase "by a quarter of the day minus the caradala," three Laṅkā-ascensions (laṅkodayas) are encompassed.
Since fifteen ghaṭīs are comprised by the three Laṅkā-ascensions beginning with Aries, they constitute the fourth part of one's own day-and-night;

therefore, one should subtract from the sequentially established Laṅkā-ascension breaths (prāṇas) one's own caradala breaths for Aries and the other signs, as produced by the latitude of one's own location.
The ascensions (udaya) of Aries and the other signs occur in their own respective regions.
The final quarter of the zodiac consists of Pisces, Aquarius, and Capricorn;
these also rise by means of the zodiacal quarter diminished by its movable portion.
By the quarter of the day together with the *cara* [ascensional difference];
here too, by the mention of "quarter of the day," the ascensions at Laṅkā for Cancer, Leo, and Virgo are taken in reverse order.
Therefore, they rise together with the *cara*-breaths of Cancer, Leo, and Virgo in reverse order.
Regarding the phrase "in direct and reverse order":
by way of direct and reverse motion, Aries, Taurus, and Gemini are diminished by the degrees of movement in direct order; Cancer, Leo, and Virgo are increased [by them] in reverse order.
These same [signs] in reverse order are Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius;
thereafter, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces are in reverse order, diminished by their [respective] caradalas.
Aries, Taurus, and Gemini are situated obliquely on the ecliptic in direct order.
Therefore, the ram rises quickly; consequently, it is diminished by the caradalāsu (the breaths of the caradalas).
The same applies to the bull and the twins.
By these, the signs beginning with Capricorn are explained.
Because Cancer, Leo, and Virgo have a different configuration [from the others], they rise slowly;
therefore, they are augmented by the caradalaprāṇas (the breaths of the caradalas).
By these, Libra and the subsequent signs are explained.

The equinoctial sine multiplied by the radius and divided by its own half-daily arc gives the carajyā; its maximum value is the caradalaprāṇas. These should be produced separately for Aries and the other signs, as in the case of the Laṅkā-ascensions.

For the purpose of determining the ascendant at the desired time by means of the rising times of the signs of one's own country, one should convert the ghaṭikās from sunrise into prāṇas and subtract from them the prāṇas of the rising times of the signs yet to be traversed by the Sun; the degrees yet to be traversed by the Sun are to be added [to the result]. Furthermore, as many sign-risings as can be subtracted are subtracted, and the corresponding signs are added to the Sun.

The remainder, multiplied by thirty and divided by the [ascendant] duration of rising (*asuddhodaya*), yields degrees and so forth; these should be added to the increased Sun. This results in the ascendant (*lagna*). In the same manner, for the night as well, one should add the elapsed *ghaṭikās* of the night to the *ghaṭikās* of the day-measure and calculate the ascendant by this method. By means of the remaining *ghaṭikās* of the night, through the inverse operation, one should determine the elapsed degrees and so forth of the Sun, and from that, in reverse order, the number of breaths (*prāṇas*) of the rising periods (*udaya*).

Those [degrees] that are to be subtracted shall be purified by that much; the remainder, multiplied by thirty and divided by the current ascendant's [longitude] in degrees, gives the result in degrees and so forth, which is subtracted from the ascendant at sunrise.
Next is the calculation of the time interval between the sun and the ascendant.
One should multiply the Sun’s untraversed degrees by its ascensional difference and divide by thirty;
the result is the Sun’s untraversed breaths (*prāṇa*).
Likewise, one should multiply the ascendant’s traversed degrees by its ascensional difference and divide by thirty.
The obtained breaths elapsed from the ascendant,
joined with the intervening breaths, divided by six, yield *vighaṭikās*; divided by sixty, they yield *ghaṭikās*.
They occur starting from sunrise. // 27 //
[The gnomon for the desired time] [Regarding the calculation of the gnomon for the desired time, he says:
Having multiplied the sine of the desired [arc] within its own day-and-night by the *avalambaka* (the vertical distance from the zenith) starting from the horizon...
The shadow-stake (śaṅku) is determined by dividing the day into its elapsed and remaining portions according to half the [equatorial] diameter. // 28 //

[The calculation of the desired sine for one's own day and night: From the ghaṭīs elapsed and remaining of the day, in the northern hemisphere, since the horizon is situated below the celestial equator (unmaṇḍala), the ghaṭīs of the ascensional difference (caradala) are subtracted from the ghaṭīs elapsed and remaining of the day; those resulting [values] are reckoned in breaths (prāṇas) starting from the limit of the celestial equator, and their sine (jīvā) should be taken.
In the northern and southern hemispheres, the caradalajyā (the sine of the ascensional difference) is added to or subtracted from the limit of the horizon.

[Therefore, there is a proportion: if this jyā exists on the circle of the diameter (vyāsārdhamaṇḍala), how much does it amount to on the half-circle of one's own day-and-night (svāhorātrārdhamaṇḍala)? That which is called the desired jyā (iṣṭajyā) for one's own day-and-night, measured from the limit of the horizon-circle, should be divided by the radius (viṣkambhārdha), that is, the semi-diameter (vyāsārdha), after having multiplied it by the lambaka (the cosine of the latitude).
When the forenoon of the day has passed and the afternoon remains, the gnomon (śaṅku) is formed;
this is the calculation of the lunar gnomon.
