At night, one should observe the shadow of the moon.

Therein, in the eastern hemisphere, the desired time-ghaṭīs of the moon are taken; however, in the western hemisphere, the remaining ghaṭīs of the moon—namely, the ghaṭīs between the setting point of the moon and the ascendant—are brought forward for the calculation of the desired time.

Having calculated the latitude-chord (*kṣitijyā*) and the ascensional-difference chord (*caradalajyā*) for half a lunar day and night, one should perform the calculation as for the sun using the breath-units (*prāṇa*) produced by the reversal of the ascensional difference.
Then, the desired chord for its own day-and-night, multiplied by twelve and divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse (*viṣuvatkarṇa*), becomes the desired gnomon (*iṣṭaśaṅku*).
Alternatively, [one may calculate] the chord of the deficient or remaining *ghaṭikās* by means of the ascensional difference.
The gnomon (śaṅku) is obtained by calculating the reverse of the caradalajyā, multiplying it by the lambaka, and then dividing by the square of the trijyā;
alternatively, one may multiply that same value by twelve times its own ahorātra and divide by the equinoctial hypotenuse multiplied by the radius (vyāsārdha).
The result is the gnomon (śaṅku).

Furthermore, in calculating the elapsed ghaṭīs of the day, the radius multiplied by the gnomon and divided by the square root of the sum of the squares of the gnomon and its shadow becomes the large gnomon (bṛhacchaṅku).
The radius multiplied by the sine of the desired [arc] on its own day-and-night circle and divided by the sine of the colatitude (lambaka) is obtained.

Therefore, in the northern hemisphere the latitude-chord (kṣitijyā) is subtracted, and in the southern hemisphere it is added. Then, having multiplied by the radius (vyāsārdha), one should divide by the semi-diameter of the day-circle (svāhorātrārdha).
The obtained value in degrees, increased by the caradala in the northern hemisphere and decreased by it in the southern hemisphere, becomes the breaths elapsed or remaining of the day;
from these, the ghaṭīs are calculated as before. // 28 //
To demonstrate the tip of the gnomon, he says: The desired gnomon, multiplied by the equinoctial midline and divided by its own verticality, [is the result].
From the line of the setting and rising [of the sun], the tip of the sun's gnomon is to the south. // 29 //
The desired gnomon— the gnomon produced at the desired time—

multiplied by the equinoctial sine (the sine of latitude) and divided by the lambaka (the cosine of latitude), gives the tip of the solar gnomon to the south of the east-west line. The distance from the base of the gnomon to the tip of the gnomon, extending along a line equally inclined toward the north, reaches as far as the [east-west] line of sunset and sunrise.
On the terrestrial circle, having tied one end of a cord at a distance equal to the interval between the sun’s zenith and the horizon (arkāgrākāṣṭha) either south or north of the eastern svastika,
one should tie the second end on the opposite side at that same [arkāgrākāṣṭha] distance;
that line, extending from east to west, is the rising-setting line (udayāstasūtra).
The tip of the gnomon is at the interval between that thread and the base of the gnomon.
The thread from the base of the gnomon to the center of the earth is the *dṛgjyā* (sine of the altitude).
The thread reaching from the center of the earth up to the top of the gnomon is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*), which is half the diameter. // 29 //
Regarding the calculation of the tip of the sun's shadow,
he says:
Multiply the sine of the maximum declination by the desired half-chord (jyārdha), and then divide it.
The jyā obtained by the lambaka is the arka-agra at the eastern and western horizons.

The maximum declination-chord (paramāpakramajyā) is the chord of twenty-four degrees, which is 1397. Having multiplied that by the bhuja-jyā (sine of the amplitude) of the desired sun, one should divide it by the lambaka (the cosine of latitude).
The resulting jyā is the arkāgrā (the sine of the sun's altitude at sunrise/sunset).
At this distance, the sun rises either to the north or to the south of the equator, and at the eastern and western points of the terrestrial horizon.
[The Equal Gnomon] states for the purpose of calculating the gnomon at the meridian circle:
"If that [gnomon] is diminished by the equinoctial [gnomon], it is multiplied by the northern altitude at the equinox."
The quotient obtained by dividing [the shadow] by the equinoctial gnomon-shadow is the gnomon-shadow in the east and west. // 31 //
By the word "sā" (that), the apakrama-jyā (declination-chord) is understood.
When the krānti-jyā (obliquity-chord) is equal to the viṣuvat-jyā (equinoctial-chord) in the northern hemisphere, then at midday the sun enters the equatorial plane (samamaṇḍala).
When the equinoctial sine is diminished by the sine of the limit of declination, then [the sun] moves to the north of the equatorial circle;
when the sine of the limit of declination is diminished by the equinoctial sine, then it enters the equatorial circle;
when the sine of the limit of declination is less than the equinoctial sine...

Then, the previously brought *arkāgrā* (the sine of the sun's altitude) multiplied by the *lambaka* (the earth-sine) and divided by the equinoctial sine (*viṣuvajyā*) becomes the gnomon on the prime vertical (*samamaṇḍalaśaṅku*). Having fixed the line of rising and setting (*astamayodayasūtra*) at the interval between the eastern and western prime verticals on the horizon (*kṣitija*), the point where the sector of degrees traversed by the sun touches the eastern and western prime vertical circles from the eastern mark— [End of sentence fragment]
One should rotate that equatorial arc on the sphere in such a way that it touches the equator at the same distance below the horizon.
Having tied a string between those two points on the equator, its half-measure serves as the gnomon; as before, it will touch the east-west line.
The distance from the north of the gnomon to the line of setting and rising is equal to the distance from the tip of the sun [to the horizon].

The gnomon at the equatorial circle, multiplied by the latitude-chord (akṣajyā) and divided by the maximum declination-chord (paramakrāntijyā), becomes the sine of the sun’s amplitude (sūryabhujajyā).

When the sun is in Aries and the other signs of the first half (the northern course), it is that same degree; when in Cancer and the other signs of the second half (the southern course), it is purified by six signs;
when in Libra and the other signs of the third half (the northern course), it is increased by six signs.
The sun becomes purified by the wheel beginning with Capricorn (*makara*).

Furthermore, on a level ground, having drawn a circle and marked the directions, one should place two points at the eastern and western limits at the times of sunrise and sunset; then, from the east-west line, [at a distance equal to the sine of the meridian zenith distance] to the south—
Having determined the third point, one should draw a circle intersecting the three points by means of two fish-diagrams;

that is the circle of the sun’s revolution. When the sun has risen at the eastern extremity of that circle and, following the path of that circle, has reached the meridian, it makes midday at an interval equal to the sine of depression (natajyā) to the south of the equatorial circle (samamaṇḍala); and in due order, on the western side, from the equatorial circle—
Having emerged, it sets at the western extremity. Where the intersection of the eastern-western line of the solar orbit occurs with the equator, that is the entry into the equatorial circle.
The distance from the center of the equatorial circle up to that point is the shadow of the gnomon on the equator.
When [the sun] moves south of the equatorial plane (samamaṇḍala) in the southern hemisphere, there is no entry into the equatorial plane. // 31 //
[The Midday Gnomon] Regarding the calculation of the midday gnomon and its shadow, he says: The sine of the degrees of altitude from the horizon shall be the maximum gnomon.
From the center, the jyā (sine) of the depressed portion is the shadow of that very gnomon.

From the point of the terrestrial equator—that is, from the location of the central cross (svastika) where the meridian and the prime vertical intersect—the sines of those elevated degrees observed when the sun is situated at the center of the celestial sphere constitute the maximum gnomon (parama-śaṅku).

The sine of the depressed degrees from that center shall be the shadow of the maximum gnomon. At the desired midday, one should apply the sun's declination degrees to the latitude degrees in the southern hemisphere.
In the northern hemisphere, one should subtract [the declination];
those become the degrees of altitude (natabhāga).
For the Moon, the degrees of altitude are those obtained by adding or subtracting the latitude (vikṣepa).
Since the moon is at its apogee (vimaṇḍala), these [degrees] are subtracted from ninety;
the remainder is the degrees of altitude (unnatabhāga). Of these, [the sine (jyā) is calculated].
The jyā of the ascensional difference (unnatabhāgajyā) is as follows:

Alternatively, the half-duration of that day’s solar rotation (svāhorātrārdha), increased or decreased by its own terrestrial jyā (kṣitijyā) according as it is north or south, multiplied by the radius (vyāsārdha) and divided by the half-duration of the solar rotation, then multiplied by twelve and divided by the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow (viṣuvatkarṇa), results in the Great Gnomon (mahāśaṅku); that is the jyā of the ascensional difference. // 32 //
[The Sine of the Deflection] To demonstrate the deflection (dṛkkṣepa), he says:
"That which results from the product of the mid-sine and the sine of the rising point, divided by half the diameter..."
The square root of the difference between the squares of those two middle sines is the observer's latitude (dṛkkṣepa). // 33 //
The middle sine and the rising sine are the "middle and rising sines.

Their product—that is, their mutual multiplication—divided by the radius (vyāsadalahr̥ta) results in a value; the square root of the difference between the squares of that result and the middle sine is one's own parallax (dṛkkṣepa).
By the use of the word "one's own" (sva), it is indicated that the parallax for the orbits of the sun and moon is distinct. // 33 //
[The Sine of the Altitude] Regarding the calculation of the sine of the altitude, he says:
"The square root of the difference between the squares of the [observer's] latitude and the [planet's] parallax is the sine of the altitude due to its own position."
At the horizon, one's own shadow is equal to the radius of the earth; from the center of the sky, it is half the diameter of the earth.
The square root of the difference between the squares of the *dṛgjyā* (sine of altitude) and the *dṛkkṣepa* (horizontal parallax) is the observer's own *dṛggati* (motion of the observer).
This arises from the influence of the earth (*kuvaśāt*), that is, from the force of the earth.

That which results from dividing the product of the *madhyajyā* (mean sine) and the *udayajīvā* (ascensional difference sine) by the radius (*vyāsadala*) is indeed the *dṛkkṣepa*, being the square root of the difference between the squares of the *madhyajyā* and [the other term].
Thus, from the square root of the difference between the squares of the trijyā and the śaṅku arising from the earth's power (bhūvaśāt), the dṛgjyā is obtained.

Therefore, because it is produced from the dṛgjyā and the dṛkkṣepa arising from the earth's power, it is said to be "from the power of the ku" (kuvaśāt). However, in the statement "its own shadow on the horizon" (*kṣitije svā dṛkchāyā*), the word "its own" (*svā*) denotes its own dṛkkṣepa and dṛggati.
The radius of the earth is 525 [yojanas]. Why does one's own shadow arise on the terrestrial sphere from the center of the sky?
This becomes equal to half the diameter (vyāsārdha).

For, due to the influence of erroneous observation (kudṛṣṭi), the visual displacement (dṛggati) from the center of the celestial equator (sama-maṇḍala) toward the eastern and western directions is either subtractive or additive (lambana);
likewise, by taking the visual deviation (dṛkkṣepa) from the center of the ecliptic (bhagola) toward the southern and northern directions, there would be a depression (nati).
He demonstrates the production of specific *jyās* (sines):
because the earth is spherical, the distance equal to half the diameter of the earth occurs at the horizon on the solar orbit and on the lunar orbit.

Having multiplied the mid-*jyā* produced on the solar orbit by the rising-*jyā* of the solar orbit, one takes the square of the quotient obtained by dividing by the radius (*trijyā*). Subtracting this from the square of the mid-*jyā*, the square root is the *dṛkkṣepa* (parallax) on the solar orbit.

Likewise, having multiplied the middle sine produced from the lunar orbit by its own ascensional difference sine, one divides by the radius (trijyā); the square of the resulting quotient is subtracted from the square of its own middle sine, and the square root of the remainder is the horizontal parallax (dṛkkṣepa) on the lunar orbit. Having subtracted the square of the solar horizontal parallax from the square of the visual sine calculated by means of the Sun’s own day-and-night circle and so forth, the square root of the remainder is the visual motion-sine (dṛggatijyā) on the solar orbit.

Having subtracted the square of the lunar horizontal parallax from the square of the visual sine calculated by means of the Moon’s own day-and-night circle and so forth, the square root of the remainder becomes the visual motion-sine on the lunar orbit.
In this manner, the visibility of other planets also occurs from the center of their respective mean mandalas.

At sunrise, during a solar eclipse, because the moon is situated below, the lunar disc is observed to be depressed to the east of the line passing through the center of the solar disc within the lunar orbit.
At sunset, it is exactly the same.

On the other side: for an observer situated on a level stretch of ground, the difference in the direction of vision (dṛggatyantara), which is equal to the radius of the earth, corresponds to a visual path-chord (dṛggatijyā) equal to the radius of the earth;
likewise, in the southern and northern hemispheres, the difference in the horizontal deviation (dṛkkṣepāntara) is the refraction (nati).

[In this regard, there is the following proportion: If, by a visual path-chord equal to the radius of the earth, a difference in the direction of vision equal to half the circumference of the earth in yojanas is obtained, then by the visual path-chord produced at the desired time...
"How much?

[Again, the rule of three proportions is as follows: "If by the *karṇa* of the true *yojana*s, *kalās* equal to the radius (*trijyā*) are obtained, then by how many are they obtained by the *yojana*s of the visual motion [= parallax]?"

Thus: here, in the first proportion (*trairāśika*), the radius (*trijyā*) is the divisor; in the second, it is the multiplier. Because they are equal, [upon their cancellation], the semi-diameter of the earth is the multiplier for the observed motion (*dṛggati*) of the sun and moon, and the result is the *sphuṭa-yojanakarṇa* in minutes (*liptā*). Having subtracted the sun’s minutes from the moon’s minutes, the proportion is as follows: if sixty *nāḍīs* are obtained by means of the difference between the true daily motions (*dinasphuṭabhukti*), [then...]
Then, by these multiplied [values], how many [units] are there?
The result obtained are the *nāḍīs*, which are the *ghaṭikās* of the visual motion (i.e., parallax).
In the eastern hemisphere, the planet is depressed in its orbit from the east;
therefore, the prior conjunction is subtracted from the planet.
Because the other hemisphere is inclined away from the observer, the conjunction will occur after an interval of time equal to that of the lambana-ghaṭikās; therefore, they are added.
This operation is performed in this manner until there is no further difference.
Thus, the minutes of parallax for the sun and moon are determined as before by the rule of three (trairāśika).
If the middle sines of the Sun and Moon are situated in the same direction, then the difference between the minutes of their respective latitudes is taken; otherwise, their sum is taken.
From that, the deflection (avanati) is obtained.

Then, having subtracted the node from the Moon at the time of the mean eclipse, the sine of the north-south arm (bhuja) of the remainder is multiplied by four and a half (4.5) and divided by the radius (trijyā); this is the displacement (vikṣepa).

The sum of the depression (*avanati*) and the deflection (*vikṣepa*) when they are in the same direction, and their difference when they are in opposite directions, is the true deflection (*sphuṭavikṣepa*). "True deflection" and "depression" are synonyms.
And by means of that depression (avanati), having brought the half-duration of the station and subtracting it from the middle transit, the remainder is the time of contact (sparśakāla).
By that [time], the procedure for parallax (lambana) is performed as before.
The half-duration of the stay (*sthityardha*) increases by an interval of *ghaṭikās* equal to the difference between the [time of] contact and the middle [time].
That [interval], moreover, should be subtracted from the middle time and the half-duration of the stay generated repeatedly until it becomes stable.
At the time of release (*mokṣa*), however, one should add the first calculated half-duration of the stay to the middle lunar day (*madhyatithi*).
As before, the half-duration of the eclipse (*sthityardha*) is increased by the interval of the parallax (*lambana*) at the middle point of the eclipse;
this is then added to the middle lunar day (*tithi*), and as before, the parallax moments are calculated.
Having increased the half-duration by that middle parallax interval, the same operation is performed again until it becomes stable.

In this manner, one should subtract from the Sun or Moon the portion of the degrees traversed by the motion of the Sun or Moon associated with the established half-duration (*sthityardha*) at the time of contact during a central eclipse; during liberation (*mokṣa*), one should add it.
These [corrections] become the times of contact and liberation.
Furthermore, when there is parallax (*lambana*) in both the eastern and western hemispheres, the half-duration, joined with the sum of those two parallaxes, becomes the true half-duration.
Having drawn a circle on level ground with a cord of the measure of the earth's semi-diameter, and having marked the cardinal directions,

one should place two points at a distance equal to the sine of the ascensional difference (udayajyā) to the north or south of the east-west line in the eastern part of the mandala; then, having stretched a cord touching the tops of the two points, one should draw a line, which becomes the sine of the ascensional difference.
Again, having made the center of the middle circle, one should rotate a circle with a cord equal to the middle sine;
that is the middle-sine circle (*madhyajyāmaṇḍala*).
From two points on the circumference of the triple-sine circle (*trijyāmaṇḍala*), one should bring two cords to the central point and thus form two lines.
That half of the intermediate chord (antarajyārdha) is likewise established on the middle circle (madhyajyāmaṇḍala) to the east, west, north, or south.
The square root of the difference between the squares of that [half-chord] and the middle circle is the versine (koṭi) of the oblique ascensional sine (dṛkkṣepajyā) on the middle circle.
Having marked two points on the great circle (trijyāmaṇḍala) at a distance equal to the amplitude (udayajyākāṣṭha) from the east and west [points], [starting from the center of the circle...]

When the interval is equal to the midday meridian-sine, one should assume the point of the oblique ascension (dṛkkṣepabindu) to the south. Having produced a fish-figure by means of the three points, one should rotate a circle passing through the three points from the intersection of the line touching the mouth and tail of that fish;
that is the solar revolution-circle (arkabhramavṛtta).
In that context, the line of interval between the center of the earth and the point in space where the sun is located is the *dṛgjyā* (sine of altitude), which serves as the hypotenuse;
the local *dṛkkṣepajyā* (sine of parallax) is the perpendicular (*koṭi*);
and the interval starting from the tip of that [perpendicular] up to the tip of the *dṛgjyā*, marked by the position of the sun, is the remaining segment.
The sine of the arc of visibility (dṛggatijyā) is that [line] from east to west;
in this way, a distinguished triangular field is produced. // 34 //
[The operation for the *akṣadṛkkarman*:
To demonstrate the state of being a debt or a credit due to the deviation (*vikṣepa*) at rising and setting, he says:
"The sine of the deviation multiplied by the sine of the latitude and divided by the co-latitude shall be a debt when [the planet] is situated in the north."
There is wealth when the moon is rising; there is wealth when it is setting; and there is debt when the moon is moving southward. // 35 //
The sine of the ascensional difference, multiplied by the oblique ascension and divided by the gnomon-shadow multiplier (lambaka), yields the result in minutes of arc.
In the case of northern oblique ascension, this is subtracted from the moon at its rising and added at its setting.

When the moon is situated in the east with a southerly declination, there is a gain; at its setting, there is a loss. This method for calculating gain and loss is equivalent to the derivation of the result from the semi-difference of the sun's motion. // 35 //
[The correction for precession] To demonstrate the nature of subtraction and addition based on the precession, he says:
"The obliquity multiplied by the declination and divided by the square of half the amplitude..."
In the northern course there is wealth; in the southern course, wealth; and in the southern direction, debt.
"Vikṣepa" (dispersion) and "apakrama" (departure) constitute "vikṣepāpakramau.
That which possesses these two qualities—dispersion and departure—is "vikṣepāpakramaguṇam.
Here, "dispersion" is understood as being momentary (*tātkālika*).

The meaning is: the cotangent of the moon increased by three signs, multiplied by the displacement (vikṣepa) and the maximum declination (paramāpakrama). [Apakrama is the declination; paramāpakrama is the maximum declination; utkramaṇa is the cotangent (utkramajyā). It means the cotangent of the moon increased by three signs, multiplied by the displacement and the maximum declination.
How is that *utkramaṇa* (ascensional difference) of the moon increased by three signs determined?
From the mention of "increased by three signs," the addition of three signs is understood.
One should multiply the *utkramajyā* (versed sine) of the moon increased by three signs.
One should divide [the square of] the semi-diameter by the square [of the sine]; the result is in *liptās*.
If the declination is northward—that is, during the northern solstice—it is subtracted; if southward, it is added.
That same result is added if the declination is northward during the southern solstice.
In the south, it is a debt; in the case of southern displacement, there would be a debt.
This same principle applies to both debt and wealth.
Since, when the declination and precession are of the same direction, the planet is obtained as increased by that much [the sum], and is subtracted from the eastern and western horizons; whereas,
when the declination and precession are of different directions, it is decreased by that much, and thus added [to the result].
This ritual action for all the grahas proceeds at their respective times of rising and setting, but not at midday or midnight. // 36 //

[The nature of the moon and others, and the cause of their perception] To describe the nature of the moon and so forth, he says: "The moon is water, the sun is fire; earth, shadow, and even darkness are indeed those."
The moon eclipses the sun, and the great shadow of the earth eclipses the moon. // 37 //
That which is this lunar orb is water as perceived by direct perception;
the sun is fire by virtue of its nature of heat;
and the earth is the ground, consisting of clay.
"Shadow on earth is darkness by its very nature.
The moon, the *candra*, obscures the sun;
the sun, situated above, is obscured by the moon situated below.
Furthermore, the great shadow of the earth obscures the moon;
there is also a difference between these two as perceivers,
since the shadow is vast while the moon is small.
The moon is diminished [in size], while the sun is vast.
[The time of occurrence during an eclipse: To explain when the two eclipses occur, he says:
When the moon, approaching its node, enters the sun at the end of a clear lunar month,
or enters the shadow of the earth at the end of the fortnight, then that is the middle of the eclipse, whether it be greater or less than expected.

The clear lunar month is the *sphuṭa-śaśimāsa*; at its end, upon its completion on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), [the moon] approaches the sun, the Āditya; "approaching the node" (*pātāsanna*) means approaching the node by way of motion along the path of declination (*vikṣepa*).
When the moon enters [the earth's shadow], when there is a solar eclipse,
or when at the end of the lunar fortnight or the full moon, the moon approaches the node (pāta) and enters the shadow of the earth,
then the middle of the eclipse occurs with either an excess or a deficiency [of time].

Since the middle of the eclipse in the eastern hemisphere is increased by the amount produced by the subtraction of the true lunar date (sphuṭatithiccheda), the ghaṭīs of parallax (lambana) must be subtracted there, because the middle of the eclipse has already passed by that much time. In the western hemisphere, the middle of the eclipse is decreased by the amount produced by the subtraction of the true lunar date; therefore, the ghaṭīs of parallax are added there.
Because it has been cultivated, there is the grasping of the middle as well. // 38 //

[The length of the Earth's shadow] He states the measure of the Earth's shadow: one should divide the distance between the Earth and the Sun by the difference between the Sun and the Earth multiplied by the Earth.
The length of the shadow of the earth is obtained from the diameter of the terrestrial globe. // 39 //
The interval between the earth and the sun is the "bhū-ravi-vivara" (earth-sun gap);
the sun's distance in yojanas is 459,585,
multiplied by the earth [factor]— that is, multiplied by the diameter of the earth, which is 1,050.
One should divide [the circumference] by the difference between the diameters of the Sun and the Earth— specifically, between 4410 and 1050— which is 3360;
that result is the length of the shadow of the terrestrial globe, starting from the diameter of the terrestrial globe, which is 143620.
In this case, the following is the operation concerning the shadow of a lamp: the diameter of the sun is the lamp, and the diameter of the earth is the gnomon.
The difference between the diameters of the sun and the earth is the "difference of the sun's and earth's diameters";
the solar yojana-carna is the difference between the shadow of the gnomon and the lamp. This is the formulation of the rule for the calculation of lamp-shadow.
The proof follows precisely from the method of lamp-shadow.
One should tie two threads on opposite sides of the solar globe's circumference and likewise two threads along the diameter of the sun and the earth at a single point;
thus, the shadow of the earth is observed to diminish progressively from the earth's diameter. // 39 //
[The diameter of the shadow] Regarding the calculation of the Earth's shadow within the lunar orbit, he says:
"The distance between the tip of the shadow and the moon, multiplied by the diameter of the Earth..."
One should know that the shadow of the earth divides the diameter of darkness into two parts. // 40 //
The distance from the tip of the Earth's shadow to the Moon is the interval between the tip of the shadow and the Moon.
The length of the Earth's shadow is 143,620; subtracting 34,377 (the Moon's radius) from this gives 109,243 as the interval between the tip of the shadow and the Moon.

This is multiplied by the diameter of the Earth (1,050) and divided by the length of the Earth's shadow (143,620), yielding 689 as the diameter of the shadow at the Moon's orbit during its own eclipse. # The diameter of the Earth's shadow at the Moon's orbit during its own eclipse.

It is as follows: if by the moon’s radius in *yojanas* (3439) one obtains the [earth’s] semi-diameter, then how much is obtained by half the diameter of darkness? Thus, the measure of the minutes of arc for half the diameter of darkness is found to be 800;19.
Thus, the calculation of the minutes of arc for the diameters of the sun and moon is performed using their respective distinct yojana-distances and ears (karṇas).
The diameter of the sun is 4,410; multiplied by the semi-diameter [of the earth] which is 3,438, and divided by the solar yojana-ear of 457,585, the resulting solar disc in minutes of arc is 33;00.
The diameter of the moon (315) multiplied by the earth's radius (3438) and divided by the moon's distance in yojanas (34377) results in the moon's disk in minutes of arc: 31;10;40.

[Calculation of the Half-duration of the Eclipse] To demonstrate the half-duration of the eclipse, he says: From the square of that half-sum of conjunctions with the moon, subtract the square of the moon's latitude.
Half of its duration is to be known as its base, derived from the daily motion of the moon and the sun. // 41 //
The meaning is that half the sum of the diameters of the eclipsed and the eclipsing bodies is half the sum of their measures (*mānaikyārdha*).
The square of that is "the square of half the sum of the moon and [the eclipsing body].
From that, the square of the moon's latitude (*vikṣepa*) is to be subtracted.
In both types of eclipses, the displacement is measured from the moon.
In a solar eclipse, the true displacement is taken as the displacement combined with or subtracted from the deflection (avanati).
Its square root constitutes the half-duration of the eclipse.
How so? From the daily motion of the moon and the sun.
By the term "daily motion of the moon and the sun," their daily traversals are understood.

For those two moving in direct motion, a rule of three (trairāśika) operation is performed by means of the difference in their daily motions: if, by the specific difference between the motions of the sun and the moon...
When sixty nāḍīs are obtained, then by means of the liptās of the half-duration, how many ghaṭikās of the half-duration are obtained? // 41 //
[The calculation of half the eclipse duration:
Thus, half the eclipse duration (vimardārdha) is to be derived. How so?
It is the square of that which remains when the radius of the moon is subtracted from the radius of the dark portion (tamas).
Therefore, that which is devoid of the activity of distraction is the root for the purpose of crushing [the afflictions]. // 42 //
Thus, for this reason,
half the duration [of the eclipse] is to be subtracted at the time of contact and added at the time of release;

furthermore, having calculated the sun, moon, and node for the times of contact and release by means of the *ghaṭikās* of half the duration, one should again determine the latitudes (*vikṣepas*) for contact and release.
By means of those two, both values for the half-duration of the stay are obtained without distinction;
the proof is seen through the process of calculation.
One should draw a circle with a radius equal to half the measure of the eclipsed disc.

That is the disc of the eclipsed body (*grāhyabimba*). Then, with the same center and using a compass radius equal to half the sum of the diameters of the two bodies, one should draw another circle; that is the circle of the sum of the semi-diameters of the eclipsed and eclipsing bodies (*samparkārdhamaṇḍala*).
Then, along the north-south line, one should extend a cord from the center toward the north or south by a distance equal to the declination (vikṣepa) according to the direction, and mark a point.

By means of the "fish" method (matsyavidhi), one should draw the east-west line. From the intersection of that line with the circle whose radius is half the contact-distance (samparkārdha), one should draw a line reaching the center.
In this way, a field that is half as long as it is wide arises; therein, half the diameter of contact is the diagonal, and the displacement is the side.
The square root of the difference of those squares is the koti; this is the half-duration [of the eclipse].

When the distance between the centers of the eclipsed and the eclipsing orbs is equal to the difference between the radii of the eclipsed and the eclipsing orbs, then that difference between the radii of the eclipsed and the eclipsing orbs is the karṇa (the hypotenuse).
The *vikṣepa* itself is the base (*bhuja*); the square root of the difference between its squares is the perpendicular (*koṭi*), which is half the *vimarda*. // 42 //
[The measure of the moon's eclipse: To calculate the remaining portion of the eclipsed part, he says: "Having subtracted half the diameter of the shadow from half the diameter of the moon."
That which remains after the distraction and is not perceived belongs to the moon. // 43 //
Subtracting half the diameter of the moon from half the diameter of Rāhu, and then subtracting that result from the lunar latitude (vikṣepa),
whatever remains is not eclipsed by the moon. During the middle of the eclipse, this applies for as much as the latitude extends to the north or south.
At that time, the distance between the centers of the two is exactly that much;
however, when there is an obliquity (vikṣepa),
it becomes greater than the difference between half the diameters of the moon and the shadow.
At that time, the lunar disc is observed to have emerged from the midst of darkness by a distance on its second side equal to the radius of the orb;
having subtracted from the lunar disc that portion which is not grasped, the remainder shall be the measure of the eclipse.
As with the moon, so too with the sun. // 43 //
[The Desired Time Portion] In order to demonstrate the calculation of the desired time portion, he says:
"The square root of the difference between the middle of the duration and the square of the displacement, diminished by the desired [time]."
Subtracting from half the conjunction, the remainder is the current degree of obscuration. // 44 //
The category of distraction (vikṣepavarga) is added to that;
"duration" (sthiti) refers to the period beginning from contact (sparśa) until liberation (mokṣa);
the middle of that is the "half-duration" (sthityardha).
Excluding the desired time and excluding the desired [longitude],
that which is the root should be subtracted from half the sum of the conjunctions and subtracted from half the sum of the orbs;
the remainder is the instantaneous eclipse.
Half the duration of the stay, diminished by the elapsed time and multiplied by the difference in velocity, divided by sixty, gives the *liptās*.
Having added the square of that many *liptās* of the displacement (*vikṣepa*) to [the previous result], it is subjected to extraction of the square root;
the root is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).
Having subtracted that *karṇa* from half the sum of the diameters (*mānaikya*), the remainder is the instantaneous *grāsa*.
By that much *karṇa*, the eclipsing body has entered. // 44 //
[The Axial Precession and the Solstitial Precession] To demonstrate the sines of precession, he says:
The axial [sine] multiplied by the *utkrama* [sine] at midday, and divided by half the diameter, is the direction [of the precession] to the south.
And at the time of contact, [the calculation] is from half the duration of the station of the sun and moon, increased by three signs, and from the [precession of the] solstice. // 45 //

"From midday onwards" means the sequence starting from midday (*madhyāhnotkrama*). The term "midday" refers here to the *ghaṭikās* occurring within the interval between the lunar day (*tithi*) and midday. In that case, within the eastern hemisphere (*prākkapāla*), the *ghaṭikās* of the lunar day are to be subtracted from half of the day.
In the latter half of the skull, [the offering] is for them during the half-day;
"at midday" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Accordingly, during a lunar eclipse, the *ghaṭikās* of the interval between midnight and sunrise are taken.

Those sixfold parts are their *utkramajyā* (versed sines); by that, the *akṣajyā* situated to the south is to be multiplied and divided by the half-extent, which is the radius (*vyāsārdha*), and the result becomes the direction (*dik*).
The Teacher stated "to the south" with reference to the rear skull-bowl,
because the front portion of the rear skull-bowl turns toward the south.
The upper part is toward the north;
furthermore, in the eastern half, the front part is toward the north, while the rear part turns toward the south.
In this way, the eastern and western portions of the lunar disc curve toward the north and south,
because "curving" (valana) is expressed by the term "direction" (dik).

Where the moon enters the shadow of the earth, as the lunar disc is being diminished there, that curvature remains in the eastern hemisphere on the northern side of the front portion of the lunar disc.
In the latter part, it is by the south;
on the other side of the bowl, it is the reverse.
The deviation occurs exactly according to the direction during a solar eclipse.
Furthermore, when the shadow of the earth is conceived as the grasper, then there is a reversal of direction for the displacement (*vikṣepa*).
"Half of the duration" (*sthityardha*) means half of the duration; it is the displacement.
Since half of the duration occurs by virtue of the displacement, [the calculation proceeds accordingly].
By that term "half-duration" (sthityardha), the parallax (vikṣepa) is expressed;
therefore, by virtue of that parallax, the calculation of the second deflection (dvitīyavalana) for the sun and moon is performed.
"Sun and moon" (arkendū): the sun (arka) and the moon (indu).
Of those two, the sun and the moon, when increased by three signs, whatever their declination (ayana) may be—
by the word "ayana" is meant the oblique ascension (krānti),
and by the word "three signs" the sine (jyā) is to be taken in reverse order.
When the sun and moon, together with three signs, are less than half a circle (180 degrees), then there is a northern directional deviation in the eastern hemisphere;
when they are greater than half a circle, then there is a southern directional deviation in the eastern hemisphere.
The ascensional difference multiplied by the obliquity of the ecliptic and divided by the radius is the sine of the declination-correction (*krāntivalana*).
On the eastern side of that disc, it is north if [the correction] is north,
and south if it is south.
On the other side of the meridian, however, the calculation of direction must be performed by inversion.

From the center of the equatorial circle, at a distance equal to the latitude (akṣa) to the south, the interval between the east-west oriented circle [the nāḍī-maṇḍala] and that point is the axial declination (akṣavalana).
From that center, it increases in reverse order.
This calculation of the displacement must be performed using the versed sine (*utkramajyā*) of the planet's depression from the center of the celestial equator.
In the eastern hemisphere, due to the motion of the visual ray (*karṇagati*), the eastern part of the disc appears to the north, while the western part appears to the south.
On the outer hemisphere (parakapāla), the eastern part [of the bimba] is shown by the southern side and the western part by the northern side;
thus one should demonstrate it on the sphere.
However, the axial deviation (ayanavalana) differs at the beginning of the northern and southern solstices.
It appears in the north during the period beginning with Aries, and in the south during the period beginning with Libra.
In this way, the drawing is performed by means of three rotations of the compass.
First, one should draw the circle of the desired radius on level ground.
Then, from that very center, one should draw the circle of the contact-radius [and the circle of the diameter].
The radius of the circle should be divided by the desired divisor. A circle with that radius should be drawn, marked with the cardinal directions—east, west, south, and north.
Having reduced the latitudes, declinations, and obliquities to minutes, their sum should be performed if they are in the same direction, and their difference if they are in opposite directions.

On the semi-diameter circle, having made a deflection (valana) toward the south or north according to the motion of the apamaṇḍala [in the western part], one should mark a point. Then, one should draw a thread reaching the center. Where that thread meets the circumference of the half-sum of the measures (mānaikyārdha), from there, having moved north or south by the amount of the displacement (vikṣepa) and having led it along the circumference, one should mark a point at the end.
Therefore, one should draw a line from that point [the center of the shadow] toward the center;
where it touches the disc of the eclipsed body, there occurs the contact: for the Sun, on its western side, and for the Moon, on its eastern side of the disc.
The center of the image of the eclipsing body, however, lies on the circle of half-contact.
During a solar eclipse, the parallax at first contact is as before, according to the direction, on the circumference of half the sum of the apparent diameters;
from its tip, the deflection is applied in the respective direction.
During a lunar eclipse, one should extend the line in the opposite direction;
from its tip, one should lead a thread to reach the center.
Wherever it touches the circumference of the object to be grasped, there is contact.
In a solar eclipse, the liberation-rotation extends toward the eastern side; in a lunar eclipse, it extends toward the western side in the reverse manner.
Then, having extended the liberation-line (mokṣavikṣepa) toward the sun in its proper direction and in the opposite direction for the moon, one should mark a point (bindu).
From the tip of that [point], one should draw a line reaching the center (kendra).
Where it touches the circumference of the eclipsed body, there is liberation (mokṣa).
During the middle of the eclipse, the parallax of the middle (madhyagrahaṇavalana) occurs due to the displacement (vikṣepa);
on the circle of half-contact, if the displacement is to the south, the parallax is to the north from the east.
The right [turn] by the far side;
in the case of a lateral throw,
the left turn by the far side.
One should extend the southern line toward the east. [In the case of a solar eclipse, the opposite should be done.
From its tip, a meridian line (south-north line) should be drawn.
From the point of intersection of the circles of their respective measures, one should draw a line reaching the center;
following that line from the center, one should mark the position of the Sun in its proper direction, and that of the Moon in the opposite direction.
Having extended the dispersion, one should place a point at its tip;
from that, one should divide the [object-image] by means of half the diameter of the perceiver's image.
First, the eclipsed disc of the object to be grasped is observed.

On the desired diagram, having produced two fish figures by means of the three points for the commencement, middle, and end of the eclipse, one should rotate a circle using a thread that passes through those three points and emerges from the mouths and tails of the two fish, meeting at the intersection of the threads.
That is the path of the center of the disc to be eclipsed.

There, having extended a thread— the measure of the desired *grāsa* (eclipse) and *karṇa* (distance)— from the center toward the direction of the path of the eclipsing body, one observes the partial eclipse for that time from the point where it touches the path of the eclipsing body, by means of a diagram drawn with half the diameter of the eclipsing body.

Having calculated the ear (karṇa) for the closing and opening [of an eclipse] using the half-eclipsed portions resulting from the contact, just as in the case of a desired immersion, the closing and opening should be demonstrated according to the method for the desired immersion. // 45 //
[The color of the apprehended image:
To demonstrate the color of the apprehended image, he says: At the end of the grasping [of the full orb], it is smoky; at the grasping of a fragment, it becomes like the moon, black.
In a total eclipse, the sun is tawny with a slight reddish-brown tint when in the midst of Tamas.
At the beginning, during the seizing and the touch; at the end, during liberation,
the moon becomes smoky.
When there is a partial eclipse, the moon becomes black;
during a partial eclipse, it appears near half-eclipsed and is perceived by all.
During a total eclipse, it is tawny, with a blackish-copper hue in the midst of darkness.
When the entire disc is covered, then it is a total eclipse (*sarvagrāsa*); at that time, it is of a tawny color (*kapilavarṇa*).
Beyond that, from the time of the *vimarda* until the middle [of the eclipse], it becomes dark copper-colored (*sakṛṣṇatāmra*).
Furthermore, during a solar eclipse, it is always black in color. // 46 //

[The solar eclipse is not to be predicted]; he says this in order to demonstrate the perception of an eclipse: when there is a conjunction with the paridhi of the sun or moon, an eighth part of the sun becomes unindicatable (*anādeśya*).
This is due to the luminous nature of the sun and the translucence of the lunar halo. // 47 //
The conjunction of the solar and lunar halos is a solar eclipse.
In this case, even if one-eighth of the solar disc is obscured,
it is not perceptible due to the brilliance of the sun.
Because the sun possesses a luminous nature,
and because the moon’s body is translucent, even an eighth part of its disc that is obscured is not perceptible.
The eighth part of the eclipsed disc, subtracted from half the sum of the measures [of the two discs], is the desired chord of the eclipse (iṣṭagrāsakarṇa).
From that group, the square root of the subtracted square of the true latitude (sphuṭavikṣepa) becomes the minutes of the half-duration [of the contact] diminished by the desired [time].
These, multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in motion, become ghaṭikās.
These [are to be applied] at the end of the lunar day (tithyanta) for the moment of contact (sparśa).
One should purify [the time];
one should also apply it at the end of the lunar day for liberation.
Those two become the times of contact and liberation. // 47 //

[The Means for Calculating Planets] For the purpose of demonstrating the means for calculating planets, he says: One should calculate the earth [longitude] from its non-separation [from the sun], and the moon from the conjunction of the sun and the moon.
Just as from the conjunction of the moon with the stars and planets, so too are all the stars and planets. // 48 //
Earth and Sun:
the conjunction of these two is the earth-sun conjunction;
from that, one should calculate the Sun.
One should calculate the moon from its conjunction with the sun;
and all the other stars and planets should be calculated from their conjunctions with the moon and the stars.
One should cause a circle to be made on a leveled ground surface raised for observation, its circumference marked with degrees of the zodiac and its four cardinal directions indicated.
Standing at its western side, the astrologer should observe the rising sun as it touches the eastern horizon.
Then, having made a mark at that spot, he should remain there until the next sunrise.
There too, he should place a mark at the point on the horizon where the sun is observed to have risen.
Thus, by means of three or four risings, the intermediate ghaṭīs should be determined using an instrument or similar device;
these are the revolutions traversed by the sun within the interval between two solar risings,
and they are precisely the minutes of arc of the true solar revolution.

By observing the shadows at midday and applying the method for calculating the sine and so forth, one should determine the two positions of the sun; the difference between these two is the true daily motion of the sun. Then, once the sun has entered Aries, the sunrises are counted until it enters the next sign, Aries.
These become the solar yogas.
Thus, when correctly observed, in the solar revolution (bhagaṇa) there are three hundred and sixty-five days and fifteen ghaṭikās.
The *vighaṭikās* are thirty-one (31); the *prāṇas* are three and a half (3 1/2). These, reduced to a common denominator in sequence, yield the numerator 210,389 and the divisor 576.
Thus, by these parts with denominators of sixty, seventy, and fifty, one solar revolution (arkabhagaṇa) is formed;
by these, the measurement of the [lunar] yoga and so forth is performed. For the purpose of accomplishing the conjunction of the sun and moon, one should observe the moon as transited by the sun.
Furthermore, for the second year, through such vigilance, there are twelve conjunctions of the sun and moon (12), four signs (4),
and twelve degrees (12).
Forty-six liptās (46),
forty viliptās (40), and forty-eight tatparas (48).
These [numbers], increased by one solar revolution and reduced to a common denominator, are 1,039,560,048 / 77,760,000; these are the lunar revolutions elapsed in a *yuga*.
By means of the rule of three (*trairāśika*): if by the passage of one solar revolution this many lunar revolutions (1,039,560,048 / 77,760,000) are obtained, then...
Then, by this [number of] revolutions of the sun in a yuga, namely 4,320,000, how many [revolutions] are there?
The result obtained is the number of lunar revolutions in a yuga: 57,753,336.

Alternatively, starting from the desired first day of the bright fortnight of the moon, one should mark a point every day at the time of the moon's rising until the completion of one solar revolution.

Thus, the number of moon-rises during the period of one solar revolution (ravi-bhagaṇa) is found to be 352; 53; 23; 28; 12. When reduced to a common denominator, this becomes 352 / 11532492 / 216000. By means of these values, the rule of three (trairāśika) is applied as follows: if there are this many moon-rises in the course of one solar revolution, [then...]
At that time, how many [revolutions of the sun] occur in a yuga?
As before, the lunar risings in a yuga are found to be 1,524,484,164.
When these are subtracted from the revolutions of the earth (terrestrial days), 1,582,237,500, the result is the lunar revolutions in a yuga: 57,753,336.

Subtracting the conjunctions of the moon with the stars and planets from the lunar revolutions, the remainder is the revolutions of the desired planet. According to the *Jāgara* [treatise], the conjunctions of the moon and Jupiter per year amount to thirteen revolutions and three signs.
Degrees: 12, minutes: 25, seconds: 33, thirds: 36.
These have been calculated in sequence as 1,033,004,016 / 77,760,000;
if this many conjunctions of Jupiter and the Moon (1,033,004,016 / 77,760,000) are obtained in a single revolution of the Sun, [then...]

Then, [to find] how many [conjunctions] there are in the solar revolutions of a *yuga* (4,320,000), one obtains the conjunctions of Jupiter and the Moon in *yuga*-years as 57,389,112. Subtracting these from the lunar revolutions (57,753,336), the remainder is the number of Jupiter's revolutions in a *yuga*, which is 364,224.

In this same manner, for Mars and the other planets as well, one should calculate their conjunctions with the Moon up until the point of completing the solar revolutions, and thereby determine the planetary revolutions.
This very method for calculating the mean longitudes of Mercury and Venus is beyond the reach of people like us.

When [Mercury or Venus] has set in the east, one should subtract half the number of days until it rises again from the days of its rising; conversely, one should add that same amount to the days of its setting.

Furthermore, when there is sunset in the east and sunrise in the west, the calculation of the whole-day (niraṃśa) day should be performed by this very same method. Between those two initial and final whole-days, the number of revolutions of the swift apogee (śīghrakendra) occurs; for Mercury, the approximate days of the swift apogee's revolution are 116, and for Venus, 584.
Having divided these [elapsed days] by 1,577,917,500, the quotient obtained constitutes the revolutions of the mean centers of Mercury and Venus;
this is the method for calculating the [mean] epicycle of the Sun's apogee.

Having determined the sun by means of the midday shadow, and having subtracted it from the mean sun for that day—if the [calculated] mean is greater, [the difference is] a debt; if less, it is a credit.
Having observed this daily in this manner until the increasing solar correction becomes constant, that correction is the maximum correction (*paramaphala*).
Thereafter, it will undergo decrease.
On the day of the supreme fruit, when the sun is at its mean position and characterized by a negative fruit, one should subtract three signs;
the remainder is the apogee of the sun's anomaly (*ravimandocca*).
One should add three signs to the [longitude] indicated by the fruit of wealth; this becomes the apogee of Saturn.
The sine of the maximum fruit, multiplied by the degrees of the circle and divided by the radius, [is the equation of the apsis].
The circumference of the sun [is determined]. The calculation of the circumference of the moon's apogee is as follows:

from the time of sunset, in the dark fortnight, by however many *ghaṭikās*—as measured by a water-clock—the moon rises, one should calculate the ascendant from the sun plus six signs using its own rising-times according to the method stated in the *Tripraśna*.
It should be performed.
That is the "clear moon" (sphuṭacandra).
That remainder from the subtraction of the mean moon at that time is the equation of center (māndaphala), whether additive or subtractive.
In this manner, one should observe daily as before until the increasing result becomes stable.
Thereafter, the calculation of the apogee (ucca) is performed like that of the sun.
One should do this every day until [the difference between] the mean and the true [motions] is eliminated.
There would be no difference whatsoever;
that very moon becomes its own exaltation (*ucca*).
Having calculated the interval between the maximum daily result and the day’s exaltation, one should calculate the interval between the maximum daily result and the sun for that day.

Then, by the rule of three: "If this difference in apogee is produced by this interval of motion, then what [is produced] by the revolutions of the sun?"—thus is the determination of the revolutions of the apogee of the Moon.
The determination of the revolutions of the Moon's node follows.

In a lunar eclipse, from the time of contact until the middle of the eclipse, there are *sthityardha* (half-duration) *ghaṭikās* produced at the time of the lunar eclipse; one should multiply those by the difference between the true motions of the sun and the moon, divide by sixty,
and they will become *sthityardha* *liptās*.
Having subtracted the square of that [lateral] component from the square of half the contact duration, the square root of the remainder is the lunar latitude (*candravikṣepa*).
That, multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by 270, converted into *kāṣṭhas*, is the arc of the [latitude] sine.
In this same manner, one should determine the [half-duration of] release (*mokṣa*)—that is, the half-duration of the eclipse—from the central conjunction.
If the planet is in an odd pada (ojapada), it is the first half of the duration;
otherwise, it would be in an even pada (yugmapada).

If there is northern declination, the arc of the [latitude] sine (bhujacāpa) is the true value when in an odd quadrant; when in an even quadrant, it is obtained by subtracting from half the circle (cakrārdha).
In the case of southern declination, one should add half the circle when in an odd quadrant.
In the case of an even quadrant, one should subtract from the circle;
that shall be the arm (bāhu).
In this manner, the remainder should also be determined by one's own intelligence.
In this manner, one should calculate another arm for the time of the [next] eclipse;
one should determine the interval between the two.
The motion of its fall (tātpātabhukti) arises from the interval between the times of the two eclipses.
From that, the determination of the revolutions of the moon's apogee is achieved.
Alternatively, one should calculate the moon's declination from its midday shadow as previously described;
the difference between that [declination] and the moon's declination for that day is the latitude (vikṣepa).
"The rest is as before" means:
for Mercury and Venus, at whatever time elapsed during the night their setting occurs, the ascendant increased by six signs is the true [longitude] of Mercury and Venus.
For the remaining [planets], the calculation is like that of the Moon, based on the time elapsed during the night.
The difference between the mean and the true [mean] positions, increased or decreased by the slow correction (manda-phala), is the fast correction (śīghra-phala).
Again, the calculation of the correction must be performed every five days;
one should then subtract it from the previous correction.

In this manner, one should first examine [the values] until the increasing [value], which yields a swift result, becomes stable. Having thus inferred by means of one's own intellect, one should establish the calculation of the [mean] anomaly and the apsis; [and from there,] the conjunctions and intervals of the lunar mansions and the planets.
The calculation of planetary displacement (vikṣepa) must be performed.
The determination of the rapid revolutions (śīghrabhagaṇa) should be carried out by means of heliacal rising, setting, retrogression, and direct motion.
Alternatively, having determined the planet by means of an instrument such as a gnomon (yaṣṭi), one should observe it again at that same time on the following day.
In the interval between those [mean positions], there is the true motion.
When that [true motion] is less than the mean motion, the planet is above the orbital circle;
if it is greater, then it is below.
The interval between those two [nodes] is the *karṇa*.

By means of that, one should observe the extreme smallness and extreme largeness of the motion [of the planet] until the completion of the revolution (*bhagaṇa*). The completion of the revolution occurs by means of the mean motion.
Thus it is.

Having observed the maximum excess of the slow motion (mānda) when its fruit is thus minimal, the maximum slow fruit (māndaphala) is the difference between the maximum and minimum semi-diameters of the epicycle (karṇa). // 48 //
[The Recollection of the Tradition] As for how the dimensions of the lunar mansions and so forth were known by the Teacher, he states this in order to explain them:
"Extracted from the ocean of knowledge of the existent and non-existent, by the grace of Brahmā."
I have, by means of the boat of my own intellect, immersed myself in the supreme jewel of true knowledge. 49.
Existence and non-existence;
existence is the auspicious, non-existence is the inauspicious;
knowledge is that by which something is known.
The supreme jewel of true knowledge: that very true knowledge is the supreme jewel, the most excellent jewel,
namely the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
"Submerged" means hidden.

"By the boat of one's own intellect" (*svamatināvā*): one's own intellect (*svamati*) is itself the boat; by that boat of one's own intellect, [the self] has been rescued from the ocean of knowledge regarding the existent and the non-existent. // 49 //
[The prescription of punishment for one who acts as a counterfeit: To establish an oath, he says:
"The work named Āryabhaṭīya is always eternal, originating from the Self-born (Svāyambhuva)."
He brings about the destruction of both merit and lifespan for one who acts as his counterfeiter. 50.

This is the *Āryabhaṭīya* of Āryabhaṭa. What is it? It is that which was formerly the *Svāyambhuva* [system], whose tradition had become utterly lost; by the grace of Brahmā—or by his own name—because it was now made manifest by Āryabhaṭa, it is called the *Āryabhaṭīya*.
That [teaching] of Svayambhū is eternal at all times.
Having grasped the meaning formulated by Svayambhū, the teachers compose their treatises;
however, because the tradition remains uninterrupted, that meaning is indeed already known.
Otherwise, how could this reasoning regarding supersensuous objects be formulated by mere mortals?
For one who creates a counterfeit or a reflection of this [work], there occurs the destruction of his merit and his life. (50)
[The concluding verse of Someśvara’s commentary:

Now, this well-spoken work, which clarifies the meaning for those of dull intellect and bestows awakening, has been rendered by Someśvara, whose mind is purified by logic, grammar, and other sciences.
This excellent and concise commentary has been composed by extracting the very essence of that exposition on the sūtras spoken by Ācārya Āryabhaṭa which was produced by Bhāskara.
Thus ends the commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya composed by Someśvara.
[The concluding verse of Bhāskara’s commentary: Those which establish objects beyond the reach of the senses...
These are the aphorisms uttered by Āryabhaṭa;
it is impossible even to state a hundredth part of their meaning, so how could anyone like me explain them in their entirety?
Thus ends the Golapāda in the Āryabhaṭatantrabhāṣya, the work of Bhāskara.
